The search for velocity-coherent sources in the 21-cm hydrogen line is crucial for understanding high-mass star-forming regions and their impact on the surrounding gas. Our study is the second in a series aimed at identifying such sources using the FAST telescope. We observed 115 regions associated with massive star-forming areas, but only one velocity-coherent source was detected. The source we found is associated with the region W51-Modulus A and is characterized by two components with narrow line widths. Our findings are consistent with the presence of compact radio jets or a jet-powered outflow. Although we did not find any new velocity-coherent sources, our work contributes to a comprehensive catalog of massive star-forming regions and aids in understanding the evolution of high-mass star-forming areas.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results in various areas, such as Krieger embeddings, survivor sets, Hausdorff dimensions, bifurcation sets, and badly approximable numbers. We show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations possess unique properties, specifically that they are winning in Schmidt games and have the countable intersection property.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics phenomena. Utilizing approximately 7,421 +/- 105 signal events from predominantly CP-odd final states (J/\psi pi+ pi-), which were isolated in 1/fb of pp collision data gathered at a 7 TeV centre-of-mass energy by the LHCb detector, researchers performed a time-dependent analysis on the subsequent decay of the Bs state. As a result, phi_s was estimated to be -0.019 +/- 0.173 +/- 0.004 radians, in alignment with the Standard Model predictions. Furthermore, this measurement was used to calculate delta_C, an estimate of the CKM angle gamma, yielding a value of -0.030 +/- 0.173 +/- 0.004 radians, with the second value representing the uncertainty of the phi_s measurement.

It is evident that deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant features from a given dataset, but they may not necessarily excel in adapting these features to datasets with different underlying characteristics. In this study, we propose a novel method that involves identifying and eliminating redundant features across various datasets. Specifically, we utilize kernel maximum mean discrepancy tests not only to assess intra-dataset feature coherence but also to evaluate inter-dataset feature consistency. By addressing the resulting challenging optimization problems via an iterative reconfiguration approach, our method enables near exact computation of the optimal solution, resulting in improved feature extraction and domain adaptation performance as demonstrated by our empirical results on a simulated and actual data sets.

We establish a phase transition framework for studying arcs and 2-distant arcs in finite fields of two dimensions. Specifically, we define an arc as a set of points $(\mathbb{F}_q^2, +, \cdot)$ where no three points lie on a line, and a set of points as 2-distant if the distance between any two points is at least two. Our main result delimits the feasible values of size $N(Q)$ for $q$-distant arcs in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$, where $N(Q)$ represents the number of points in the arc, as $q$ tends towards infinity.

A traditional method in number theory, known as the inclusion and exclusion formula, is often utilized to derive a formula for counting the number of equilateral triangles in a regular triangular grid, known as the triangular numbers. By applying the inclusion and exclusion formula, we find that the sum of the triangular numbers, calculated as the nth triangular number, T(n), equals n(2n^2 + n)/6. This formula can be verified through two distinct proofs, one involving an induction approach and another relying on a determinant evaluation. Although these methods are considered significant in mathematical reasoning, their relative complexity makes them less than ideally suited for younger or novice mathematicians, particularly those in the lower divisions of an elementary school. Therefore, this paper aims to introduce a novel and straightforward method for deriving the formula for the sum of the triangular numbers, based on a simple and well-known identity in the world of combinatorics, known as the product rule. By applying this rule, we find that the sum of the triangular numbers, calculated as the nth triangular number, T(n), equals (3^n + (-3)^n)/6. This method is considered to be more accessible and suitable for a group of novice mathematicians, particularly in the lower divisions of an elementary school.

Graph Neural Networks have excelling capabilities in handling graph-structured data but fall short in providing understandable explanations for their predictions. The prevailing explanation methods primarily apply feature importance to explain model decisions but, due to inheriting issues from their underlying models, fail to effectively cover graph-based data. In order to address this, we developed XGraph, an innovative method for generating transparent explanations that utilizes an independent explanation model, separate from the primary GNN model, trained to accurately replicate the classification results of GNNs while generating more reliable explanations. The approach employs a combination of global and local features, scored through attention-based mechanisms, to provide clear and understandable explanations for predictions made by GNNs on graph-structured data.

The galaxy cluster, RXCJ0232.2-4420, holds a unique position as it has one of the smallest known cool core proportions among low-redshift HSC clusters, yet its subcluster, located at a redshift of 0.28, possesses one of the largest proportions of cool core systems among similar redshift range objects. We conducted a detailed study using the Chandra telescope to observe the two component systems within RXCJ0232.2-4420 and obtained spatially resolved data on the gas temperature, gas mass, and X-ray luminosity for each. We discovered that the larger system has a temperature range between 3.46 and 4.29 keV, an X-ray luminosity of 4.69 x 10^44 ergs per second, and a gas mass of 2.23 x 10^13 solar masses. We further determined that the two systems merged around 1.35 billion years ago, according to our timing estimates based on X-ray luminosity data and similar to what was previously established using optical data. We found the smaller system has a temperature range between 3.29 and 3.93 keV, an X-ray luminosity of 2.04 x 10^44 ergs per second, and a gas mass of 7.44 x 10^12 solar masses. We calculated a global mass of 2.04 x 10^14 solar masses for the merged cluster

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, was developed and has demonstrated superior performance on various benchmark datasets. In this work, the linear component of the LMU is replaced with a more efficient fractional formula, and the unit is adapted for use in handling time series classification tasks. Our research indicates that the fractional LMU achieves performance comparable to the real-time LMO, while operating at significantly reduced computational and memory costs. Furthermore, the results show that the fractional LMU achieves classification accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art models, including the LSTM and Transformer, on several benchmark datasets, while operating at a computationally efficient rate $\mathcal{O}(N\log N)$.

The search for feebly interacting particles is a crucial area of study in searching for dark matter as well as understanding the fundamental physics of neutrinos and Higgs bosons. The ALPS project is working on a next-generation collider-based experiment to detect particles that interact with matter very weakly. This research proposes a new, highly efficient way to detect such particles using a novel approach at a high-energy physics collider. By analyzing data from the LHCb's electron-positron collider, researchers found minimal limitations on the possible creation of long-lived particles, even with masses above 90 GeV. This research sets new standards for how to design experiments searching for such particles in existing data from electron-positron colliders.

Language plays a vital role in a culture's fabric, deeply intertwined with human migration patterns. Investigating the migration dynamics through the naming game with migrating entities reveals how migration affects language development. (i) In scenarios where all agents are mobile, a collective phenomenon emerges that promotes language homogenization. This effect is analogous to the Langton's ant-driven emergence of order from chaos. (ii) When only multilingual individuals move, monolingual groups or "islands" form. Unmigrated speakers within these isolated groups tend to learn the surrounding language, ensuring linguistic continuity within each group. (iii) When monolingual "islands" encounter each other, language divergence occurs, given enough time, leading to the presence of multiple languages within the system. Our research provides a new explanation for the spontaneous creation of multiple languages by exploiting the interplay between migration and language evolution.

PINN algorithms have made significant breakthroughs in solving various complex PDE-based problems. Despite their success, they lack a solid theoretical foundation, particularly regarding convergence rates and sensitivity to data. This research bridges this gap by deriving a theoretical framework for PINNs that establishes a direct link between training losses, function approximations, and radial basis function kernels. The resulting convergence rates prove to be dependent on network width, condition number, and the frequency of given data points. Through various numerical experiments, we validate the theoretical findings and uncover unique characteristics of PINNs when dealing with distinct types of features within partial differential equations. As a result, we are able to explain previously observed paradoxes and reveal new surprises. Specifically, we find that PINNs can converge for high-frequency features given sufficient width, but will inevitably face convergence difficulties no matter the width when low-frequency and high-frequency features are combined.

We examine a two-wave system in the context of partial Kelvin-Voigt damping. Specifically, we analyze a boundary-coupled system consisting of wave equations in the half-space, one with damping and the other without, coupled at the boundary through a viscoelastic link. Building upon theories of weak solutions for wave equations, we establish a weak solution for this coupled system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that within a certain scope, the solution we derived satisfies the equation and adheres to the boundary conditions we established. Ultimately, we show that the system's energy decays at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{2}{9}}$, and this rate can be optimized.

Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications. However, traditional deep RL methods are hindered by two major limitations: they often struggle with learning from scarce, low-dimensional data and lack robustness against unexpected sensory disruptions. New deep RL algorithms, developed to counter these shortcomings, draw inspiration from biologically-inspired motor control theories. These models incorporate a predictive forward simulation model, typically drawn from optimal motor planning theories, that helps separate task-relevant from task-irrelevant data. By utilizing a forward model to simulate possible outcomes, to generate artificial data and reward signals, these algorithms can effectively leverage higher-dimensional and more noisy artificial tasks to facilitate learning. We introduce novel algorithms grounded in this approach, based on the principles of reach-avoid problems and optimal planning in the realm of safety, and demonstrate their efficacy in comparison to state-of-the-art methods on multiple challenging benchmark tasks, specifically balancing a pole on a cart and navigating an uncertain robotic arm to a target.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip. Our method relies on a specific combination of quantum squeezing and normal-order interactions between photons within multiple resonator modes. When an applied pump exceeds a certain threshold, we observe significant unidirectional signal transmission between modes. Notably, the efficacy of this nonreciprocity can be maximized, achieving near-total transmission with minimal loss, and can be enhanced by incorporating nonresonant cavities. Additionally, we demonstrate that this nonreciprocity can be optimized for both small and large input powers. We further propose a design based on a combination of nanobeams, Bragg mirrors, and dielectric materials that can implement this unidirectional light transmission with high transmission efficiency.

We focus on a type of function, known as concave kernel functions, defined as $f(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1:k}$${\alpha}_i(\mathbf{x})\phi_i(\mathbf{x})$, where the settings of $k$, $\alpha_i$, and $\phi_i$ are variable but the functions are restricted to a specific group $\mathbb R^n \rightarrow \mathbb R$. Under certain conditions, it can be proven that the functions have isolated local maxima. A method to verify these conditions is provided and, as a result, we can determine the set of all concave kernel functions with isolated local maxima. Furthermore, we can use this information to establish the set of all concave kernel functions with isolated local minima.

The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects for directly detecting dark matter particles weighing less than GeV/c$^2$. Its ability to analyze numerous isotopes within its target material is a distinctive advantage, allowing for the optimal identification of dark matter interactions through the use of multiple measurement methods. This research focuses on demonstrating the experiment's potential to effectively identify the $^{117}$Ce isotope using Ammonium Ceric Nitrate and explores the prospects of using this isotope in CRESST experiments.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, an ill-posed problem, resolved by imposing a Gaussian Mixture Latent prior. This prior utilizes a kernel mixture structure, utilizing the Expectation-Minimization algorithm, in conjunction with a Closed-form Maximum A Posteriori estimator. The proposed model is capable of adapting to diverse image statistics, effectively handling both regularized and non-regularized deblurring tasks. Furthermore, the model can address multiple blurred images associated with distinct blur kernels, referred to as Overlapping Groups Multiplet deblurring. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated through comparisons with established benchmarks and real-world data in multiple applications such as super-resolution, color image deblurring, demotion of blur in face recognition, and analysis of retinal images with complex statistics.

This paper introduces two crucial concepts, the associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair and the covariant Rota-Baxter pair, which contribute significantly to the solution of the BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation. A new equation, the double curved Rota-Baxter system, is then formulated using these concepts and the BiHom-pre-Lie module structure. The study not only confirms the existence of the solution to the equation but also explores its relation with the BiHom-pre-Lie module, yielding various homogeneous solutions, particularly for the two-step BiHom-pre-Lie module. By establishing a connection between the BiHom-pre-Lie module and the double curved Rota-Baxter system, eight different homogeneous solutions are obtained, with two of these solutions unique. The research also confirms that the solution to the equation is equivalent to a BiHom-pre-Lie module covariant with respect to the BiHom-Yang-Baxter system. A new algebraic structure, the pre-Lie bimodule, is defined and the solution to the equation is found to be a pre-Lie bimodule covariant with respect to the BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair, providing a general method for obtaining solutions to the equation.

Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software
developers. Hoare logic, in particular, facilitates the structured creation
of verified programs by encapsulating algorithmic requirements. Various
admissions criteria determine which programs can be certified by Hoare logic.
The development of Hoare-like logics for unbounded program systems addresses the
initial limitations of classical Hoare logic, enabling the verification of systems
whose transitional dynamics are influenced by past program states. This text focuses
on advanced, space-intensive verification techniques, including the application of
closed and open systems theory to Hoare logic. It surveys key Hoare logic
extensions that guarantee infinite program runnings and examines the
characteristics, advantages, and shortcomings of each. Some of these extensions
allow for the incorporation of program goals and flexible time constraints,
enabling the verification of infinite program cycles. Hoare logic's extended
applications enable the formal validation of long-running software programs,
including those found in process algebra and game theory.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that allows efficient propagation of values among nodes. The valuation of Canopus over existing protocols, such as PBFT, PoWA, and RAFT, in terms of energy usage, network bandwidth, and computational time, was also demonstrated. The evaluation was based on real-world consensus issues and was executed using 100 nodes, with the results indicating that Canopus outperforms PBFT by 60%, PoWA by 91%, and RAFT by 68% in terms of energy usage, network bandwidth, and computational time respectively.

Recent studies using neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, 
which can't distinguish between individual headgroup and tail components of a lipid, 
have found a significant non-lamellar tendency in lipid bilayers when the cholesterol content 
is high and the ether-linked phospholipid concentration is low. However, these earlier methods 
failed to show clear evidence of lamellar phase bending moduli in lipid mixtures, 
which are now known to be an important aspect of membrane function. In this current research, 
we utilize solid-state magic angle spinning 13C NMR, allowing differentiation between 
headgroup and tail components, to analyze a mixture of palmitoyl-2-phosphatidylcholine, 
stearoyl-2-phosphatidylcholine, and cholesterol. Our results indicate that this lipid mixture 
forms a single homogeneous phase with lamellar structure, and we utilize numerical simulations 
to demonstrate that this phase exhibits non-crystalline dynamics similar to biological membranes. 
Notably, our study shows that mixtures of this type exhibit a significant non-crystalline dynamics 
related to cholesterol content, which is in line with earlier research suggesting that this 
dynamic is linked to membrane function. Moreover, our results suggest that specific lipid 
interactions may be necessary to produce this dynamic, which is distinct from pure lipid 
bilayers that exhibit non-crystalline dynamics.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian. It looks at a spatially homogeneous, flat FRW model and finds that its minisuperspace is defined by the Hamiltonian's constraints, which are equivalent to those of the standard LQC model for the matter and gravitational degrees of freedom. By contrasting the two models, the research determines the total particle density at which quantum gravity begins to take effect and finds that critical matter density ratios apply universally across all matter types. Additionally, the research calculates and compares the gravitational and matter supermomenta, which provides insight into the order of quantum gravity effects in relation to the scale factor. Finally, the research investigates the LQC model's dynamics during the universe's inflationary phase and finds that its behavior differs significantly from that of either the classical FRW model or the quantum deformed LQC model.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a specific
energy range from 78 to 166 EeV. This comprehensive dataset is made available 
for close examination, alongside nine events used to establish the energy scale 
for each detected primary particle.

Deep neural networks are increasingly being used in robotics but they often ignore how their output affects the world, making their integration into real-world robots problematic due to safety and efficiency concerns. In particular, robotic algorithms that rely on model predictive control require the evaluation of many possible trajectories during planning, which can be time-consuming when considering the impact of the network's output. One way to speed up this process is to approximate the effects of the network's output using a collection of pre-simulated scenarios, a technique known as trajectory anchoring. This method involves storing a large database of simulated trajectories and updating it whenever the network's parameters change, a task that can be computically intensive. To make this process more efficient, we propose a novel update strategy that involves partitioning the balance tree of the database to pinpoint the trajectories that need to be re-simulated and to determine where new trajectories should be inserted. By using a data structure that allows for the efficient partitioning of a balanced tree and for the insertion and deletion of nodes, we can significantly reduce the computational cost of the updates. This strategy is implemented in the C++ programming language and is evaluated in this paper.

The traffic prediction field faces a significant challenge regarding model robustness, particularly in handling unexpected scenarios. Breaking down test data into smaller overlapping patches can improve model generalization, but the optimal patch size remains unknown. This paper investigates the effects of testing models with varying patch sizes on their performance and robustness. Using real-world traffic data from Chicago and New York, we evaluated how different patch sizes affect traffic prediction accuracy, model complexity, and robustness under unexpected conditions, such as severe weather. Our findings suggest that testing models with overlapping patches of a limited number of cells can effectively assess their capacity to handle unexpected scenarios. This patch-testing approach can facilitate the identification of models with enhanced generalization and robustness, even without requiring additional training.

In recent years, the study of Gray categories has revealed its valuable uses in higher category theory. Constructed from tricategories with 2-equivalences, Gray categories serve as an efficient tool for simplifying more complex higher category structures. This report introduces a new concept, pseudo Gray categories, developed from pseudo monoidal 2-categories, which share similar properties to Gray categories. Further investigation of pseudo Gray categories and their corresponding 2-functors has been conducted, along with a demonstration of their utility in simplifying pseudo monoidal 2-categories. This report also establishes connections between the concepts of pseudo functors and functors with 2-natural transformations, as well as their relationships with monoidal 2-functors and functors with 2-natural transformations.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods have significant errors when dealing with non-standard hippocampus configurations, such as hippocampal sclerosis, causing them to lose precision in the hippocampus region when detecting non-standard cases. In contrast, a deep set-based approach incorporates structural information for HippoSeg, resulting in more precise and versatile segmentation even in complex HippoSeg scenarios. By transforming hippocampus shape sets into point set maps, HippoSeg is capable of accurately segmenting diverse HippoSeg types. In evaluations, HippoSeg showed improved performance compared to other methods, such as Multi-Atlas Based Registration and deep learning-based approaches, for standard HippoSeg types and superior performance on non-standard HippoSeg types when compared to other methods that also utilize structural information for improvement.

We scrutinize a claim that involves a two-path interferometer where three people walk through it simultaneously without any two using the same path at any given time, a phenomenon referred to as the bus experiment. Using a classic mathematical approach, we find that the desired outcome can indeed be achieved by simply having each person cross the path whenever they encounter it. However, we also develop a more in-depth mathematical description, formulated within the framework of a fundamental mathematical structure called a category, and demonstrate that the initial outcome is a consequence of a specific type of mathematical transformation known as a composition that does not adhere to a generally accepted logical consistency known as compositionality. We further argue that the initial conclusion remains valid even when accounting for the systematic distortion caused by individual human steps.

Our research identifies the cosmic ray nucleon collision as the primary mechanism creating the inner proton radiation belt within low Earth orbit (EO). The proton radiation belt's formation can be explained by the equilibrium achieved between proton pho-ton production and proton stripping from the inner belt. A specific examination of the Electron-Beta Spectrometer (EBS) on the APX-10 satellite revealed the presence of high-energy protons with energies exceeding 10 MeV, which radially oscillate around 200 km at 30-minute intervals, corresponding to Earth's orbit. By contrast, less energetic particles at energies below 1 MeV are more evenly distributed around Earth due to their reduced escape velocity. The observed proton radiation belt appears to extend beyond geosynchronous orbit, with a possible upper limit of 36,000 km, and contains particles up to 20 GeV in energy. A theoretical simulation of this phenomenon indicates that protons within this radiation belt experience frequent interactions with the Earth's atmosphere, resulting in approximately 50% escape velocity at 200 km altitude. Consequently, the proton radiation belt is in a state of continuous change, with particles either being added to or lost from the belt, depending on their energy.

A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates directly with the limitations of achievable performance gains. This 
paper proposes a novel three-phase training approach for improving network 
expressivity, comprising pre-training with sample expressivity, followed by 
transfer learning to adapt to target datasets with reduced expressivity 
requirements, and finally fine-tuning to optimize performance on specific 
tasks while ensuring expressivity is within safe limits. Experimentation with 
three datasets demonstrates superior performance by showing that this method 
achieves better generalization and performance outcomes at lower model 
complexity compared to standard neural networks.

To protect user data in low-rank matrix completion tasks, we develop a novel
noise-based method ensuring differential privacy. This method introduces noise
drawn from a specific distribution handling outliers, generated using the
double Huber loss function, and demonstrates differential privacy, along with
guaranteed performance metrics for both noise magnitude and sensitivity.
Specifically, we establish bounds for the relative recovery error and the
rank-sensitivity of the reconstructed matrix, as well as its minimum singular
value. Additionally, we investigate how our mechanism's performance is affected
by parameters like matrix size, precision, and the degree of outliers, and
show its efficiency by comparing it with an alternative method on synthetic and
real-world datasets.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, referred to as 'astrodust', and tiny particles, known as PAHs, come in various distinct forms. The evidence suggests that a uniform grain composition is most consistent with the observed patterns of infrared polarization, and the established ratio between optical and infrared polarization. A detailed analysis reveals that a combination of astrodust and PAHs accurately replicates the properties of galactic extinction and emission from interstellar dust while adhering to existing constraints on dust abundance and infrared spectral characteristics. The associated models have been made publicly accessible and are applicable to a wide range of astronomical objects and settings.

Research into exoplanets has so far concentrated on stars much larger than our own sun, however, planets orbiting these smaller stars have been harder to detect.  The close proximity of these stars to their companion planets means their brightness diminishes rapidly as they approach their companion stars, thus we can expect these smaller stars to occasionally block the light coming from their companion planets as they orbit their parent stars.  By using data from the Kepler space telescope we have discovered several instances of these smaller stars having companion planets whose light is blocked by their parent stars, resulting in decreased brightness, which can be referred to as eclipse-tide variations.  By using these variations we have estimated the mass and orbital distance of these planets.  As a result of our research we have discovered several planets orbiting these smaller stars, which have smaller masses than our own solar system, which have smaller minimum mass estimates of  \s{0.1 M_J} and larger estimates of \s{0.9 M_J}.  From our research we have found that in systems containing a large inner planet, which have smaller mass estimates of \s{0.2 M_J} and larger estimates of \s{0.8 M_J}, which have their orbital distances at least two times greater than their parent stars' radii, which result in decreased brightness, which can be referred to as eclipse-tide variations, which have larger mass estimates of \s{0.9 M_J} and larger orbital distances at

Consider the rules of a popular light-switching game played on a simple graph with vertices of clickable lights. Each click affects the state of the chosen light and its neighboring lights. A sequence of strategic clicks leads to winning, which means turning off all lights in a given configuration. Researchers have developed an analysis of this game played in a grid graph with open boundaries, using an infinite sequence of steps. Analyzing the clicks as operations on words, the researchers found that winning configurations can be described as those made of two types of words through a composition of click operations. This theoretical framework allows the researchers to determine which configurations can be won in a given grid graph of size m by n.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied color schemes. Specifically, this approach extends the influential Swin U-Net model to systematically address common image processing issues before performing segmentation tasks. These image processing challenges, such as noise reduction, deblurring, demosaicing, and color enhancement, are treated as preliminary image restoration tasks. The proposed model is highly adaptable, allowing users to easily select the desired image processing method prior to segmentation. Comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the superior performance of the new model in comparison to the current state-of-the-art image segmentation models.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy resulting from approximations. This paper suggests reordering these steps, combining them into a single iterative process where in each iteration more precise insights about the program's behavior are gained and used to improve the accuracy of the analysis. It is demonstrated that by alternating between the same operators in analytical and coanalytical interpretations, the limit of the analysis converging to the exact result can be reached. The study also identifies situations where this iterative approach tends to stagnate, resulting in a less precise approximation compared to a more thorough iteration-based calculation.

A new classification of topological phonons has been proposed in recent years and several materials exhibit topological phonons in their structures. Clusters of topological phonons can form and influence each other's topological characteristics. An atomic framework is used in this work to define topological phonons, where each atom's localized eigenstates are utilized. The study introduces a method for determining clusters of topological phonons within a given atomic framework and applies it to snowflake crystal structures under stress. The results show that clusters of topological phonons exist in non-trivial phonon spectra of stressed snowflake crystal structures and dictate the phonon topological characteristics. An analysis reveals that snowflake crystal structures under certain levels of stress host unique clusters of topological phonons.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods due to their adaptability in generic metric spaces. Among these methods, the k-nearest neighbors approach is particularly popular and versatile, which we further extend in this paper by introducing novel outlier detection techniques based on the emerging paradigm of doubly robust learning in machine learning. Our new methods can be viewed as an improvement on existing k-nearest neighbors techniques by incorporating density estimation more efficiently, utilizing machine learning models pre-trained on the data. Moreover, we also developed a doubly robust estimator for the optimal number of nearest neighbors. Our experimental findings demonstrate that these techniques outperform traditional methods and even exhibit robustness to model mis-specification.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering the unfair discrimination that individuals may face due to their connections. This shift has prompted researchers to explore fair graph neural networks, incorporating node-level fairness into the model's training. This work assesses and addresses neighborhood fairness within GNNs by defining it as a measure of fairness based on the scores produced by graph neural networks, incorporating the scores of a node's neighboring nodes. This study examines three approaches to incorporating neighborhood fairness into GNNs using in-processing, where fairness is incorporated directly into the model's training, resulting in more generalizable and fair models. These methods involve modifying GNN architecture, selecting sensitive and sensitive node pairs, and optimizing for neighborhood Gini coefficient, fairness constrained optimization, and transfer learning for fair representations. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of in-processing neighborhood fairness in reducing disparities while improving model generalizability, and these approaches can be applied to a wide array of downstream tasks.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The resulting approximations demonstrate a comparable level of accuracy, with SMIM exhibiting a slight advantage within the context of this study.  To further assess the accuracy of these methods, some examples include an analysis of temporal profile differences between approximate analytical solutions and exact numerical simulations, as well as comparison with exact analytical solutions where possible.  Ultimately, this research suggests the SMIM as a preferred choice for obtaining reliable and straightforward analytical insights into the dynamics of reversible enzyme reactions.

Squark virtual states in gluino decays could potentially be the primary contribution to hadronic output signals in searches for supersymmetry, especially at the LHC. We're focusing on gluino pair production paired with a jet, studying how to identify this process despite background challenges using advanced analysis methods. By incorporating novel observables and machine learning tools, our research shows that hadronic output signals can be effectively extracted from data. Furthermore, our findings suggest that hadronic gluino decays can probe gluino masses up to 3.5 TeV or squark masses up to 3.8 TeV, even with virtual squark masses near their mass counterparts. We also demonstrate the capability to identify the type of squark mass virtuality through its distinct impact on hadronic output signals.

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences, show that bubble collapse can be hindered by more optimistic forecasters. Nevertheless, our analysis reveals a critical flaw in these theories as they fail to account for the interplay between the remaining optimistic forecasters and the growing disparity in their estimates. In an effort to rectify this shortcoming, we develop a new class of expectation models accommodating mixed signals. These models, in turn, give rise to a broader class of financial bubbles that can coexist with a market of arbitrageurs. Through a new approach, we investigate the conditions necessary for the emergence and longevity of these bubbles, along with the amount of arbitrage generated. Our findings indicate that bubble formation is more likely when early arbitrageurs exert smaller influence and more heterogeneous arbitrageurs are involved. Additionally, we show that as time progresses, the remaining optimistic forecasters contribute to increased arbitrage quantity, aligning with empirical research findings.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation methods. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to simulate quantum harmonic oscillators based on a many-body wave function formulation, where the wave function was initially normalized to exactness, allowing for reliable simulations of quantum dynamics.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however current methods often rely on complex review processing techniques which can be difficult to replicate reliably. This paper presents a novel approach to review-based rating prediction that relies on a sentiment analysis tool called VADER, known for its simplicity and high accuracy. By integrating VADER into a Convolutional Neural Network designed to process reviews directly, we have created a lightweight and efficient model that achieves better results on the TripAdvisor hotel dataset compared to existing methods.

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity and uneven distribution of CS data. Cross-domain data sharing presents a non-trivial solution to this issue. This study introduces L2CS, a large, self-supervised, automatically created dataset for CS NLP. L2CS encompasses 2.67 billion sentences in three CS languages (es-ve-EN) and includes six diverse tasks. L2CS demonstrates superior performance when compared to existing CS datasets and state-of-the-art CS models in es-VE and es-ES tasks across all six tasks. Furthermore, it shows that using CS data can enhance English NLP tasks, such as neural machine translation and information access. L2CS data is accessible at https://github.com/c0van/L2CS.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary of a particular open set within a closed surface is not Topologically compact when using the compact uniformity, and we demonstrate that a related subgroup of homeomorphisms of a particular surface is not compact within the strongest topology in which it can be compact.

We're investigating integrable boundary conditions that can be geometrically interpreted as D-branes within specific theoretical models of conformal field theory, involving both classical and quantum aspects. Initially, our analysis focuses on three notable cases: the shahabian boundary, the Triebl-Horowitz boundary, and the DPP boundary, with the aim of establishing precise relationships between Brane and Field Theories for these cases. We also explore whether these interpretations extend to the related Triebl-Horowitz and DPP Brane Geometries.

As tasks increasingly rely on computer execution, the demand for reliable solutions is rising across various domains, including engineering and computer graphics. A fundamental component of addressing these challenges is the mesh, a geometric framework consisting of basic elements that facilitates problem-solving through numerical computations. With the shift towards real-world applications, mesh meshes have become essential for ensuring the accuracy and precision of simulated results. To meet these needs, researchers are developing new methods for mesh construction, aiming to combine accuracy with simplified analysis and visualization. In this context, the focus is on hexahedral elements, known for their versatility and suitability for a wide range of computations. A new mesh generation technique utilizing hexaheral elements is presented, tailored for computational domains featuring curved boundaries. This approach leverages a flexible hexahedral element construction framework, allowing for smooth domain representation and high numerical efficiency. To address the inherent flexibility of the elements, the method incorporates a stiffening mechanism, minimizing the effects of numerical errors and resulting in accurate simulations and fast convergence rates. A primary objective of the research is to provide a versatile and efficient mesh construction approach, adaptable to a broad class of computational problems. This aim necessitates a flexible hexahedral mesh, accommodating both flat and curved domain boundaries, with minimal and uniform error distribution. To achieve this, the method combines element bending, similar to minimal surface algorithms, with a new component, the straight dihedral distance, evaluating and prioritizing element edges along the boundaries. This innovative component, introduced in this study,

The task of relation extraction aims to identify and extract significant connections between entities within a text, which can be crucial in knowledge graph construction and knowledge triplification. This task has seen significant advancements with the introduction of various relation extraction models, especially with the emergence of deep learning techniques. However, the extraction of multiple relations from a single text, also known as multi-relational extraction, has been relatively underrepresented in recent years. This study proposes a novel approach to tackle this challenge by employing a graph convolutional network to analyze the relational patterns within a text, utilizing a distant supervision triad model to define candidate relationships, and leveraging attention mechanisms to differentiate between various relationships in a single text. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, yielding a 6.7% improvement in F1-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art method on the SemEval 2016 task 7 dataset. Additionally, the extracted relationships and relation embeddings are utilized to create a relation knowledge graph, showcasing the potential for triplification based on relation extraction outcomes.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables and load capacitance, the proposed model incorporates parameterized equations derived using Curve Fitting Toolbox in Matlab to accurately capture these dynamics. Distinguishing itself from prior models driven by empirical observations, this analytical approach endeavors to understand the underlying physical intricacies of inverter delay. Consequently, the proposed model offers enhanced accuracy, particularly suitable for modeling the behavior of inverter delay across diverse technological nodes where a thorough SPICE netlist analysis would be excessively laborious.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
using the most up-to-date information about the consequences of your actions.
In a broad array of constantly changing and physically-based environments, the
utility of future actions depends on past actions and current circumstances.
We've discovered that finding a reliable, up-to-date policy for these types of
environments is an unchanging problem: any effective policy derived from recent
data will be identical to one that uses the most current information.
To address this challenge, we've created an algorithm that approximates a reliable,
up-to-date policy by imposing a limit on the variations in utility predictions
following each action, and we've demonstrated its effectiveness in a simulated 3D
navigation environment.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious. A new study employing a parametric mapping approach to compare functional data supports two possible explanations for this organization: a spectrum of animacy to inanimacy and a distinction between living thing and inanimate thing representation. Our results show that a one-dimensional representation of animacy fits the data well, but including an inanimacy extreme improved fit, suggesting that the ventral temporal cortex animacy structure is more complex than previously thought. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the living thing/inanimate thing distinction influences visual processing in a more prominent way than the animacy/inanimacy distinction, measured by differences in voxel count and representational similarity analysis. However, whole-region analysis revealed similar precision for both distinctions. Moreover, whole-region analysis failed to support the living thing/inanimate thing distinction, but the results for the animacy/inanimimey distinction hold even after controlling for visual features. The study's results offer insights into how the ventral temporal cortex represents visual information with varying levels of animacy.

In various scientific simulations, approximating key characteristics of problems is crucial, such as concentration profiles, temperature distributions, and pressure patterns. To achieve accurate descriptions, researchers often apply high-order numerical methods, which involve solving transport equations for scalar fields. This paper introduces an innovative approach based on convex optimization for obtaining approximate solutions up to a specified numerical error threshold. This method can be adapted to multiple optimization problems, allowing for the incorporation of additional factors like spatial data constraints, the influence of noise, and differing levels of error tolerance. Convex optimization's robust mathematical properties enable efficient and effective solutions, while also providing rigorous guarantees for the accuracy of approximations and efficient handling of large datasets.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV in different observed states. Observations also suggest that the source exhibits a time evolution of parameter values over several days. Furthermore, research has shown that the hardness-intensity diagram can be explained by changes in the inner disk boundary radius and the electron temperature in the corona, while the flux-dependent photoionization model of the iron line explains the time-dependent properties of the iron line. Additionally, research has identified quasi-periodic oscillations in the hard X-ray band, typically occurring at frequencies between 2-4 Hz, which are associated with the transfer of matter between the inner disk and the corona.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to being brittle due to their potential for overfitting on the policies of their training partners. As a result, they may adapt strategies centered on preconceived expectations of other agents' actions rather than truly reacting to their behaviors. To address this issue, we developed transfer-friendly single-agent models that can effectively learn from each other through multi-agent interactions, without the need for modifications in the agent architecture or training environment. By leveraging these models, we achieved significant transfer success in a communication-based cooperative setting, surpassing existing approaches and demonstrating the value of being transferable within the framework of multi-agent reinforcement learning.

We introduce MatRec, a pioneering approach for large-scale visual material 
identification, capable of handling diverse everyday materials across a range of 
technologies, from seamless smartphone scanning to massive industrial sorting. 
To our knowledge, MatRec stands alone as the first to successfully recognize 
materials beyond the usual 'wood','metal','glass' categories, with results 
including: by accuracy, MatRec surpasses existing solutions on four prominent 
databases and outperforms pre-trained models on two others; by efficiency, 
MatRec achieves up to a 10-fold increase in frames processed per second; and by 
coverage, MatRec expands material recognition capabilities into unseen domains. 
MatRec's unique success stems from a carefully curated dataset with 2000+ classes 
across 20 material categories, accompanied by a novel network architecture tailored 
for visual material correlation. MatRec's source code will be openly shared on 
https://github.com/asharakeh/MatRec.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. Furthermore, we examine the correspondence between categorified representations and 2-term representations of Lie 2-algebras. We then discuss the cohomology theory developed by Luecking and the Maskin-Wolf framework for 2-term representations. Our discussion ultimately focuses on the categorification of the 2-term cohomology algebra and its implications for Lie 2-algebras.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise matches between images and then group them into sets of features. This approach is inspired by the self- and cross-attention mechanisms in the Transformer model. It offers several advantages, primarily due to the ability to consider all image pixels equally, without bias towards areas with higher texture. Additionally, we can accurately determine the scale of matching features, without relying on costly iterative methods. Our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in image geometric matching, particularly in situations with low-texture backgrounds. Experimental results demonstrate that it requires significantly fewer computation steps, yet achieves higher accuracy on non-maximum suppression and object detection, while also enabling the existing pipeline to run end-to-end without the need for external loops.

The ratio of polarized intensity at Faraday rotation angles is a valuable tool for eliminating biases associated with unresolved magnetic fields, particularly in evaluating the line-of-sight magnetic field component. Although this ratio is not influenced by Faraday harmonic structure or the faraday rotation angle, it remains susceptible to noise and systematic errors originating from the initial polarization position angle measurements. We assess various methods to correct the line-of-sight magnetic field bias caused by inaccurate polarization position angle measurements, taking into account the polarized intensity ratio's applications in analyzing the magnetic fields of BL Lac objects, radio galaxies, and quasars.

To mitigate the strain of peak energy demand on power suppliers, promoting a pricing strategy that incentivizes consumers to shift their high-energy usage during off-peak hours is essential. Real-time energy pricing has been shown to be effective in achieving load shifting, but its adoption has been limited due to concerns about over-sharing peak energy demand data. Non-recursive Bayesian independent component analysis is a suitable method for promoting load shifting by accurately reconstructing and predicting a power supplier's peak demand without relying on detailed load data. By applying non-recursive Bayesian ICA to a two-profiler scenario, load shifting can be efficiently achieved without compromising consumers' privacy, as demonstrated in our accompanying video.

We examine the thermodynamic characteristics of the Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet gravity coupled to a scalar field, focusing on a black string solution obtained through a Liouville-type transformation. By employing a suitable transformation, we derive an exact string black hole solution generalizing the previous findings. Our analysis yields analytical expressions for various thermodynamic parameters, allowing us to investigate the impacts of the Gauss-Bonnet parameter and coupling on the thermodynamic properties. Additionally, we provide evidence for a phase transition and examine the behavior of the entropy density with respect to these parameters.

The results demonstrate that the power-law decay rates found in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem for discrete systems directly correspond to pointwise scaling rates of a spectral measure with a spectral value of one. Moreover, assuming weak convergence, when no spectral gap is present, the convergence rates of the time-average in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem rely on sequences of infinite time as they tend to infinity.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is crucial for understanding its chemical evolution and the origin of star formation. Through the use of data from the LAMOST-ELSA project, we have selected 77 metal-poor stars with a surface temperature between 4600 and 5100 K and an absolute visual magnitude between -1 and +3. By combining the LAMOST data on line strength with the latest versions of the MIST and BaSTI models, we have calculated the masses, ages, and initial mass fractions of these stars based on two different metallicity scenarios. Our results show that 33 of these stars have a mass between 0.9 and 1.8 times the mass of our Sun. When our calculations are compared to the predictions of the MIST model, we have found that the mass functions of our stars overlap partially with the population II and population III distributions. However, our data do not match the predictions of the BaSTI model due to differences in metal abundance. Our findings also indicate that the mass loss due to stellar winds has a significant impact on the initial mass fractions of our stars. When our calculations are compared to the predictions of the MIST model, we have found that the mass fractions of our stars in the high metallicity scenario are generally lower than in the low metallicity scenario.

The length of global fire seasons has been studied by analyzing monthly burnable fuel maps and climate data. These maps are created by combining 500-meter satellite observations of global vegetation and fuel moisture conditions. They calculate the monthly fuel moisture content and the Burnable Fuel Moisture Index (BMMI) which indicates the burnability of fuels. The BMMI is used to identify regions where fuels become burnable due to drought or low rainfall. The Burnable Fuel Moisture (BFM) dataset is then calculated by subtracting normal precipitation from the BMM dataset in areas where normal precipitation is expected. This dataset shows that in most regions, fuels do not become burnable. However, in a few regions, fuels have become burnable over the past 20-30 years. The study found that approximately 60% of global regions have fire seasons that last no more than 2 months while 12% of regions have fire seasons that last 5 or 6 months. The study found that the Burnable Fuel Moisture (BFM) is the best predictor of actual fires. The relationship between BFM and actual fires is positive. The study found that the BFM is highest in regions with semi-arid savannas and woodlands. The BMR approach can be used to estimate the length of a fire season by identifying the BMR that best explains the frequency of fires. We've conducted a comprehensive examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures were applied to 85 languages, standardizing the data, and then we analyzed the methodologies without any preconceived ideas. The investigation involved 85 languages, spanning 24 families, with the data treated as independent replicates. The methods used to estimate morphological complexity were all previous participants in the WMTL challenge except for two innovative proposals. The principal component analysis revealed that one of the methods was heavily correlated with the others, indicating a common underlying aspect. When we applied the first principal component to the challenge, the results showed that four of the methods would have ranked the languages identically. The proposed statistical methods were tested against data outside of this study and showed positive outcomes, suggesting their effectiveness. Interestingly, some established methods were found to be ineffective. The analysis of the WMTL challenge results showed that two new methods would have allowed for a greater number of languages to achieve perfection, as well as improving the overall performance.

Researchers have proposed self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) as a possible model for addressing galactic core density issues in cold dark matter (CDM) models. Substructure density profiles in SIDM models, however, indicate over-densification relative to standard CDAM models. We examine the impact of sidm parameters on substructure formation and investigate the effects of interactions on tidal stripping during satellite galaxy absorption into primary host galaxies. Preliminary findings suggest tidal stripping is reduced in SIDM models, yet satellite density profiles show over-densification relative to standard CDAM models, potentially resolving galactic core density issues without requiring increased HOF masses.

This paper focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solutions of the equations. Given incomplete information, we use two primary sources: initial assumptions about the solutions and partial measurements from the equations. Based on these sources, we have developed methods to generate effective approximation subspaces and analyzed their performance. By identifying the optimal performance limit and providing simplified methods to achieve it, we have made strides in addressing the challenges associated with reducing the dimensionality of PPDE solutions while accounting for incomplete information about the equations and their solutions.

This research introduces the m-ar-K-FastICA method for feature extraction when data is missing or randomly selected, building upon the Kelly's fastica algorithm. The system dynamically adjusts to accommodate varying numbers of data samples or redundant features, categorizing data into distinct classes based on its characteristics. The proposed approach identifies key features from data through a statistical analysis and uses these to identify distinct sub-sets, represented as ellipsoids, in the data set. The features are then selected and ranked based on their ability to distinguish between classes, with the top features used for classification purposes. When applied to various data sets, the system consistently outperformed traditional feature extraction methods, with improved accuracy, simplicity and reliability. Specifically, the system outperformed fastica by 12% for snp, 8% for dueke, 23% for wine, 32% for breast, 5% for colon, 9% for leukemia, 3% for cmc, 21% for diabetes, 18% for dermatology, 6% for iris, 21% for letter and 8% for tu-dibvs in terms of classification accuracy.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographic locations is crucial, particularly during emergency situations or sudden events. It encompasses detecting occurrences like natural disasters, riots, and high-profile sports events. Social media analysis has emerged as an effective approach for monitoring these events. Our proposed system leverages real-time social media data from multiple sources, employing clustering and event detection techniques informed by data distribution patterns. This innovative mechanism allows event data to be divided and processed across distributed servers, enhancing system scalability. Our event detection framework incorporates an advanced algorithm, which we have experimentally validated using Twitter data representing diverse events and demographics. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in accurately identifying trending events, minimizing false positives, and demonstrating robustness across different event types and user demographics.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions for the measure-valued elliptic PDE $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \; \mathcal{L}^N.$ Given certain moderate growth conditions on the matrix function $A(x)$ and the measure $Q$, our very weak solution $u$ satisfies $\mathrm{W}^{1,p}$-Soboleity regularity with an optimal value of $p > 1$. This result addresses an unresolved question in the field, initially investigated by M. Willem in a 1984 paper, and later by several other authors including J. M. Ball and R. V. Kohn, P. Le Bisconte and M. A. Aleman, and M. A. Aman and J. M. Do Nascimento. Our proof builds upon their work, specifically leveraging the ideas presented in R. V. Kohn and L. Wang's 1999 paper and later in M. A. Aman and J. M. Do Nascimento's 2013 paper. Our findings also encompass a specific instance of the PDE that has been studied by J. I. Dunning-Dunham, M. B. Glaser, and M. A. Aman and J. M. Do Nascimento among others.

By employing the evolutionary method, our research has involved an extensive examination of the phase diagram of binary Ni-Co systems and identified numerous equilibria and transition temperatures among Ni$_3$Co$_{12}$ and Ni$_2$Co$_3$. Our findings reveal that compounds rich in cobalt exhibit higher stability at elevated temperatures due to increased electronic entropy. Based on the calculated thermodynamic properties on the pF2 energy scale, our results suggest that $\beta$-Ni$_2$Co$_3$ exhibits a transition from hexagonal to orthorhombic structures at high pressures, whereas $\gamma$-Ni$_2$Co$_3$ remains stable in an orthorhombic structure across the entire pressure range considered in this study.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. Each ad impression resulting from user interaction is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids typically based on the value of the ad impression and estimated winning price. However, existing bidding strategies often overlook the uncertainty in winning an auction, in which a low win rate may result in a substantial cost per win. In this paper, a novel bidding algorithm, referred to as MCB, is introduced to address this issue. MCB involves simultaneously considering the value of an ad impression and the cost of winning an auction, achieving a balance between revenue and cost to provide a more comprehensive bid valuation. MCB can be applied to a broad range of distributions and is demonstrated to be efficient in both processing speed and accuracy, using a live campaign as an empirical validation and comparing it against current industry standards.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of remotely generating Wigner negativity in one subsystem given another's specific measurement outcome. Research has demonstrated the utility of quantum steering in enabling controlled Wigner negativity in one system based on another's state. Yet, the relationship between quantum correlations and Wigner negativity remains unclear, particularly in the case where one system's Wigner function exhibits conditional negativity.

We have developed a resource theory framework for studying nonclassical properties in quantum states. This theoretical framework enables the derivation of two key inequalities: one that sets a lower limit on conditional entropy and another that sets a lower limit on logarithmic negativity. Our findings show that when quantum correlations are insufficient to meet the conditional entropy inequality, they are sufficient to meet the conditional negativity inequality. Notably, the relationship between quantum correlations and Wigner negativity becomes apparent when the latter's sufficiency is met - it results in the conditional generation of Wigner negativity. Our research also demonstrates that when conditional entropy is insufficient to meet the requirements of the inequalities, the relationship between quantum correlations and Wigner negativity becomes apparent under specific circumstances - namely when specific bounds on logarithmic entanglement are insufficient and when certain properties of a Gaussian state are exhibited.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, leveraging min-entropy, and extend it to the context of quantum key distribution. Utilizing the proposed lemma, we establish a secure boundary for a dual-threshold QKD system incorporating random non-uniform seeds. Interestingly, our analysis reveals that the unpredictability of the non-uniform seeds' distribution may compromise the system's security, even with the pre-existing threshold. Moreover, our analysis shows that the width of the secure window is inversely related to the magnitude of non-uniformity. These findings underscore the necessity of seeds generated from randomness extractors to ensure the secure operation of QKD systems.

We examine the diffusion equation for population growth proposed by Feller in 1951, which describes a population's velocity as being proportional to the population size and also diminishes with increasing velocity. This model can be seen as a special instance of the generalized logistic equation, which has been studied by Armitage and have found that it exhibits oscillatory behavior when the population grows rapidly enough. We now provide a direct proof of this phenomenon by relating Feller's model to a particle system where larger particles move more quickly, thus allowing us to infer the diffusion equation from this particle system. We also discuss how this model might be applied to real-world scenarios.

In this work, we introduce a new method to study multi-phonic interactions in waveguide QED systems by employing effective vertex functions. By deriving these functions from exact Green's functions, the waveguide QED environment is simplified into an equivalent quantum Rabi model, where the action of photons on coupled resonators can be described through a set of equations based on the vertex functions and coupling coefficients. The introduced approach allows for a unified treatment of non-trivial photon scattering problems by adjusting a limited set of parameters. The versatility and efficiency of this method will be demonstrated by comparing it with other existing methods in treating non-trivial photon scattering problems under different conditions. Furthermore, we will showcase how to use this method to build a master equation for the long-time dynamics of the system, and we will also explore how to improve the approximation by including a wider range of transverse fields in the corresponding Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian.

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter is by utilizing boosted dark matter interactions. The framework for light dark matter interactions involving no spin is well established, but a comprehensive framework has been lacking for including spin in light dark matter interactions. Our research develops a novel approximation to describe boosted dark-matrix element calculations accurately, which results in significant changes to the proton structure factor in comparison to scenarios without spin. Interestingly, our approximation reveals that the proton structure factor can become time-dependent in certain situations, but remains independent of the dark matter velocity when interactions occur via a single resonance or through an effective field theory. Our model also shows that the time-dependent structure factor can potentially violate principles of Lorentz invariance. Furthermore, our research indicates that the cross-section for boosted dark matter interactions may exceed standard models by orders of magnitude, which could make possible detection at facilities such as the DarkSide-20k experiment or future liquid xenon experiments with even lower xenon densities.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances. Yet, it remains largely an open problem to effectively employ these detectors in the presence of significant carrier phase errors. This study proposes an innovative approach to mitigate the adverse impact of carrier phase errors by incorporating additional, tailored terms beyond conventional differential detection. The new method, called enhanced differential detection, involves tracking the receiver's and transmitter's respective carrier phase states, with the latter being readily available in most communication systems. By doing so, the proposed scheme significantly reduces the detrimental influence of carrier phase errors, leading to elevated detection accuracy in diverse channel scenarios and at lower signal-to-noise ratios. Notably, the proposed detection method does not necessitate any additional power allocation or bandwidth, and it remains compatible with established, reliable continuous phase modulation systems. Simulation results validate the efficacy of the proposed detection method, with further research needed to explore its practical implementation in modern communication systems.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create a user interface for human labelers that facilitates the implementation of this framework and allows the representation to be learned effectively. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method achieves equivalent performance with optimal comparative evaluations, thereby enabling the utilization of comparative evaluations on larger-scale datasets. The code and dataset will be publicly accessible.

We discuss nucleon structure functions and their role in understanding the internal composition of nucleons. Recent progress on quasielastic electron-nucleus scattering is reviewed, particularly focusing on calculating inelastic form factors using diverse methods.

In typical topological systems, significant disruptions trigger a phase shift, but we have developed an adjustable version of the Toric code that remains stable under even extreme external influences, characterized by a "critical line" where no phase shift occurs, and exhibits resilience against non-linear distortions. This creates an unusual scenario where a region of weak irregularity within the system's boundaries actually enhances its resistance against more complex disturbances. This phenomenon is facilitated by the interplay of two types of irregularity present in the adjustable Toric code. Our research focuses on the underlying mechanisms and applications of this discovered effect.

We investigate the large $N$ behavior of characteristic polynomials of random Hermitian band matrices with a finite and fixed bandwidth. These matrices evolve from the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble as the matrix size grows, assuming the bandwidth grows more rapidly than the square root of the matrix size. Our research reveals that the limiting distribution of complex eigenvalues is unaffected by the specific distribution of matrix entries, and is equivalent to that of the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble. This result holds under the condition that the variance of the probability distribution is finite. Our findings are verified through numerical simulations.

Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level dialogue text struggle to comprehend dialogue context, particularly in extracting the underlying semantic meaning. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce the use of Abstract Meaning Representation as a means of pre-training dialogue models. AMR, a concept-based representation form, facilitates the understanding of semantic information. By leveraging parallel AMR and dialogue datasets, we pre-train a transformer with both dialogue and concept knowledge. This pre-trained model delivers superior performance in a variety of dialogue tasks, as showcased in the results from the Dialog-State Tracking Challenge. Specifically, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SemEval 2018 dialog datasets, with a notable improvement of over 5%. Moreover, we demonstrate that the pre-trained model generalizes effectively to the Dialog-State Tracking Challenge 7 datasets, with a significant enhancement of more than 3% in the performance.

To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, algorithmic interpretability must be measured.  A wide array of concepts have been proposed to capture how much sense our interpretations of algorithms make.  Unfortunately, the field lacks a unified understanding of what this means, and the terms used have diverse and often ambiguous meanings.  To bring clarity, we introduced a comprehensive framework for evaluating the interpretability of algorithms, one that encompasses multiple perspectives and reflects the inherent complexities of intelligence.  Our framework, encompassing both qualitative and quantitative aspects, is composed of properties that are essential for successful measurements, as well as those that are desirable.  The former properties guarantee that the results of our measurements are reliable, unambiguous, and applicable across a wide range of algorithms, while the desirable properties guarantee that our interpretations accurately reflect the algorithms' underlying logic.  By categorizing and evaluating the different concepts of interpretability, our study reveals that many of them fall short of achieving the desired properties, although some measurements come close.  Furthermore, through the development of a simple example, as well as a more in-depth analysis of the FLCP constraint in neural networks, our study demonstrates the importance of accurately evaluating the properties of our measurements, as well as the need for further research in this field.

Anomaly detection without labeled data is an increasingly significant challenge due to the advantages of unsupervised methods in terms of cost savings and scalability.
