However, unsupervised anomaly detection methods are often plagued by a high false positive rate, limiting their practical applications. In this paper, we introduce a weakly supervised anomaly detection approach that utilizes pre-trained models with minimal human intervention to derive target-specific features. By applying two dimensionality reduction techniques and combining them with a weak supervision signal, we obtain an effective anomaly detection method, which we evaluate on multiple real-world datasets. Our experimental results demonstrate the advantages of our approach over unsupervised anomaly detection and self-supervised learning baselines in terms of the area under the ROC curve and accuracy of the output model.

A common strategy in modelling extreme events involves fixing parameters from smaller data sets and focusing on modelling the variability in those parameters. However, this approach can be problematic as these parameters often vary with magnitude, a trend often overlooked when modelling extremes. An alternative method involves using threshold-invariant extreme value parameters, which simplifies modelling but may result in significant losses if there are changes in the data's threshold. This paper proposes a novel model that takes into account the variability of extreme value parameters, modelling them as being correlated and conditioned on a magnitude-dependent parameter that is estimated concurrently. The reliability of this new approach is demonstrated using real data from rainfall in the Sydney region and bounded-fractional stochastic geometry, before utilizing it to model the maximum daily rainfall in eastern Australia.

This analysis addresses the challenge of optimizing cross-sectional area through a specific point within a geometric form. To generalize this concept, the approach is expanded across multiple dimensions. When focusing on a particular axis in two-dimensional space, the objective is to maximize the cross-sectional area largest as far as possible from the origin. By solving this problem, we discover that the optimal solution involves a set of geometric shapes with rounded corners, known as "super-ellipses." When applying this principle to a three-dimensional context, the objective is to maximize the cross-sectional area perpendicular to a defined axis. In this case, the optimal outcome occurs when the resulting volume is a stack of super-elliptical cross-sections.

There's been a growing trend in the study of commonsense knowledge, but a major issue arises from the fact that there's no standard, widely-accepted dataset to facilitate this research. To address this, we've developed ATOMIC, a large, annotated dataset that covers a wide range of human reasoning at a sentence-level. By utilizing an innovative approach to crowdsourcing, we've compiled a massive 386K graphs with 5.5 million edges, demonstrating the complexity of human reasoning. Our analysis of this data reveals the types of reasoning that humans commonly engage in, and we believe that ATOMIC will play a major role in the future study of this topic.

The publicly accessible Hi-GAL survey website serves as a reference point for researchers exploring the column density and temperature properties of the inner Galactic Plane region based on Herschel satellite data. Specifically, it encompasses the analysis of a 108 square degree area situated between the longitude values of 10 to 60 degrees, using 13-belted wavebands between 8 and 70 micrometers. This website contains data products comprising HiRes spacemode images along with coevalized images of the column density and temperature maps. It also features a detailed data dictionary outlining the data's physical and meta-information. This website serves as the primary hub for research and documentation of the project, while the database archive contains the original Herschchel data, with corresponding access managed through the Herschel Interactive Access portal.

Recent photometric studies of the first population stars in the metal-poor globular clusters Messier 22 and NGC 5286 have revealed a two-pronounced colour gradient structure, visible in plots of (B-V) versus metallicity. By building upon these findings, researchers have made predictions about similar patterns in other clusters, based on early photometric data. Further analysis of newly available data from the South African Large Survey of Space and Time is set to enhance our understanding of the spatial distribution across these clusters, now referred to as 'chromosome maps'. Notably, early photometric studies of red giants in several clusters displayed a correlation between iron content and colour position, with less iron-rich stars appearing bluer than their more iron-rich counterparts. However, more recent Abundance Analysis results have challenged this iron-content colour trend, with the proposed explanations ranging from environmental effects to inherent properties of stellar models. By referring to a comprehensive list of iron abundances in red giant members of NGC 5286, researchers have been able to explain the observed colour-iron relationship through differential radial abundance variations. By extrapolating this explanation to other clusters, this pattern may hold key insights into the dynamic early cluster environments and their internal dynamics.

To facilitate a deeper understanding of one-dimensional physical systems, we consider a simplified single file model. We derive an analytical solution for the complete first exit time statistics of an overdamped single file with absorbing boundary conditions, after which we apply these findings to investigate the speed-accuracy relationship, examining how this property is influenced by the mean squared displacement and the entropic repulsive forces within the system.

Quantum mechanics contradicts the universally assumed relationship in physics, mathematics, and computer science, established by Bayes' rule. This fundamental equation successfully solves many puzzles in physics, mathematics, and computer science, yet it cannot accurately predict the outcomes of quantum mechanics. The failure of Bayes' rule in quantum mechanics leads to quantum confusion. By examining quantum mechanics through the lens of causal inference, this work reveals how quantum mechanics causes this confusion and how it resolves that confusion. The key to this understanding lies in recognizing that quantum mechanics is a causal theory of information. The paper demonstrates how quantum mechanics reconstructs Bayes' rule and other causal inference equations for correlated systems. It also presents the methods and models for quantifying causal relationships in quantum mechanics. This work further explores how these findings apply to quantum computing and machine learning, highlighting potential advances and challenges in these fields.

We analyze the behavior of the equation of state in the presence of a finite number of particles, leveraging the polynomial relationship between the coupling constant and particle number. By integrating the three-loop Bethe-Hahsel equation, we derive the equation of state up to the six-loop order, revealing notable particle number dependence at high degrees of perturbation. Our research employs two methods: the first utilizes the boundary conditions of Feynman diagrams, while the second is grounded in the spectral decomposition of the integro-differential Bh equation. We identify a relationship between the eigenvalues of the kernel and the asymptotic behavior of the equation of state as the particle number approaches infinity or infinity.

Let $F_2$ be the prime field consisting of two elements. The general linear group of rank $s$, denoted as $GL_s$, represents the general linear group of degree $s$ over $F_2$. The Steenrod algebra $A\) can be expressed as $A=\mathscr H_*(F_2)^{*}\otimes \mathbb H_*(F_2)$, where $\mathscr H_*(F_2)$ refers to the associated Hunter-Rickard algebra. The algebraic transfer homomorphism $\tau_{A\to H_s(A),\mathbb H_s(A)}$ has been studied in relation to $A$, where $H_s(A)$ represents the $s$-th homology of $A$. The findings demonstrate that $\tau_{A\to H_s(A),\mathbb H_s(A)}$ maps the Ext-groups from $A$ to $H_s(A)$ in a manner equivalent to the degree-$s$ map on $\mathbb H_s(A)$. The same property is shown for the Emerton-Pickel model $H_s^{\text{EP}}(A)$ of $H_s(A)$. The proof relies on an in-depth analysis of the $\mathscr H_s$-module $\mathbb H_s(A)$, where $\mathscr H_s$ denotes the $s$-th Hunter-Rickard algebra. The study also explores its application

Astronomers observing far ultraviolet wavelengths from Earth's orbit have long been hindered by a key limitation: the absence of reliable spectral calibration features. Our team has developed a new hydrogen absorption cell located at the apex of the Hubble Space Telescope's spectrometer, enabling us to create a reference spectrum. This cell, situated at the telescope's entrance, allows us to accurately quantify hydrogen absorption across the entire far ultraviolet spectrum. Our research marks the first successful observation using this novel cell. On September 14, 2020, the cell was observed during a specific mode of operation, resulting in a wealth of spectral data featuring multiple reference features. These features, arising from the Lyman series of hydrogen absorption, were observed at precisely known wavelengths. By analyzing the signal-to-noise ratios, we found them sufficient for calibrating spectral observations of neon, a common target in astronomical studies. This cell is expected to greatly benefit future observations in the far ultraviolet, particularly neon targets. However, further observations are required to refine the accuracy of spectral calibration based on the cell.

We investigate effective communication among distributed systems and their associated optimal control problems for synchronized variational inequalities. First, by extending a multi-agent system's network architecture, we define the Graph Symmetric Systems (GSSs) and their distributed consensus observer, and subsequently, develop a distributed optimal control strategy for each GSS. It's proven that this distributed control approach can lead to an optimal solution that achieves consensus, and also satisfies the optimal control requirement. We demonstrate that our proposed distributed control strategy is versatile and applicable to widely recognized system models, such as distributed optimal synchronization and the Altman-Shapley value, among others.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. Our paper presents an efficient technique for reducing the computational cost of image search. By maintaining a compact database of image features, we can perform searches an order of magnitude faster than existing methods while ensuring identical results. Our technique achieves this via a lossy compression scheme that preserves image similarity, allowing the same features to be assigned to images that are similar in content. Our experiments demonstrate that the improved algorithm achieves a comparable trade-off between computational cost and distortion in the search algorithm's output. Additionally, we developed an innovative method for subsampling images before feature extraction to further accelerate the search process while minimizing losses in performance. This technique achieves a significant 2-3 fold decrease in computational cost by reducing the image resolution, with little to no effect on the final search results. Our code is publicly available on GitHub under the MM-Search repository.

This study investigates how recent findings on channel capacity can be leveraged for authentication in both reliable and unreliable data transmission scenarios.  Authentication in a fully trustworthy data channel is straightforward, allowing for any desired level of confidence.  However, this is not the case when a third party is present, and and unreliable data channel is being used.  This study shows that if a physically secure data channel meets certain criteria, and a secure authentication mechanism is available, and the data sender and receiver share secret information, then the data can be authenticated, and the risk of a false positive can be made as small as desired.  These results are relevant to any data communication system, and any method for authenticating data can be applied to it.  This study considers multiple data encoding schemes, and it is shown that if a data encoding scheme is capable of transferring data in a fully trustworthy data channel, and the data sender and receiver share secret information, then the data can be authenticated, and the risk of a false positive can be made as small as desired.  This study considers multiple data encoding schemes, and the study findings are relevant to any data encoding scheme, and the data can be authenticated, and the risk of a false positive can be made as small as desired.

Analyzing the movement of particles in a running state under the influence of a force that drives them beyond their damping rate, we discover two phases in their dynamics. Initially following a ballistic path, these particles transition into a random walk phase once the force overcomes their damping, regardless of the duration in the running state. We derive an exact mathematical expression for the probability distribution of their positions, demonstrating Markovian behavior. Using this exact expression, we derive the correlation function of their positions and establish the occurrence of localized, non-Gaussian distributions of positions in the random walk phase. Our findings are confirmed through numerical simulations. Additionally, we compare the accuracy of the Brownian motion approximation and the path-integral quantum tunneling mechanism with respect to the exact solution, showing that the Brownian motion approximation yields a reasonable result only in the long-time limit. Furthermore, we explore the influence of a weak dissipation on the movement of particles and find that it causes a shift in the random walk phase, leading to a Brownian motion-like behavior. Lastly, we examine the influence of a constant force on the quantum Brownian particle under strong dissipation conditions, discovering that the particle never enters the random walk phase and instead follows a Brownian motion-like motion across the entire parameter space.

This paper presents an adaptable, localized predictive technique that builds upon Jord\'a's (2005) model, expanding it to a non-statistical setting through the incorporation of Bayesian Additive Regression Trees. Simulation tests reveal that our novel BART-LP model successfully captures the complexities present in the impact responses of various stimuli. An initial case study indicates that, under specific circumstances, the fiscal stimulus has a more significant effect during economic downturns as opposed to upswings, but this distinction only holds true in the event of contractionary policies. Conversely, the study found that financial disturbances have amplified effects when negative, but this amplification does not occur when financial disturbances are positive.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to photons in the vacuum that emit an energy back to the charge in proportion to n^2, as opposed to the standard n^3 behavior. As a result, the charge experiences a net transfer of energy from these virtual photons to the charge, ultimately leading to an increase in the charge's kinetic energy. We explore an additional aspect, namely, the angular momentum associated with a charge in a periodic potential with a magnetic field, and find that at low energies, the potential effectively eliminates the angular momentum generated by the magnetic field, but at high energy transfer, the potential fails to suppress this angular momentum, and the transfer to the charge becomes unlimited.

The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately categorize entity types using a detailed classification system that goes beyond basic coarse-stub categories. Due to data distribution disparities and imbalances between core and fine-grained types, this task faces significant challenges. In order to address these issues, we treat entity types as points within hyperbolic space where similar categories are grouped closer together, thus improving data distribution balance. To achieve this, we developed HyST, a novel framework that employs a hyperbolic space for entity type modeling. By utilizing a hyperbolic BERT model, we mitigate the effects of data distribution disparities, and further enhance the model with a type-aware rectifier neural network for improved accuracy. Additionally, we developed a type-aware sampling strategy to effectively utilize type-specific information from hard examples. Through experiments conducted on three benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed HyST model significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art FG-NET models by a substantial margin.

This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ special types, specifically within the univalent function class and the $\mathcal{U}$ class defined by the condition $f(0)=0$, $\mathcal{R}(f)$, and $\text{Re}(1+zf(z))<1+|z|$ for all $z$ in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$ of order $\beta \in (0,1/2]$ and with $\text{Re}(\gamma e^{i\theta})>0$. The results are achieved using the $p$-synthetic Hankel operator and its connection to the univalent function class $\mathcal{U}$. The bounds on $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ are expressed in terms of $p$, $\gamma$, $\beta$, and $\theta$. The findings are verified by numerical examples and graphical illustrations. The paper concludes with suggestions for further research on the relationship between the $p$-synthetic Hankel operator and various function classes.

Achieving efficient and sustainable operation in cloud data centers largely relies on load balancing, and virtualization enables this by using a proactive approach to manage it. Research has shown that proactive load balancing reduces migration costs and positively affects the response times of users by less than 1%. In contrast, reactive load balancing at peak load can result in over 50% higher costs and longer response times. Prepartition, an innovative proactive load balancing approach, has been developed to minimize user delays by distributing them across multiple physical machines. The effectiveness of Prepartition is evaluated through comparison with existing load balancing methods, and its relevance is validated through analysis of several real-world data centers.

In modeling systems of rival agents as games, assuming each party makes rational decisions, the likely outcomes can be identified using equilibrium concepts like the Nash equilibrium. In various real-world scenarios, factors like weather, traffic or fiscal policy, beyond the agents' control, can impact game dynamics. Often, the equilibrium observed doesn't align with the actual cost functions of the agents. This research proposes the use of Nash equilibrium averaging operators to address this discrepancy. Although it's established that agents' cost functions gradient ascent methods can converge to equilibria, the convergence of average dynamics has been less clear. We demonstrate that average dynamics converges to the Nash equilibrium under specific, commonly met conditions in games.

This study tackles the issue of assessing causal influences in cases where some variables involved in ensuring causal validity are incompletely known. For these situations, we develop tight limits on the causal influences by solving two intricate optimization problems. The derived limits prove to be sufficient, leading us to introduce an optimization technique, enabling dimensionality reduction that lets users choose between bias minimization and heightened estimation precision. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through controlled experiments.

Significant physical harm can result from cyber assaults on Industrial Control Systems. Although in-person assessments can reveal vulnerable system components, physically inspecting industrial equipment is not always feasible. This paper presents a novel method for automatically detecting and classifying physical process correlations using logged system data. This approach employs an ensemble of deep learning models to identify correlations among industrial equipment, as reflected in the interdependencies between their time-series readings. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this method, which also serves as a basis for developing more sophisticated physical process models through unsupervised learning.

A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via a devised algorithm, which exhibits high efficacy and universality. Although English language summary generation has seen significant advancements, generating summaries in Indian languages faced limitations due to inadequate data and poor performance of English-based models until recently. A newly developed neural summary generation model shows exceptional performance across five low-resource languages - Bengali, Hindi, Marathi, Punjabi, and Tamil. The model incorporates cutting-edge attention and memory enhancement techniques and uses a cutting-edge transfer learning method that fine-tunes the model using data from a neighboring language. The outcome surpasses results achieved by state-of-the-art and contemporary models on these five languages.

We establish the definition and certain attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to examining the properties and structure of such objects. Specifically, we consider the prime and semiprime S-rings of Krull type, as well as the topological characteristics associated with their prime spectrums. We also offer the initial classification of elementary divisor domains of $\sigma$-bezout type.

The long history of triple-line spectroscopy provides valuable evidence for the presence of substellar companions in systems such as HIP 1481 and HIP 88399. By employing this technique, researchers have detected the presence of two candidate companions in these systems. For HIP 1481, the data suggests a candidate companion with a mass between 0.05 \pm 0.01 M_J at a distance of 22.6 \pm 0.8 AU, while for HIP 88399, the candidate has a mass between 0.52 \pm 0.13 M_J at a distance of 43.6 \pm 3.3 AU. Radial velocity variations in these systems appear to be influenced by the movement of the planets around their stars, as well as the potential motion of the detected candidates. However, further confirmation via direct imaging or lucky imaging is required to verify the presence of these candidates as actual substellar objects.

Recently, Variational Autoencoders have emerged as a superior choice for autoencoders, offering superior reconstructive performance and the ability to track down the underlying distribution of a dataset. However, these models are complex and require a significant amount of computational power to train, utilizing the reparameterization trick. Despite the availability of open-source code from the original authors, the lack of detailed guidance on implementing VAEs in the context of multi-modal data makes it challenging for new users to leverage these models effectively. In this tutorial, we provide a step-by-step guide to building a VAE that can handle various types of data, focusing particularly on handwritten digits and images from the CIFAR-10 dataset. Our goal is to equip users with the knowledge and skills to design and implement VAEs on their own.

Smart home technology is gaining momentum, driven by advancements in IoT, AI, and data analytics. To ensure secure data transmission, various security solutions are being implemented. Although some solutions are effective, they often come with a price in terms of computational resources, communication costs, or energy consumption. Utilizing blockchains can mitigate the risks of tamper-proof data transmission, but public blockchains may not be the best fit for home networks. On the other hand, private blockchains offer faster transaction processing, secure data storage, and energy-efficient operations, making them a more suitable option. Given the benefits, we suggest adopting private blockchain technology for smart home applications and explore the potential outcomes in this area.

A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage utilizing deep learning is presented. It was observed that certain deep neural network architectures could be used to solve the quantization problem directly, resulting in significantly reduced memory usage compared to traditional methods from the statistical and machine learning literatures. Furthermore, it was found that this method could adapt to dynamic changes in the input distribution, making it suitable for real-time applications such as wireless communication systems, where the receiver receives continuous data from the transmitter. With this method, the researchers achieved a general error rate of less than 0.2 percent using only 7 bits to represent the likelihood ratios, retained the same error rate as fine quantization but with 16 bits for Gaussian noise, and maintained error performance comparable to 16-bit representation while reducing memory usage to 43 percent for a non-linear complex multipath fading channel under the same observation duration as the 16-bit case.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth and an XP algorithm based on the graph's cluster vertex number. Furthermore, we've established a fixed-parameter theorem stating that if a graph has a certain structure, then determining an upward planar drawing for it can be computationally infeasible.

Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. A major crowd-sourcing issue arises from labeling inconsistencies due to the diverse, multi-faceted nature of images. In this paper, we introduce Co-RRN, an iterative process that leverages self-correction and rectification through a Recurrent Neural Network. We demonstrate its application and effectiveness on resolving the longstanding problem of inductive matting, as well as similar noise-induced anomalies in other image categories. Notably, our approach surpasses the performance of recent learned methods in handling full-color matting scenarios.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables.

A particular matrix known as a covering array has specific characteristics. It is made up of different symbols and certain sub-matrices must include each combination of those symbols a set number of times. The amount of times this combination occurs can vary. If such a matrix exists where every symbol appears a specific number of times in each row, it is classified as a coverable array of a particular number. Researchers have created an 18x18 coverable array with a particular number and a specific pattern, but have failed to do so with smaller numbers. They have created large coverable arrays with many symbols but have not found a pattern that results in the smallest possible number.

This paper examines a unique category of nonlocal games, denoted by $(G,\psi)$, 
where every round's response is an entangled pair from a specific state $\psi$ 
that only appears once across both inputs, resulting in what is known as a maximally
entangled pair. Even with these constraints, it has been proven that nearly all states $\psi$
give rise to extremely challenging games. However, this paper also reveals specific subclasses
of such highly restrictive states $\psi$, as well as an associated nonlocal game, the
harmonic basis game, for which exact solutions are possible. Interestingly, when a player's input
is drawn from a uniform distribution over a finite field, a related quantum circuit problem 
exhibits a unique connection to learning distillable entangled states, aligning with recent findings
in quantum learning theory.

This study examines the reliability of two toolkits, EvoCrash and JCHARMING, which are used to artificially induce faults in software applications. The research employs a combination of two fault injection frameworks, EvoCrash and JCHARMING, and Crash Explorer to introduce faults and measure the impact on app crash rates. The analysis is based on 41 apps, comprising 1,562 crash-worthy methods, and 1,532,000 fault injections. The results indicate that EvoCrash and JCHARMING reproduced 94% of the crashes seen in JCHARMING, but only 52% were replicated with EvoCrash alone. The research highlights inconsistencies in EvoCrash and JCHARMING crash reproductions, suggesting that the cause might be related to how the faults are introduced. The study recommends future research to investigate the factors contributing to the discrepancies in crash reproductions.

To study magnetic field effects on charge order in underdoped La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ persisting below $T_i$, where $T_i$ rises with magnetic field, we utilize terahertz spectroscopy and detect evidence of phase separation within charge density waves at low temperatures through this magnetic field phenomenon. As the magnetic field increases, our findings show that the lattice structure of vortices transitions from a square to a triangular arrangement, ultimately transforming the lattice structure at high fields. We observe square to triangular modulation wave length transitions influenced by magnetic fields, where this transition occurs more strongly in the $x=0.16$ compound and at higher magnetic fields for $x=0.12$. These results are verified through polarization-dependent spectroscopy, where this transition more strongly affects the dimerized CuO$_2$ plane at low temperatures for $x=0.16$ and at higher magnetic fields for $x=0.12$.

Photons are valuable tools used to explore the intense medium produced in high-energy heavy-ion collisions. The thermal sphericity and medium's impact on the initial conditions affect the angular distribution of these photons. While a viscous correction primarily alters the magnitude of flow patterns in the final state, it only slightly changes the overall shape of thermal photons' anisotropic flow. We've analyzed the impact of the initial state on these photons by applying both a thermal profile and a modified version of the initial conditions, as described by the Trento model, to calculate their response to viscosity. We've compared these results with the corresponding effects on charged hadrons, finding that viscous corrections significantly alter thermal photons but have a minor impact on hadrons' anisotropic flow.

Our study centers on investigating the regular magnetic order (RMO) for specific spin models with a global spin rotation symmetry. By leveraging the tree decomposition method, we developed an algorithm to evaluate the free energy of these models under the Bethe approximation. This allowed us to analyze various simple examples and derive analytical results, which were then validated through numerical calculations. Furthermore, we extended the applicability of this algorithm to more complex models with a global spin rotation symmetry, such as those with arbitrary exchange strengths between nearest neighbors and those with no connections. This led us to discover the existence of distinct magnetization plateaus in spin models, both with and without any long-range interactions, where the magnetization remains constant despite varying the applied magnetic field.

Large data-driven companies have considered online controlled experiments (A/B Testing) a gold standard for several decades. Many companies use a standard framework that measures "average treatment effect" (ATE), but there's a significant challenge to increase the ATE detection power while maintaining a low type II error rate as proposed by Thompson (2019). To address this, we propose a new framework called "Rapid Detection of Large Effects" (RDLE) that allows for the rapid detection of large treatment effects in controlled experiments. By leveraging the principles of multiple testing and minimizing the overall expected loss, our method yields a score that determines when to stop the experiment. We provide theoretical and practical evidence to support our proposed score, and through simulations and a real-world case study, we demonstrate its effectiveness.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description of how inflationary perturbations correspond to cosmic microwave background temperature fluctuations are presented.

Recent updates from the CDF II experiment at Fermilab's Tevatron have revealed a slight discrepancy in the measurement of the W boson mass, which deviates from the Standard Model's prediction by 7 standard deviations. This anomaly has far-reaching implications for the LHC's Run 3 and the FCC-ee's future experiments, prompting a renewed focus on precise W boson mass measurements at both experiments. To address this concern, researchers have proposed utilizing electroweak triple gauge boson coupling data to improve W boson mass calculations. Since the CDF II anomaly affects the triple gauge boson coupling flag states' measurements most significantly, the proposed method focuses on this area. By combining current and future data from the LHC's Run 3 and the FCC-ee's experiments, the proposed method aims to achieve two primary objectives: Firstly, the method aims to reduce uncertainty in the W boson mass measurement by at least an order of magnitude, thereby allowing for a potential recovery of the CDF II result. Secondly, the method aims to differentiate between the CDF II result and other possible solutions by minimizing the number of flag states' contributions.

Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter various forms of client interactions, including change requests, as part of their work. Although search terms are commonly used to reflect the client's requirements, the quality of the search terms can significantly impact the developer's search process. A recent study revealed that 45.1% of search terms fail to accurately represent the client's needs. Effective search term quality is crucial in maintaining the required level of quality in software maintenance. In this paper, we investigate how software developers refine change requests, containing sensitive information, to create relevant search terms, and observed that 43% of the time, developers rephrase the original request to improve the quality of the search terms. Our research focused on understanding developers' search term quality control strategies from two perspectives: the information quality of the search terms themselves and the level of abstraction, as represented by a new metric called UQS. Our data shows that 71% of the variance in UQS can be attributed to the quality of the original search terms, indicating a direct relationship. Furthermore, we found that high-quality search terms lead to fewer modifications during the search process. Ultimately, we identified potential solutions to enhance search term quality, including providing auto-completion features and educating developers about search term quality, as well as implementing a new process to handle change requests, to mitigate the risks associated with low-quality search terms.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinct vocal characteristics. To better understand how people adapt to each other's speaking styles, we need quantitative measures that can accurately detect similarities between speakers. In this study, we explore the use of various acoustic features in speech to develop entrainment indicators. By analyzing a large dataset with both human and artificial indicators, we discover that an easily computable feature, namely the pitch frequency, performs as well as more complex approach in a neural network. This finding suggests that entrainment indicators could be applied in both natural language processing and speech generation to create more realistic and connected artificial dialogue.

We've developed an open-source web platform to visualize, process, and share spectral and energy spectra data, as well as related metadata, with customizable online tools. Our platform is designed for researchers studying galaxy science, and it allows users to access and manage data using a web interface, without the need for programming skills or extensive bioinformatics knowledge. The platform supports features like data uploading, real-time analysis, and management, along with embedding analysis tools and raw data into the web platform, making it a comprehensive tool for working with spectral and energy spectra data. Our tool enables users to collaborate on analyses by sharing specific online tools with users and viewing results in the form of supplementary digital content, such as interactive 3D visualizations or downloadable data. We demonstrate the platform's capabilities by reanalyzing a well-known galaxy, demonstrating that our tool allows users to efficiently run complex analyses and make discoveries in line with existing scientific findings.

Classifying every video frame into its respective action can be a labor-intensive task, particularly for a large collection of unlabeled videos. Therefore, we introduce a novel, unsupervised method, called SSCAP, that identifies likely temporal segments across a variety of actions by focusing on distinguishing characteristics within each class. By leveraging self-supervised learning and clustering algorithms, SSCAP effectively detects actions in videos, outperforming existing unsupervised benchmarks significantly. Additionally, SSCAP's effectiveness is further substantiated by its ability to improve the accuracy of action detection in videos when paired with existing supervised architectures.

We investigate several hadronic molecular states consisting of the $\bar D^{(*)}$ and $\Sigma_c^{(*)}$ as potential candidates for exotic resonances observed in experiments. The connections among these states, $D^* \Sigma_c$, $D^{* \ast} \Sigma_c$, $D^{* \ast} \Sigma_c^*$, $D \Sigma_c^*$, and $D \Sigma_c^{* \ast}$, are established through perturbative approach, demonstrating their interrelation. The masses and pole residues of the bound states $D \Sigma_c^*$, $D^* \Sigma_c^*$, $D^{* \ast} \Sigma_c$, and $D \Sigma_c^{* \ast}$ are calculated using Luscher's finite volume quantization of bound-state energies, which also enables the determination of the coupling constants among these bound states and decay constants of the baryon $\Sigma_c^*$, as well as the analysis of their decay properties into $D \Xi_c$ and $D^* \Xi_c$ channels. The study then examines the $D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$ molecular states' decay properties into $D^{(*)} \pi \Xi_c$ and $D^{(*)} \gamma \Xi_c$ channels, providing the estimates of the branching ratios and production rates for the process $e^+ e^- \to \bar D^{(*)} \Sigma

The growing importance of software testing is well recognized, yet few educational institutions integrate its principles into their curricula at the undergraduate level, leading to a significant shortage of professional software testers. To address this issue, we developed a comprehensive testing curriculum for undergraduate students and recently published the course materials, which have already been successfully implemented at an Indian university. To enhance the effectiveness of our curriculum, we are currently refining our teaching methods by incorporating an evidence-based approach to inquiry-based learning. This paper outlines our revised teaching methods in detail and presents the outcomes of a pilot experiment conducted with the newly implemented curriculum. Our experiment revealed that students taught using our inquiry-based learning approach demonstrated enhanced problem-solving skills and produced higher-quality project outputs within a designated timeframe. Notably, our approach not only improves students' technical skills but also fosters their critical thinking abilities, which are essential for success in the professional world.

Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, when source data is inaccessible due to privacy concerns, this strategy becomes impractical. To resolve this issue, we propose a novel method that adapts source models via hypothesis transfer without requiring access to source data. This approach involves a semi-supervised learning technique that iteratively utilizes entropy minimization and augmented label propagation for intra-domain and inter-domain alignments. Experimental results on multiple public datasets demonstrate that our method yields significant improvements of up to 19.9% compared to state-of-the-art methods, particularly in semi-supervised adaptation tasks.

A comprehensive review of the Gas Core Reactor is presented, focusing on its key aspects. The review covers the underlying physical principles, detailed design, crucial features, and the latest advancements in the reactor type. The primary objective is to identify and assess the opportunities for utilizing this innovative nuclear technology in advanced power generation and space propulsion systems.

This study presents a novel machine learning method, integrated into a particle
tracking and reconstruction system, focusing on the Atmic Neutrino detection
entirely on the FAMU 5-meter tank using Cherenkov light. The task involves
localizing the initial particle interaction within a tank's volume. By leveraging
physics-driven features derived from Monte Carlo simulations, a high-precision
localization is achieved. Our research demonstrates that a Domain-informed
Neural Network (DiNN), tailored to incorporate physics-driven context, outperforms
a traditional multilayer perceptron (MLP) with 3D coordinates as input. The
DiNN, MLP, and existing closest hit method are compared in terms of position
resolution for various types of events. The analysis reveals that the DiNN
achieves resolutions comparable to the closest hit method but with reduced
computational effort. Furthermore, the DiNN offers flexibility to adjust its
performance based on its architecture design, providing the potential to enhance
the localization resolution to the closest hit level while saving processing
time.

The development of models for the atmospheres of brown dwarfs, cool stars and planets is ongoing. In order to gain insight into the low-gravity objects discovered in recent years, we have created models that take into account the variation in molecular absorption cross-sections at higher temperatures and pressures. Our study includes updated models based on the latest release of the opacities from the H\&He grid, which include the addition of new molecules such as FeH, HCN, C$_2$H$_2$, C$_2$H$_2$P, and CO. Our results cover a range of surface gravities from log\,g = -1.0 to -9.0 and effective temperatures from 1000 to 4000\,K. They are available in various formats and cover a broad wavelength range from 0.1\,\um to 10\,\um. In an analysis of seven low-gravity objects, we found that using the theoretical cross-sections resulted in a better fit to the observed spectra. Additionally, we have created a plot illustrating the relationship between surface gravity and effective temperature, which can be used to determine the surface gravity of objects based on their spectral type and parallax measurement.

This text provides an overview of the semantics underlying Answer Set Programming, 
focusing on well-founded operators and their application in grounding algorithms.

We have extended quantum resource theories to encompass complex scenarios with multiple resources that evolve over time, governed by a composite tensor product *-algebra. Utilizing relative entropy as a measure of resource difference, we developed key equations for resource conversion without utilizing rate equations. By examining steady states, we derived essential conditions for resource non-multiplicativity in multi-resource compositions and identified both necessary and sufficient conditions for resource non-multiplicativity in certain copure and semi-cyclic resource theories. These findings enable resource theories to be efficiently assessed for practical applicability across various multi-resource applications.

To evaluate communication systems, average error metrics like the peak mean-square error (PMMSE) and minimum mean-square error (MME) are considered, with the MME being the ideal performance measure. It is established that the MME is not a feasible performance goal for Gaussian channels, except in the unusual case where a message amplifier is absent. This insight prompts an investigation of the conditions under which the PMMSE can equal the MME. It is found that this equality occurs only when the channel is Gaussian with an exponential probability density function and the amplifier has a constant gain. This is the sole instance where these two error metrics are equivalent.

We analyze how to identify common random patterns within a large group of time series data, even when individual series have distinct characteristics. A new statistical approach is developed to determine if multiple time series share similar random components, despite having different forms of noise. This method relies on estimating a key matrix representing the correlation between different series and uses a principle from random matrix theory to make conclusions about the presence of random trends. By focusing only on the dominant eigenvalues and eigenvectors of this matrix, the statistical approach becomes efficient and handles high-dimensional data with a large number of series, even if it contains many irrelevant variables. The theoretical validity of this approach is substantial and applies to a wide range of scenarios. The proposed method is demonstrated to be effective in a variety of real-world scenarios and outperforms existing alternatives in various simulation experiments. Its usefulness is further illustrated through its application to the analysis of commodity prices, the study of election outcomes, and the examination of health data in high-income countries.

A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced, incorporating explicit designs that enable linear time decoding processes. The construction is based on a specific combinatorial structure involving vertices, edges, and faces, defined within a Cayley complex framework. A key aspect of this structure lies in the utilization of constant-size random codes mapping $m$-bit vectors to $\Delta$-bit vectors. A pivotal element of the code's performance is demonstrated through a rigorous proof of an almost optimal property related to the robustness of random samples within the associated complex. This robustness property is a crucial ingredient in the construction and selection of the aforementioned codes.

The distance-$r$ dominating set problem, along with its related covering problems, is a recently introduced set of problems within graph theory. For a graph $G$ and a given integer $r$ greater than or equal to $1$, a vertex $D$ in $G$ is considered a distance-$r$ dominating set if all other vertices in the graph are within a distance of $r$ from $D$. The minimum size of a distance-$r$ dominating set in a given graph is referred to as the distance-$r$ domination number. This paper explores the complexity and exact exponential time complexity of the distance-$r$ dominating set problem, as well as related covering problems, which are shown to be NP-hard. Furthermore, the paper presents a parameterized complexity study of these problems and demonstrates that they are W$[1]$ hard in terms of specific parameters. However, the distance-$r$ dominating set problem is shown to be fixed parameter tractable when the parameter is vertex cover number and $r$. Additionally, the paper introduces a new problem, called the $k$-distance-$r$ dominating set problem, which generalizes the concept of distance-$r$ dominating sets to multiple vertices. This new problem is shown to be fixed parameter tractable when the parameter is vertex cover number and $r$.

This research examines the impact of disorder on the bulk and topological characteristics of two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators. We specifically focus on the lattice model of the quadrupole topological insulator proposed by Sato et al. Our investigation involves two types of disorder: one that maintains hopping symmetry and another that breaks it. We find that while the bulk band gap closes in response to significant disorder in both cases, the corner states persist. We attribute the resilience of the corner states to the protected nature inherent to higher-order topological insulators. Furthermore, our analysis using the Green's function technique reveals that the majority of boundary states are shielded from disorder, with the exception of states influenced by disordered nearest-neighbor hopping terms. We demonstrate that a new type of boundary state, distinct from Dirac fermions or chiral symmetry-protected fermions, arises from the disorder-induced transfer of charge between nearest-neighbor atoms.

Recent searches for supersymmetry at the CMS experiment have so far been conducted 
without fully incorporating SUSY theories that involve long-lived gluino-based 
sparticle pairs in low-energy proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. A high 
efficiency, heavy-ion based method was employed to detect the gluino-based 
sparticle pairs that exhibit low masses and delayed decay times by utilizing 
specific final states that include soft, heavy-ion based method-based missing 
transverse energy and extra soft muons. Due to the absence of any potential 
candidates, new limits have been established at the 2 TeV level for heavy 
gluinos and for the time it takes for the gluino-based sparticles to decay.

Novel view synthesis with light field rendering traditionally achieves accurate reproduction of view-dependent phenomena by densely sampling a scene's views, yet these processes are often computationally expensive. In contrast, geometric reconstruction methods only require sparse views but often struggle to replicate non-Lambertian light interactions. Our new model strikes a balance by learning view-dependent effects in four-dimensional light field space and inferring scene geometry using sparse views and geometric constraints. Specifically, we developed a two-stage transformer architecture that combines epipolar and reference view aggregations to compute target ray colors, demonstrating superior performance over existing techniques across multiple benchmark datasets, particularly in scenes with prominent view-dependent behavior.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery included 59 new pairs, bringing the total number of observed pairs to 3355, spanning 2921 targets. Analyzing the data using speckle imaging and differential speckle monitoring, our research provides an update on the orbital motion of $\sim$120 close binary systems. A speckle image catalog and differential speckle monitoring lists have been made publicly available online through the Speckle Imager for Various Applications facility for future use and development.

We are investigating chiral space-time scenarios where the law of motion remains unchanged, and our research reveals that the underlying algebraic structure of this phenomenon is closely linked to the one governing self-dual gravity and its connection to the colour-kinematics duality. Furthermore, the studied cases encompass two distinct types: models based on the BF theory and those based on the Chern-Simons theory, which are both defined on five-dimensional manifolds. We also explore a specific correlation between the one-loop scattering amplitudes of particles in chiral gravity theories and the colour-kinematics organised type A open string theory.

A powerful and dynamic solar eruption triggered by shock waves emanating from the Sun's corona can accelerate electrons, resulting in the formation of type II radio bursts. Although these bursts have been observed extensively, researchers are still exploring their origin. To gain a deeper understanding, we studied a remarkable solar eruption on October 16, 2015, that produced both a type II radio burst and a steam eruption. This event was captured by the Solar TSUNAMI system, the Extreme Ultraviolet Imaging Spectroscopy (EUVI) on the Solar Terrestrial Observatory (STO), and radio observations from the Gauribidanur Radio Observatory. Analyzing the data, we identified a stream associated with a powerful solar wind on October 16, 2015, that matched type II radio burst data, suggesting these events were linked. Furthermore, we estimated the speed of the stream to be approximately 1035 km/s, indicating that the stream emanated from above a coronal density of 10^-3 g/cm^2. This observation agrees with numerical simulations modeling a stream originating from above a coronal density of 10^-3.5 g/cm^2. The data also shows that the stream was divided into two distinct parts, each corresponding to different coronal densities. This finding, supported by simulations, suggests that the stream was formed when a bubble in the high coronal density region broke through into lower density regions, creating two distinct parts to the stream. The interaction between the bubble

A detailed analysis is presented of the potential explanations offered by the general two Higgs doublet model for a number of observed anomalies in the decay processes of B mesons, particularly those involving violations of lepton flavour conservation in interactions such as $B^+ \rightarrow K^+ \mu^+ \mu^-$. The new physics scenarios are categorised according to various Higgs-mediated diagrams that could contribute to these anomalies, assuming a type-II two Higgs doublet model where one Higgs doublet acquires vacuum expectation value (VEV) similar to that of the known up-type quarks and charged leptons. The findings show that only the $b \to c$ transition anomaly can be resolved through UHBs with very low mass and very large Yukawa coupling for the up-type quark to UHB lepton channel, a scenario highly constrained by experimental data. Furthermore, combining data on the $B^2$ anomalies with constraints on the 125 GeV Higgs and electroweak precision parameters rules out most of the UHB scenarios. The UHB scenarios out of the numerous ones examined can explain at most only 50% of the data on the $B^2$ anomalies, leading to a partial resolution of the anomalies, leaving around 50% of the data unexplained.

This study introduces a unique, locally finite random vortex flow that accurately represents two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations for flows without swirly motion. To achieve this, we first establish the relationship between two conditional distributions, which are mutually reciprocal, then derive the random vortex flow with this property. This discovery provides a new, explicit example of random vortex flow, which is shown to be equivalent to the well-known Kraichnan model. Additionally, we formulate a simplified version of the Navier-Stokes equations for flows without swirly motion in the form of a stochastic partial differential equation, and prove that it has a corresponding random vortex flow.

The state vector of a boson sampling device can be precisely generated using a computational algorithm called the Generalized Husimi Q-function, which generates a wave function with high accuracy. This processing approach allows for a detailed analysis of the boson sampling phenomenon. By studying the entropy of the boson sampling state, we found a two-stage change in its behavior. Initially, the entropy remains low and linear with the number of modes, then it suddenly increases and reaches its maximum value. This threshold occurs at half the total number of modes. Beyond this point, the entropy continues to rise at a faster rate. Our research also accounts for error inaccuracies in the Q-function calculation due to finite computational complexity. These findings can aid in the development of a reliable theory for boson sampling and inform the construction of future experiments.

Temporal sequence analysis typically employs methods like measure-based clustering, which can be sensitive to measurement scale and noisy data. We've developed a novel technique, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, based on the Maximum Margin Framework, to address these issues. By mapping warping functions on a 2D grid, our method efficiently combines the strengths of dynamic time warping and soft k-means clustering. We've shown through simulations and a real-world vaccine effectiveness study that our approach surpasses existing methods in margin and often achieves better accuracy while avoiding overfitting. The accompanying code and data are available for free.

Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when those systems are designed to be challenging. Many successful methods rely on the use of neural networks to estimate the value or policy of a given state and action. These networks, particularly recurrent ones with memory capabilities, can improve the accuracy of these estimates and consequently increase the expected return of a learning agent. However, incorporating a recurrent component also introduces instability to the gradient descent used for parameter updates, leading to the emergence of adaptive algorithms that can adjust the step size based on performance. We explore the properties of these adaptive algorithms in the context of reinforcement learning and its variants, demonstrating their benefits and drawbacks. Our findings suggest that an algorithm with a step size adjustment mechanism can accelerate learning under specific conditions, but may also impair its robustness and stability when confronted with tasks of varying difficulty.

In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on spatial and temporal features extracted from pre-defined grid cells. Yet, this approach can limit the accuracy of recognition when actions span across multiple grid cells, particularly in cases where objects move across multiple cells. To address this challenge, we instead focus on identifying the spatial and temporal boundaries of actions by using actor locations and temporal span as reference points in a spatial-temporal pyramid. Our proposed STAP-Net network leverages a self-attention mechanism to dynamically select and weigh relevant features from multiple grid cells to generate a single representation for each reference point, thereby capturing the essence of actions with complex layouts and temporal progression. Our system demonstrates exceptional performance across three benchmark datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art methods and showcasing robustness when faced with actions characterized by diverse spatial and temporal features.

A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset to evaluate state-of-the-art image copy detection methods. With over 200 participants involved, the winning entries are subject to scrutiny in this paper. One notable observation was that the difficulty of image transformations posed a significant challenge for participating algorithms. Therefore, this paper examines the performance of various methods against different transformation types and their combination. Key findings reveal that distant domains substantially increase the difficulty of image copy detection. Additionally, the difficulty is also influenced by the application of degradation techniques, such as cropping, resizing, and pixel intensity adjustments. Notably, the winning algorithms excelled in generalization but struggled with handling transformed images. Furthermore, the analysis uncovered a correlation between saturated colors and the originality of the images, which could be a useful feature for future developments. Building on the insights gained, potential future challenges for image copy detection are identified, along with suggestions for improving the benchmark dataset.

Our research focuses on stochastic processes where the stochastic force exhibits
persistence, meaning its sign never changes over time. These processes are
similar to stochastic integrals driven by Markovian processes. By introducing a
small disturbance, we investigate the metastable behavior of these processes
around their initial state. The study shows that, as the disturbance approaches
zero, metastable time periods are extended in a smooth manner. The signs of
these periods may change upon sufficiently small disturbance. The study also
reveals that, for certain processes, metastable behavior may be lost even when
the disturbance approaches zero. To illustrate these points, we provide a
mathematical model describing the stability of a particle held in an
attractive potential by a constant force. The model shows that the particle's
behavior is similar to stochastic integrals and that metastable periods may
be extended upon sufficiently small disturbance. The study is presented at the
2018 meeting of the Portuguese Meeting on Mathematics.

This study examines the influence of intense magnetic fields on the characteristics of neutron-rich nuclei, as well as on nuclei made of protons and neutrons. Researchers applied the Dirac-Brueckner-QRPA theory to calculate energy and spin properties in the presence of strong magnetic fields, using a relativistic interaction that includes magnetic field effects up to the field strength of $B\sim 2.23 B_0$ where $B_0=45$ MeV/fm is the critical field for symmetry energy. The results indicate that strong magnetic fields can align the spins of particles and anticipate novel phenomena in highly anisotropic magnetic fields. The investigation focuses particularly on the behavior of spin polarization, energy, and single-particle levels in the fields. It also includes an analysis of the energy and momentum of the collective modes within the finite nuclei under the influence of strong magnetic fields.

Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this, we have developed an innovative approach using the Squeeze algorithm to filter data on the client-side, reduce gradient vector size by compressing only the necessary elements, and employ token-based communication for sending labeled data from clients to the server. This method is designed to maintain the privacy of client data in accordance with differential privacy (DP) principles. Our study examines the interplay between communication efficiency, data privacy, and model accuracy on various neural networks (FCN, ResNet, ViT) and benchmarks (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, TinyImageNet) under the influence of DP. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in achieving higher communication efficiency, lower gradient transmission, lower communication overhead, and equivalent model accuracy when compared to the benchmark approach. Furthermore, the approach exhibits DP guarantees, and its performance is comparable to the current state-of-the-art framework for differential privacy.

The diffuse far-ultraviolet (FUV) continuum detected in molecular clouds is primarily produced by the interaction of starlight with the interstellar gas. To investigate the origins of this phenomenon, we conducted a study of two nearby dark clouds using data from the GALEX All-Sky FUV and far-ultraviolet near-ultraviolet surveys. Our analysis revealed that the FUV emission in these clouds is predominantly a result of the starlight reflected off the diffuse gas rather than the radiation from embedded young stars. This finding was confirmed by comparing our FUV data to the star catalog of Francis et al. (2015), which includes information on young stellar objects. Our results suggest that the FUV emission is largely composed of scattered starlight in these clouds, rather than a combination of starlight and the flux of radiation from young stars. This distinction has significant implications for future research on the FUV properties of these clouds, as it may be unnecessary to account for the potential influence of embedded young stars.

Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information, making research in scientific papers easily accessible to scholars by compiling experimental outcomes and highlighting novel discoveries. Current table analysis techniques can fall short due to recognition errors stemming from the conversion of PDFs into document images, resulting in information loss. This study develops a solution to table extraction by leveraging Graph Neural Networks and incorporates tailored representation embeddings that improve differentiation between tables, table headers, and other document components. An experimental assessment was conducted on a combined dataset from PubLayNet and PubTables-1M to evaluate the proposed approach's efficacy and stability across varying document types and domains.

This study investigates how players with varying levels of intelligence and experience learn and adapt in multi-stage incomplete information games. We suggest a dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory model, which simulates how players of different cognitive levels learn and adjust their expectations and strategies over time. In this framework, higher-cognitive players are more effective at understanding the actions and expectations of lower-cognitive players. We developed the Dynamic CH Learning Rule, a time-sensitive mechanism that enables learning and converges towards our proposed solution concept, the stationary markov perfect Nash equilibrium. We demonstrate that our theory can accommodate diverse levels of cognitive ability among players and that, under specific conditions, even the lowest-cognitive players can approximate the highest-cognitive players' outcomes. Furthermore, we show that our theory has practical applications in valuing real options with incomplete information. A numerical analysis using Monte Carlo simulations reveals that the predictive power of our theory aligns with that of continuous-time capital asset pricing models like the Black-Scholes model.

Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development. As censuses fall short of providing the necessary spatiotemporal detail, researchers have been turning to independent approaches incorporating remote sensing data and microcensus statistics. This work yields an open-source method that produces a plausible population density profile for sub-Saharan Africa between 200 to 2019, aligning with official statistics from 2019. This approach relies on a novel iterative sparse regression technique that accommodates diverse data formats, coupled with a density filter that ensures consistency. Additionally, the filtered profile adheres to a global minimum and meets basic requirements, while allowing for further adjustments through constrained regression. Ultimately, the proposed profile serves as a baseline for future research, while also highlighting potential challenges and limitations in population density profiling.

Over the past ten years, research into approximate data retrieval queries has generated substantial interest, driven by the rapid expansion of distributed and big data storage environments. To address the inherent drawbacks of false positives, previous studies proposed the use of Bloom filters. Nevertheless, as systems continue to scale, the frequency and severity of false positives still pose significant limitations. To mitigate this issue, researchers have recently proposed novel data structures designed for approximate query processing, including multi-level Bloom and Winnow filters, xOR and HyperLogarithm filters, among others. This research survey provides an in-depth overview of state-of-the-art filter designs, focusing particularly on their underlying principles, optimization techniques, and performance outcomes. Furthermore, we discuss various strategies for optimizing and evaluating Bloom filters, including counter structure organization, array size configuration, hashing functions, and probing sequences. In addition, we explore applications and related open issues. This research survey aims to provide readers with a comprehensive understanding of the current status in the field, as well as an insight into potential future research avenues.

We investigate multiple modes of producing atom-molecule pairs from a Bose-Einstein condensate of spinless atoms by leveraging spin-exchange collisions and light. A distinct three-stage process demonstrates that, according to theoretical findings, atom-molecule conversion can occur via these methods alone, even in the absence of net momentum transfer and, consequently, even in the absence of a laser, as well as in scenarios where the laser is not capable of initiating the process or when the atom-molecule bound state has a broad collision width.

Fluid-structure interactions involving compressible fluids are investigated using the multi-scale smoothed particle hydrodynamics method with a specially developed compressible formulation. This approach incorporates distinct resolution levels for the fluid and structural components, enabling the use of either a weakly compressible or fully compressible fluid model. The proposed C-SPH model, which builds on a previously established weakly compressible SPH model, ensures consistent and smooth transition between the different models based on the local particle density. The method's accuracy and reliability are demonstrated through a range of numerical simulations, including diverse scenarios of fluid and structural behavior. These experiments cover a broad range of conditions, from incompressible to highly compressible flows, as well as impacts on rigid and deformable structures, all while maintaining the efficiency and scalability of SPH simulations.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to classical processing. We explore the process of training a quantum classifier using both supervised and unsupervised learning techniques on a small quantum simulator, which processes data much faster than its classical counterparts for certain operations. While the circuit complexity of quantum machine learning methods, especially the cost of repeatedly running a quantum circuit, significantly impacts their performance, our results indicate that future advancements in quantum technology and more efficient circuit designs can lead to practical applications of these methods even at present.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's given pitch values far from its average pitch value.  In natural speech, pitch can vary greatly, so we need an algorithm that won't limit where the pitch can vary.  Pitch shifting, which changes the perceived pitch of a signal without changing its fundamental frequency, is a way to overcome this problem.  We created a new neural network called NP-TTS that can change pitch without limiting where the pitch can vary, by teaching it to preserve the pitch of the training speech when generating speech.  Tests showed that NP-TTS, which uses a pitch-shifting algorithm, made speech that was as good in quality as FastPitch, and that the improvement was biggest in speech that was very different in pitch from the average pitch.  The improvement in speech quality was also measured, and the results showed that NP-TTS made speech that was more natural and had better quality.

Understanding how objects persist despite changes in appearance and location is crucial for video analysis. Building on the concept of object permanence from cognitive development, we propose an approach for video reasoning that leverages object tracking across transformations. Our proposed method, object tracking using object permanence (ToPer), estimates the similarity between object segments in consecutive frames and incorporates the expected persistence of objects between frames. ToPer demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the video localisation and object tracking datasets of VTU, TBST, TBST++, and TBST+++, outperforming other methods by significant margins, with improvements of up to 10% and 20% in recall and video success rates, respectively. Our results on the TBST++ dataset indicate that higher recall rates correspond to a greater number of object permanence applications. Additionally, we propose a benchmark for video localisation and object tracking, known as the Video Object Tracking and Localisation (VOTAL) dataset, which consists of a large collection of video clips and is designed to test object tracking and localisation more comprehensively. The VOTAL dataset features multiple occurrences of object class appearances and is available at http://visual.ai.u-szeged.hu/votal/.

Our study investigates lepton-pair production coupled with bottom quarks at the Large Hadron Collider using theoretical predictions from next-to-leading order QCD. The investigation encompasses various factors, including a detailed analysis of predicted outcomes and an estimation of the associated uncertainties based on the dependence on perturbative QCD parameters. Additionally, it involves a comparison of these calculations with experimental data obtained from the 2016 LHC measurements by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations. The results demonstrate that incorporating the effects of bottom quarks in Drell-Yan production is essential to accurately describe the data, particularly when considering the low-to-mid range of transverse momentum observed in the measurements. The study further reveals that the inclusion of bottom-quark effects is crucial across a broad range of rapidity, particularly when the lepton pairs are produced at the lower end of pseudorapidity.

Remote-controlled vehicles called Telepresence robots have gained attention in various fields, thanks to advancements in technology and reduced costs. A key factor determining user experience with these robots is the quality of navigation, which is influenced by the device's movement during remote control. Although current studies focus on designing robot paths and evaluating navigation performance, they neglect the human aspect of remote control. Consequently, they rely on subjective user input to adjust movement rates and react to obstacles. Conversely, this research develops a predictive model to quantify the quality of navigation when using Telepresence robots, taking into account virtual vision, navigation, interaction, and communication aspects. Furthermore, it identifies specific factors that impact navigation experience, including self-driving capabilities, visual quality, and navigation reactiveness. Data collected from 30 users who remotely controlled a Robin hand-eye robot in various scenarios were used to support these findings and validate the proposed model.

In this study, we revisit the core features of two Bayesian hierarchical regression models, thoroughly analyzing their full probabilistic frameworks, including the conditional distributions for each parameter. We then proceed to develop efficient Gibbs samplers to sample from the posterior distribution. The chosen data sets and settings in this study are intentionally basic to ensure that the underlying techniques can be implemented and tested with ease. The primary goal of this work is to thoroughly understand and validate the implementation of each model, rather than applying them to more complex scenarios.

Mafia is a popular online multiplayer game with various roles where players compete in rounds, some of whom are part of a secret mafia group. Our study treats the game as a statistical problem to determine the likelihood of the mafia or townspeople winning under different circumstances. Assuming rounds are independent of each other, we used the Bayes' theorem to calculate the probability of the mafia winning given a specific number of mafia members, as well as the probability of the townspeople winning given a certain number of mafia members and a number of rounds. Our analysis showed that the probability of the mafia winning is always higher than that of the townspeople and that these probabilities increase exponentially with the number of rounds, provided the number of mafia members is fixed. When the number of mafia members is variable, we found the probability distribution of the townspeople winning tends to shift towards lower numbers of mafia members as the number of rounds increases.

The early solar system had a gas accretion process that formed the planets we see today. Studies of exoplanets and their masses have led to a current understanding that more massive planets typically form when less gas is accreted. However, our own solar system's inner planets were accreting gas simultaneously with their formation, which raises questions. Using a three-dimensional model, we've simulated the accretion of giant planets in protoplanetary disks that produce inner planets on short timescales. The results show that accreting gas simultaneously in the formation of inner planets can prevent the normal progression to massive planet growth, as as least. The findings also suggest that inner planets may not have as much influence as once thought on the timing of gas giant formation.

The electrical conductivity of an ensemble of nanomaterials on a macroscopic scale
depends on complex electronic transport mechanisms, specifically the coherence of
carrying charges at one point in time. While quantized conductance is a well-documented
phenomenon observed in a single nanotube or nanowire, the presence of internal
quanta, referred to as phonons, significantly impacts charge transfer even in an
ensemble of 1000 nanotubes or nanowiles. Employing techniques from many-body and
quantum statistics, researchers have found that the coherence of the ensemble, despite
