the presence of internal quanta, allows for coherent energy transfer through the system
even when interactions with the environment are considered. Experimental observations,
such as the freezing of electrical conductivity at extremely low temperatures, can be
explained by theoretical predictions, specifically the theoretical freezing of electrical
conductance as theoretically predicted.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in relevance and importance, affecting the quality of the cluster. By weighing each feature differently and incorporating an adaptation of the Silhouette method, the objective function of the algorithm aims to optimize cluster separation while minimizing intra-group variations. The efficacy of this method is evaluated through multiple synthetic data sets and real-world applications, including text classification and DNA sequence analysis. The results show promising performance comparisons to established state-of-the-art clustering techniques.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Although they effectively handle complex patterns by dividing input data into distinct segments, traditional algorithms used to train MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, taking a long time to learn the model parameters. To overcome these limitations, we have developed an innovative algorithm that determines MoE model parameters in a more efficient and reliable manner. This new approach, specifically designed to handle infinite hidden layers within neural networks, can be used to recover the underlying MoE model even when the experts themselves contain complex structures such as recurrent connections, convolutional components, or data augmentations. We have thoroughly tested our algorithm's effectiveness by applying it to a range of MoE neural network subtypes, verifying its ability to accurately recover MoE models across various settings.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry.

In our investigation into the universe's early stages and the properties of fundamental particles, global symmetries have long been respected in the fields of Particle Physics and Cosmology. These symmetries, however, can cause problems during inflation because the gravitational waves generated would be too large. The possibility that a global symmetry might be broken spontaneously, thereby generating a potential obstacle for the inflationary model in the form of topological defects where the symmetry is still intact, presents an interesting scenario. We investigated a specific inflationary model in which this occurs and found that the gravitational waves generated during inflation could be minimized or avoided altogether. The conditions required for this phenomenon to occur are not only physically plausible, but also create a mechanism that could also account for the universe's current observed state.

This study offers a new method to distinguish between blue horizontal branch and blue straggler stars in the globular clusters Rup 190 and NGC 2808. Using our approach, we were able to correctly identify the blue horizontal branch stars in Rup 190 and found that BHB and BS populations in NGC 2808 have a mass difference of approximately 0.10 solar masses. A mass function of the BHB stars in Rup 190 and NGC 2808 indicates a higher mass value, which also differentiates them from the BHBC stars in those clusters. The resulting mass functions have a higher uncertainty at the lower mass end compared to the overall cluster mass function. The approach developed here can be applied to the globular cluster M22 to verify previous findings of the mass function difference between BHB and BHBC stars. The approach developed can also be applied to the globular cluster M22 to verify previous findings of the mass function difference between BHB and BHBC stars.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, establishes the "b-principle" associated with such functions, and confirms that this principle holds true for a specific type of map functions classified as oriented colored semi-submersions.

The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to draw from past experiences and adapt them to unfamiliar situations. Typically, the process begins by training the DNN on a multitude of diverse tasks and then retaining the optimized model parameters, known as the expert, which can be applied to a variety of downstream tasks. Although this approach has been found to be effective for a limited scope of tasks, its effectiveness significantly diminishes when the downstream tasks become diverse and numerous due to a significant drop in transferability. Contrary to the traditional notion of expertise, novel findings indicate that the optimal DNN performance on downstream tasks is not necessarily achieved by maximizing the similarity between the learned features and the desired outputs, but rather by balancing the similarity with the downstream task outputs and the dissimilarity with the source task outputs. Based on this understanding, a new DTL framework, called Differentiable DTL (D^2TL), was developed to optimize the similarity between the source and downstream tasks using a global similarity function and the global dissimilarity function, while considering the impact of the source task outputs distribution, the downstream task outputs distribution, and the impact of the source task outputs distribution on the global dissimilarity function. Through a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed framework on the CIFAR10 dataset, which consists of various downstream tasks, the results indicate that the proposed framework, which uses a differentiable function to optimize the similarity between the source and downstream

The efficiency of information propagation in intricate systems heavily relies on their structural organization. In network structures, clusters are systematically arranged, thereby boosting the propagation's efficiency. To investigate this, we introduce a model simulating information spread through complex networks, complemented by an optimization approach to fine-tune the network's efficiency. By simultaneously adjusting the network's architecture and the weights of individual edges, our method aims to minimize the required time for information to reach all nodes. The information diffusion model we've devised is versatile and can be applied to a variety of scenarios, including both linear and non-linear systems. The approach to optimizing the network is also universally applicable and may be extended to various problems, such as adjusting synaptic weights in artificial neural networks.

Under specific conditions from Floer theory, we derive numerical measures that quantify 
the proximity of two Lagrangians based on their angular separation and relative position within the symplectic form. 
These conditions are applied to homogeneous Lagrangians of a prequantized sphere, enabling the analysis of their angular relations 
and ultimate collision when the angular difference becomes infinitesimally small.

The reliability of a discrete-time channel model heavily depends on the precise definition of discrete nonlinear interference points. The gap in current channel memory characterization, specifically regarding continuous versus discrete interference, is addressed in this paper. By linking channel memory with the G-noise model and introducing a normalized version of White interference, we develop generalized criteria for determining discrete nonlinear interference points. The results show that channel memory is largely determined by the spacing between key interference points, particularly when the White interference ratio is far beyond the noise floor. Furthermore, we establish a guideline for choosing discrete nonlinear interference points in various channel models, including unbalanced M-QAM, square M-QAM, and hybrid square/non-square M-QAM systems. The findings are verified through numerical simulations, presenting a possible extension to existing channel models.

The widespread adoption of Android as the global leading operating system makes it an appealing target for malware. To counter this threat, security experts continuously develop advanced detection systems based on machine learning and deep learning. However, skilled hackers counter these systems by adapting their malware samples to bypass detection through a variety of evasion attacks. This study focuses on problem-space evasion attacks on Android malware detection systems. The paper reveals hackers modify the behavior of their malware to evade detection by altering their interaction with the system, without any modification to the malware's binary code. We present the first known evasion attack on Android malware detection, which modifies the app's API call set to evade detection. This study showcases the first successful implementation of this attack, which shows that malicious apps can avoid being detected in malware-based analysis by modifying their interaction with the system without altering their code.

Service-Oriented Computing (SOC) utilizes services as fundamental components, where advancements in understanding services and their descriptions have a profound impact on SOC. Historically, services were viewed as traditional methods that execute behind remote procedure calls. However, services have evolved into entities with distinct personalities, capabilities, and management styles. A service is characterized by its management entity, defined as the entity responsible for administering the service provider and consumer interactions. A notable trend involves service management entity centralization, where the service management entity functions as an intermediary, thus sparking the concept of microservices. This paper examines the evolution of services in SOC, with a particular focus on service management entity centralization and its effects on microservices, an essential topic in SOC research.

Recent experiments employing thermal Hall conductivity have provided substantial evidence for the existence of several topological orders, including the Pfaffian, $\nu=1/2$ state, which however poses a challenge in being realized as a ground state due to its complex quantum fluctuations. In this study, a detailed thermodynamic analysis of the Pfaffian topological order is presented using a Bethe ansatz method within the framework of the su(2)_L-su(2)_R quantum group symmetry. As a result, thermodynamic properties in both the planar and finite thickness limits are derived along with thermal Hall conductivity. Importantly, this analysis overcomes long-standing limitations of earlier non-interacting theories. Our results demonstrate that while the Pfaffian remains an adiabatic anyon model, its suitability as a ground state is supported under particle-hole symmetry. Moreover, precise measurements of the thermal Hall conductivity can unambiguously identify the Pfaffian's presence, distinguishing it from competing topological orders such as the anti-Pfaffian and $\nu=1/3$ states.

Our analysis indicates that primordial binary black holes with masses within hertz spring to life when the rest mass density of baryons in the universe drops below a certain threshold, creating an opportunity for their formation to leave behind gravitational waves detectable by the LISA within our lifetime. Black holes in less-dense universes fail to emerge because either the velocity of particles becomes too great, preventing the formation of self-gravitating clusters, or the clusters themselves are unable to overcome their own repulsion. Black holes in the most dense universes emerge successfully, but their masses grow too large for LISA to detect. The window for forming these binary black holes is particularly narrow, lasting only from the point at which neutrinos lose their ability to free-stream until the point at which baryons begin their own free-streaming period, lasting a mere 1 second. The formation of these binary black holes follows a predictable, universal pattern, giving rise to a range of possible masses that follow a distinct, predictable pattern. The formation of these binary black holes is a natural outcome of the standard model of cosmology, and their masses are fixed regardless of the specifics of the universe in which they form. The masses of these binary black holes fall within a narrow, predictable range of 10^11 to 10^13 grams. The masses of the most massive and the least massive possible variants are each limited to a single, precise value of either 10^11.2 grams or 10^13

The complex nature of protoplanetary discs makes their precise reproduction through computer simulations crucial for gaining insights into planetary formation. A recent study used the ATHENA code to model how ring-like disturbances in a disc's pressure affect the formation of planet cores, considering scenarios involving both smooth and turbulent discs. Interestingly, researchers discovered that in areas where the disturbance is most intense, cores can form more efficiently, under specific conditions, of course. Furthermore, as cores grow into planets, their minimum possible mass could be as low as 0.5 M Jupiter, influenced by disc turbulence. Finally, as planets orbit within these disturbances, their orbital positions could dictate their ultimate mass, presenting a potential pattern in which planets increase in mass over time.

This study investigates the relationship between the limits of artificial neural networks'
computational capabilities and the learnability of various tasks within the context of
optimization-based learning methods. Firstly, we demonstrate that the time complexity
of reaching an optimal solution using a minimax optimization technique is influenced by the
network's degree of overparameterization. This discovery is built upon the discovery of
an upper time bound, known as an "optimality threshold", that caps the time required to
reach an optimal solution for a given dataset. Notably, this bound can be interpreted as a
quantitative measure of "representational power" for the network. Our results suggest that
overparameterization can expedite model training under certain conditions, but only up to a
certain point beyond which performance actually deteriorates. Moreover, we found that the
"optimality threshold" can be used to characterize not only the time it takes to reach an optimal
solution, but also the minimum number of parameters required to perform a specific task.
Our study, which leverages a simple framework known as "Learner-Task-Network" (LTN), aims
to contribute meaningfully to the ongoing debate between the "bad optimizers" hypothesis and
the "bad initializations" hypothesis. Our findings imply that the limitations on the capabilities
of neural networks may be an inherent characteristic resulting from the specific learning tasks these networks are attempting to perform.

We have obtained results that provide a broader application of the Solel-Wyser model for Bohr sets, which in turn expands on a finding by Bergelson, Morris and Schaubberger. Our solution addresses a question initially posed by Bergelson, Morris and Wierdeman and yields an explicit minimum size requirement for sets that satisfy specific criteria related to Bohr sets. Specifically, for a countable discrete abelian group $G$, when given a closed subgroup $H$, and a set $E$ with positive density in $G$, it can be determined if there exists a subset $A$ of $E$ with a specific size such that the sum of the elements of $A$ whose images under a given homomorphism $f$ fall within a given set $B$, equals $E$, and this occurs when $B$ is a Bohr set of some size relative to $f$ and $H$, with a size relationship that holds in all non-trivial cases. Furthermore, when considering $G = \mathbb{Z}$ and $f = \text{id}$, it can be determined if there exists a set $A$ with a specific size such that the sums of the elements of $A$ whose images fall within a given set $B$, equal $E$, and this occurs when $B$ is a Bohr set of some size relative to $1$, with a size relationship that holds in all non-trivial cases.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where multiple customers share similar itineraries. We refer to this challenge as the high-pooling rate (HPR) problem. In this context, ridepooling services struggle to achieve optimal pooling rates without significantly increasing customer detours. We approach this issue by establishing a mathematical programming model that identifies the most efficient and realistic routes given pre-existing road networks and customer requirements. Our model takes into account various constraints such as road directions, detours, and customer specifications. We also introduce two solution methods: a two-stage algorithm and a column generation method. Our model and algorithms are tested with real-world data and the results demonstrate their practicality and efficiency. Furthermore, we conduct a case analysis to evaluate the impact of return trips on pooled routes and identify opportunities for improvement within the high-pooling rate problem.

In the digital age, multi-modal data have become a crucial resource for E-commerce. However, the various formats in product data present significant challenges in processing. Currently, research methods primarily rely on visual information and are difficult to apply in scenarios outside this domain. To address this limitation, a new approach called ModEL is proposed, focusing on semantic feature learning for multiple data types. By using a common latent space for different representations, ModEL demonstrates effective learning on multiple data types. To support innovative applications in E-commerce, ModEL is evaluated through tasks like matching large datasets and generating synthetic data. To enable more research on diverse product data, a new benchmark called PDMB is created, including high-resolution images, detailed text descriptions, and product barcodes. The benchmark enables more realistic product synthesis and data augmentation. The source code and datasets for ModEL and PDMB are available online at https://github.com/ericskiedan/ModEL and https://github.com/ericskiedan/PDMB respectively.

A significant function in most algorithms for analyzing brain scans is attributed to unsupervised learning, particularly in non-linear exploration. A novel approach, Deep InfoMax (DIM), offers considerable potential in exploring brain structure. In this study, a modified version of DIM is applied in examining the structural connectivity of white matter through diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). This modified method employs a contrastive learning strategy with random walk-based objectives to enhance exploration. Performance is evaluated using the Challenge on Exploring White Matter Non-Linearity (CWNL) dataset, which includes multiple subjects, variants, and objectives. Notably, the modified DIM achieved superior results compared to the original DIM and other state-of-the-art methods, according to metrics such as mean square error (MSE) and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the CWNL dataset. The modified DIM's objectives exhibit notable correlations with axial diffusion coefficients (FA, mean ADC) and radial anisotropy (RA), underscoring its effectiveness in non-linearity exploration of white matter non-linearity exploration.

Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task known as text classification, which is widely utilized in numerous real-world applications.  Characteristic of all NLP applications involving text classification is the use of word embeddings as input to the model.  Word embeddings are positioned in a high-dimensional space such that similar words are closely situated.  Researchers have developed the concept of Retrieval-Augmented Machine (RAM), a pre-trained language model capable of learning word embeddings through an attention mechanism.  Unlike standard word embeddings, RAM's embeddings are sensitive to the context in which words are used.  This research investigates whether RAM's contextual embeddings can enhance the performance of text classification tasks.  To achieve this, the study introduces an innovative score metric known as the Influence Score (I-score), which assesses the impact of context on word embeddings.  Through experiments on the Google RCV dataset, the researchers found that incorporating the I-score into the model architecture resulted in improved performance and increased interpretability of the results.  The findings suggest that the I-score can effectively capture the contextual influence of words in text classification tasks, demonstrating its potential as a valuable tool in enhancing the robustness and interpretability of text classification models.

We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model on a square lattice, employing the variational Monte Carlo method. An effective spin-orbit constant is considered in the paramagnetic phase, and our findings reveal that the interaction's increase reduces this constant, making comparison with the insulating phase's value challenging. However, an increase in the spin-orbit constant's value, analogous to that observed in Ce$_3$Bi$_4$Al$_{11}$, results in a metal-insulator transition occurring when interactions surpass a certain critical threshold. Furthermore, an analysis of the density of states shows that the occurrence of a metal-insulator transition is a result of the interband interaction's increase, and the formation of a local effective center of symmetry within the $t_{2g}$-orbital subspace is responsible for the enhancement in the effective spin-orbit constant in the insulating phase.

A dark matter candidate with a mass similar to the present day age of the Universe could remain largely intact and make up a significant portion of baryonic mass within the Universe. If a dark matter particle decays into standard particles that hold information about its velocity, this would result in the particle's energy loss being limited to a small fraction of its current mass energy. Consequently, its velocity would cede only a tiny portion of its current kinetic energy over time. As a result, dark matter particles with a mass less than approximately one-trillionth the mass of a proton could remain largely intact and retain velocities above the speed of light escape from the Universe, even with a lifetime significantly shorter than the age of the Universe, especially when considering the massive MACHO components that make up the dark matter. This implies that our galaxy, the Milky Way, could potentially harbor dark matter massive MACHOs with a mass range between $10^{-12}\; \mathrm{g}$ and $10^{-55}\; \mathrm{g}$ that are on the verge of disintegrating.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate safely and efficiently in diverse environments before being released to the public, it is crucial to assess their performance in varying scenarios, including unseen distributions, against realistic benchmarks. However, the standard practice of evaluating a model's performance on its training or validation set does not adequately address these concerns, as it provides no indication of how the model will perform in real-world, unseen situations. In this paper, a novel estimation method, distribution shift estimation (DSE), is introduced to approximate a model's performance in shifted environments using a single, representative dataset. DSE identifies and focuses on central tendencies within data distribution, allowing it to effectively predict a model's performance across a wide range of shifted scenarios. Furthermore, the study highlights several key aspects of distribution shifts, including the impact of shifted scenarios on model performance, the benefits of assessing generalization performance, and the limitations of models that excel in simulated environments but struggle in real-world scenarios. Through a series of experiments, the DSE method demonstrated strong predictive capabilities for a model's performance in shifted environments with a correlation coefficient of 0.88, while also identifying key challenges and characteristics of distribution shifts.

High-fidelity simulations of nucleic acids require precise simulations that account for every atomic movement. Achieving such high-accuracy simulations using standard simulation methods is challenging due to the large system sizes of nucleic acids. Our research demonstrates how to enhance simulation accuracy by employing a Nose-Hoover chain to regulate bond lengths and bond angles, in addition to existing optimizations for torsional potentials and atomic movements. We found that this approach leads to negligible deviations from optimal performance in nucleic acid simulations with up to 128 nucleotides. Our results enable high-accuracy all-atom nucleic acid simulations with minimal adjustments needed for existing codes.

The Asymmetric Numeral System (ANS) was introduced in 2013 as an entropy coding technique, which has since been refined through several optimized variations. This research examines two distinct table-based ANS encoders - the standard version and the multi-level variant - and applies the principles of precise initialization to eliminate redundant data, specifically to the table-related encoder outputs, resulting in a total of $\lceil \log_2(255.5n)\rceil$ and $\lceil \log_2(127.5 \cdot 2^{k-1}+127.5)\rceil$ bits of redundancy, respectively, for $n$ input symbols. Additionally, the findings also offer solutions to two related decoding problems.

The dielectric characteristics of micro- and nano-emulsions are significantly influenced by ion interactions, leading to varied dielectric behaviors depending on electrolyte concentration, as illustrated by dielectric relaxation studies of hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide in glycerol. In contrast, ion interaction within water-based emulsions results in dielectric responses analogous to ion-free systems, despite slight shifts in dielectric constants. Additionally, hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide in glycerol induces dielectric transitions when mixed with water, triggering ferroelectric behavior and crystallization of the cations upon dilution. Notably, this study presents a novel method for detecting cation crystallization visualized through X-ray scattering and confocal microscopy.

In our earlier work, the range of heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules was determined, and a predictive model based on resonant quark-antiquark pairs was established. This paper presents additional support for this model of heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules. Several notable heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules, such as X(3872), Zc(4050), and Zc(4200), are used as examples to demonstrate the model's effectiveness. Utilizing the properties of these molecules, the model's parameters were refined. As a result, the model's reliability in predicting the mass spectrum of heavy-antiheavy hadronic molecules has been further validated.

Research on military drones is growing in importance as a swarm can be a
useful asset in warfare, and recent analysis based on 302 English and
Russian publications reveals significant advancements have occurred between
2014 and 2019, particularly among studies published in 2019 and 2020.
A notable increase has been observed in the application of artificial
intelligence compared to earlier periods, and our research categorizes
publications according to drone types, application areas, and the
complexity/depth of content. By comparing our results with existing reviews,
we highlight some disparities and areas for further research, and by
examining references cited in each group, we identify the most frequently
cited publications and draw insights from their content.

The Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation functions provide valuable information about the early universe and small-scale structure. Analyzing the correlation functions between quasars and galaxies at specific cosmological distances can place constraints on several cosmological parameters. By using a large dataset of $z_{\rm source} = 3.8$ and $z_{\rm source} = 5.1$ measurements, it has been found that including the full shape of 3D correlation functions significantly improves constraints on cosmological parameters. Moreover, it has been observed that including the 3D correlation functions of monochromatic quasar samples changes the constraints on cosmological parameters compared to using only the 1-point and 2-point data. The inclusion of 3D Ly$\alpha$ data can potentially reveal new information about the cosmological model by accounting for higher-order correlations related to quasar biases and the breaking of statistical homogeneity.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where a beam of particles undergoes an unconventional manipulation, swapping its horizontal and longitudinal beam patterns at the A0 Photoinjector. The new experimental setup, featuring a specially designed deflector accompanied by curved beamsplitting components, has enabled the first observation of a distinct phase shift between the particle beam's trajectory and its time-of-flight.

Predicting pedestrian trajectories is crucial for enhancing public safety and self-driving technologies. The key challenge lies in developing a forecasting model that's both adaptable and robust, capable of accurately predicting short-term movements while considering long-term goals. Existing top-ranking models for pedestrian prediction are either complex and difficult to scale or overly reliant on distant neighbors, neglecting nearby cues. To address these issues, we propose POLAR, a new framework that's designed to be both efficient and effective. The model consists of two interconnected components: a local feature extraction module that identifies key spatial cues and a global prediction module that integrates these cues to forecast pedestrian paths. The key innovation here is the model's ability to adapt the weightage of these local cues dynamically as the pedestrian moves, rather than fixing them beforehand. By leveraging self-attention mechanisms, we create a dynamic framework that's both computationally efficient and capable of handling complex behaviors. When tested across multiple prediction timescales, POLAR outperformed existing top-ranking models, with significantly improved performance and scalability.

Over the past thirty years, various theoretical models have been developed to
analyze intricate systems. These models encourage a system to adapt and
improve its performance over time. One notable concept, the complexity of
recurrent neural networks, was introduced by Fortnow and Lipton in 1994, and
involved backpropagation as a learning mechanism. In our research, we revisit
this idea using a different learning technique, Hebbian learning, which allows a
system to eliminate errors without external guidance. We show that some of the
previous bounds remain valid, while others need revision, and establish new
limits on the complexity of recurrent neural networks based on this new learning
method. Additionally, our study focuses on incremental Hebbian learning, which
involves learning and memorization processes without the need for external
guidance. We also explore an extension to the complexity bound, which takes into
account the number of steps a system needs to achieve convergence.

This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for facilitating communication between humans and a swarm of robots. Our solution involves merging a compact hand gesture recognition model with the advanced \emph{ros2} system to enable a swarm of robots to execute complex actions in response to distinct hand signals. Our experiment, utilizing a series of hand gestures that instruct different swarm behaviors, was successfully implemented with three Turtlebot3 robots. This enabled these robots to automatically adjust their distances and evade collisions with obstacles in various simulated environments as well as in a physical testing setup.

The study aims to assess the performance of composite deep learning models consisting of Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for identifying diverse White Blood Cell types, a feat that could revolutionize automated medical diagnosis and blood analysis in pharmaceutical and healthcare settings by analyzing image samples, thereby aiding in disease diagnosis for patients.

A crucial aspect in designing quantum gates involves the ability to manipulate quantum states in a precise manner within a given time constraint. Recently, a protocol known as counterdiabatic inference was proposed to create gates from smooth, inflection-point-based trajectories. However, this method requires solving a time-varying Schrödinger equation, making it computationally demanding. In this work, a simplified approach called reduced counterdiabatic inference is presented by approximating the inflection points using fewer points, thereby reducing computational complexity and achieving faster convergence. Additionally, this method's effectiveness is theoretically validated and numerically demonstrated through the calculation of spectra and switching times for various systems, including a two-level system and a harmonic oscillator.

Color-neutral images constitute a vital section of data for image processing research. Due to their diverse applications, efficient techniques for transforming them into grayscale images are highly sought after in both research and industry contexts, particularly where preserving color information is crucial. Existing methods, however as far as research shows, do not adequately address this challenge. To fill this gap, we introduce two new approaches for converting RGB images into their grayscale equivalents. These novel transformations are developed within the framework of Spectral Graph Theory, a unique field where image processing concepts are mathematically linked to graph theory. The clear structure of this theory also enables the creation of more efficient randomized algorithms, a common practice in modern image processing. Our contributions are threefold: (a) we introduce a new grayscale transformation based on the Laplacian matrix of the color lattice; (b) we develop a new transformation derived from the Laplacian of the color distribution; and (c) we evaluate the performance of our methods, comparing their effectiveness with other existing techniques.

This research develops an expression to decompose infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions into a sum of exponentials along with a corresponding error term. Building upon this, a corresponding infinite series is derived for functions in $C^\infty$, which converges to the original function under specified conditions on the remainder term. Subsequently, these results are applied to solve differential equations of higher order, and in the case of initial value problems, the convergence of associated infinite series solutions is established.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, such that it meets the conditions set by Alexandrov for an upper curvature bound, we demonstrate that an almost conformal harmonic map from a surface to the pair (S, d) results in a branched covering. Consequently, if (S, d) is topologically equivalent to the two-dimensional sphere S^2, then (S, d) is proven to be conformally equivalent to S^2.

We've created the highest-specification electron positron pairs in a laboratory setting by leveraging the Breit-Wheeler process, in which gamma rays collide with electrons. Our experimental setup utilized a beam of near-monochromatic, high-energy ions to create a photon beam that was then focused and concentrated before being made to collide with individual electrons. As a result, we were able to produce electron positron pairs and record their creation in great detail, noting that these pairs were produced close to their point of origin and close to the collision's time frame. Our findings align well with theoretical models that have been developed for this phenomenon.

In a forthcoming letter, we examine the production of the Standard Model Higgs boson via associated production with a W boson in a type of Two Higgs Doublet Model where the Higgs bosons primarily interact with the Standard Model vector bosons via tree-level diagrams. The Higgs boson is represented by the lighter CP-even state, and its heavier CP-even and CP-odd counterparts can be produced via tree-level diagrams with the same multiplicity as in the Standard Model. However, the coupling between these states and the W boson, as well as the one between the charged Higgs boson and the electroweak gauge bosons, are independent of the Two Higgs Doublet Model parameters, resulting in a more restrictive scenario compared to other models. We have analyzed the associated WH production in the presence of the background top quark and anti-quark originating from the proton-proton collisions, as captured by the ATLAS and CMS experiments, focusing on the differential cross-sections of the decay modes $H\to b\bar{b}$ and $H\to WW^*$ to further determine the effects of the tree-level diagrams on the cross-sections. We discovered that even with the tree-level diagrams that are identical to the Standard Model, the model still exhibits deviations from its benchmark scenario. These deviations can be quantified with the precision of a few percent, suggesting that the analysis of the associated WH production may be an effective means of identifying new physics beyond the Standard

We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by shape expressions. These shape expressions, a form of DTD-like constraints, define the structure of resulting RDF graphs. The key element in our approach is typed IRI constructors, which enable the assignment of unique identifiers to RDF subjects, a crucial aspect in data integration. By incorporating typed IRI constructors, we ensure the precise mapping of relational data to RDF format, allowing for the assignment of specific types to IRI identifiers. A special type, referred to as the 'blank' type, is used for anonymous subjects, anonymous subjects that will not be assigned a specific IRI. The process of data exchange is defined through source-to-target functions, which map relational data to RDF structures, and these functions are constrained by shape expressions. The concept of strong and weak validity is introduced to determine if the data exchange process successfully maps the source data to a valid RDF structure, and this validity is verified by checking the shape expressions' constraints. The determination of validity is essential, as only strong validity guarantees the success of data exchange. Furthermore, we investigate the complexity of recognizing strong and weak validity, and the minimization of data exchange solutions, and demonstrate that these problems exhibit high complexity.

A new field of shape-constrained nonparametric regression is rapidly growing across various disciplines including economics, statistics, operations research and artificial intelligence. In the context of productivity and efficiency analysis, this research area can be categorized into two main parts: one related to monotonically-constrained performance analysis and the other concerning the estimation of shapes. Notably, recent applications extend beyond productivity and efficiency evaluation, encompassing other fields such as visual perception and time-series forecasting. The diversity of recent advancements in this area is noteworthy, with techniques encompassing kernel-based methods, kernel-free approaches, multivariate analysis, dynamic forecasting, neural networks and deep unsupervised learning. The integration of artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly essential for productivity and efficiency analysis, as well as in other areas of conic classification and time-series data organization.

The majority of research into the creation of bosons at the Large Hadron Collider assumes the colliders' initial state and final state. However, there is a missing link in these studies - the identification of bosons through decay processes, which are crucial for research but have been overlooked. This study develops an innovative method to identify bosons at any point in the decay process and uses it to examine the development of jet substructure observations in various detector environments. The results demonstrate that the method can precisely determine the mass of produced bosons with an estimated resolution of 100 MeV or better in experimental conditions similar to those of the LHC.

Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work investigates how the self-attention mechanism in pre-trained models extracts grammatical relationships from sentences. By analyzing layer-wise performance and attention patterns in the model, we found that the self-attention mechanism's ability to generalize grammatical relations is hindered when dealing with unfamiliar inputs, as compared to those with similar structures. To address this limitation, we developed a novel approach that utilizes linear projection matrices for queries and keys in the self-attention mechanism. By selecting specific attention patterns for grammatical relationships, our method enables the model to focus on syntactic relationships without compromising semantic accuracy. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving an 4.3 f-score improvement on the Penn Treebank, a 12.6 f-score improvement on BEA, and a 7.7 f-score improvement on CoNLL.

The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). For non-English languages, the scarcity of large-scale resources hinders ASR performance. In this study, a newly created German acoustic model is fine-tuned using various data sources. The model achieves significant improvement when augmented with the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus, bridging the performance gap with the best existing English models. Additionally, this research introduces a new Wikipedia corpus comprising high-quality spoken data. The corpus features all German dialects and is suitable for use in ASR and speech synthesis applications.

The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and dual star evolutions, however through 73 VFTS spectra analyses it has been observed that Be-type stars have higher rotational speeds. Calculations of Be-star's projected rotational speeds gave them an average velocity of 319km/s±, with 75% of values above 200km/s. This is significantly higher than typical B-type stars with lower mean velocities of 69km/s±, with 75% of values below 140km/s. Be-star's rapid rotation could be a result of dual star activity where a close companion's gravitational force causes the star to spin faster. Alternatively, Be-star's could be a result of single star evolution, characterised by a specific mass range of 10-15 solar masses, with an estimated mass distribution of 55%±6% and 45%±6% respectively. Be-star's rapid Be-star's rapid rotation could be a result of dual star activity. Alternatively, Be-star's could be a result of single star evolution, characterised by a specific mass range of 10-15 solar masses. Be-star's mean luminosity was 0.8 to 1.2 times that of a typical B-type star, although with an uncertainty of 0.1 in magnitude. Be-star's with an identified companion, the Be-star's velocity was 230km/s±, with an estimated mass of 14.6 solar masses.

To translate ASR output into written text, inverse text normalization is utilized.
Existing ITN techniques, whether rule-based or neural modeling approaches, often
involve complicated annotations and data preparation, including the need for costly,
domain-specific, high-quality training examples. In contrast, our proposed data
enhancement technique efficiently creates large amounts of accurate spoken-written
pairs from unrelated text data with minimal manual annotation. Furthermore,
our model specifically designed for spoken-written synthesis has shown superior
performance compared to conventional sequence-to-sequence models.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs.

Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas such as medical imaging. A promising approach, partial dependence plots, can provide insights into individual variables' influence on a model's predictions. However, these plots are typically reserved for binary classification models, limiting their application in areas like medical diagnostics where labels are scarce. In the case of multi-class and regression tasks, multiple values are associated with different observations, making partial dependence plots less effective. To address this challenge, our research introduces a novel visualisation technique called Integrated Partial Dependence plots. This method creates distinct regions for different classes based on I/O plots, thereby enhancing understanding and analysis of models' behaviors in scenarios with multiple outputs or labels. Our method was demonstrated to be efficient in terms of computational cost on models such as U-Net and VGG16 for tasks involving large datasets of medical images.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We address this question by compiling a comprehensive topological classification of one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems with and without correlation effects. Our investigation shows that correlation-induced symmetry breaking leads to a significant topological classification change from a point group type to a more complex one. Specifically, topological solitons in the non-Hermitian Lie fermion chain can be either modified or completely destroyed due to correlation effects, which arise from the competition between the local hopping term and the jump term. We further propose an innovative method to directly visualize the phase diagram through a self-dual fermion model, which effectively condenses complex topological structures into manageable and transferable forms. This work not only sheds light on the role of correlation effects in non-Hermitian topology but also provides a valuable approach for uncovering topological structures in complex systems.

Our current research builds upon our previous findings where we identified acoustic characteristics essential to synthetic speech perception as warm and competent. We now aim to explore how these derived vocal attributes contribute to their creation in synthetic voices. We've developed a multi-step model that transforms input attributes into corresponding acoustic features for the Tacotron speech synthesis model, using either individual or paired attributes as input. Additionally, we've established benchmarks for synthetic speech warmth and competence across various speech synthesis systems and found them in natural human speech. Notably, we've discovered that state-of-the-art synthetic speech still lags behind natural human speech in warmth and competence.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and addressing the neutrino mass conundrum is examined.  An analysis of the underlying particle interactions and their stability is performed, resulting in the determination of the dark matter mass range.  By analyzing the dark matter and anti-dark matter annihilation into $W$ boson pairs, a lower bound of 2 MeV on the dark matter mass is derived, and an upper mass range of under 1 GeV, and possibly up to 500 MeV, is proposed.  Additionally, a stability analysis of the new particles reveals that, in the dark matter mass range of interest, the global lifetime of the system can surpass the age of the universe if the dark matter mass is higher than 80 MeV, and possibly within the 2-50 MeV range as well, and possibly even for masses as low as 20 MeV under certain conditions.

We re-examine the application of the geometrical collective Bohr-Mottelson model to nuclear structure, with a focus on the minimal length introduced by Mignaco and other researchers. We develop a mathematical framework based on the deformed algebra of quantum phase space, rederive the surface degree of freedom collective potential and derive the corresponding Hamiltonian. We then apply the generalized Galan i Seoane quantization rules, previously established within the deformed q-deformed Weyl algebra, to obtain the complete set of collective equations. We solve these equations for a particle and a deformed harmonic oscillator, demonstrating that minimal length collective effects transform the fixed potential into a surface one and alter the corresponding classical action, resulting in modified quantum energies compared to the standard case. We verify these findings for a nucleus like the $^{208}$Pb, with a minimal length of about $b_0 = 2.45$ fm.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained attention due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends the concept of Golay complementary matrices and their corresponding polynomials to higher dimensions, with a focus on developing suitable higher-dimensional analogs. Novel constructions of high-dimensional Golay complementary matrix sets are presented, including special subsets that can be utilized in omnidirectional precoding applications. Additionally, promoting finite algebraic number fields and their Galois extensions can lead to new discoveries in this area.

In our proposed method, a novel approach for detecting changes in multi-dimensional hyperspectral images is presented. Traditional binary change detection operators are typically applied to three-dimensional spectral vector representations of these images after being divided into individual bands. Nevertheless, this process results in a considerable loss of information. To mitigate this limitation, a feature fusion deep convolutional autoencoder framework is developed, enabling the direct utilization of three-dimensional hyperspectral data while preserving detailed spectral features through a novel bottleneck reconstruction loss function. The framework incorporates change detection via an binary label comparison module, leveraging pixel labels from multiple image patches to generate change maps. Comprehensive evaluations on diverse datasets reveal the efficacy of our method in preserving intricate spectral information and its superior performance relative to established techniques.

A comprehensive study explores the connection between residual entropy and viscosity using an innovative machine learning-driven approach. This research provides an in-depth comparison between the underlying thermodynamic properties and the complex entropic features that drive the variation in viscosity across diverse temperature and pressure conditions in molecular fluids. By utilizing residual entropy as a proxy for entropic factors and employing an unsupervised machine learning algorithm, we map the energy subspaces of Lennard-Jones and water molecules to uncover the hidden residual entropy landscape. This residual entropy landscape successfully captures the inherent dynamics of these fluids, thereby accurately predicting their comparative viscosities across the entire range of temperatures and pressures. This novel approach not only offers a straightforward method for estimating viscosity but also provides valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of complex fluids, allowing for a deeper understanding of the physical phenomenon and the development of highly efficient and accurate models.

We are proposing a new model for the universe's evolution, which results in a cyclic pattern at a large scale. This model is compatible with the laws of physics as they are currently understood. Unlike other theories, our approach does not involve dark energy changing over time. Instead, the universe's expansion folds back onto itself due to a cosmological constant. With the laws of physics as they are currently understood, combined with certain initial conditions from the early universe, our model's results reveal a pattern in which the universe expands and then folds back onto itself over and over again. Each cycle has similarities but also some key differences. For example, each cycle has a period of rapid expansion known as the 'big bang', but also some areas where the expansion slows down and then speeds up again. This model's predictions show a pattern that matches recent observations of the universe's expansion, which suggest a slowdown. However, further observations, particularly those related to the light from distant galaxies, may eventually result in a more detailed understanding of the model and its potential predictions.

A new superdeterministic theory of quantum mechanics known as Invariant-set theory is being proposed. This idea brings concepts from areas like chaos theory and dynamical systems into play, suggesting that initial conditions have inherent limitations. Although the theory doesn't involve hidden variables, it attempts to explain quantum phenomena without relying on local realism. We'll show how to construct this theory by applying the noncommutative geometry framework of Connes, offering a potential solution to the quantum-interference problem raised by Bell's extension of Einstein's superposition principle. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that Invariant-set theory is capable of generating nonlocal correlations strong enough to exceed the scope of Bell's theorem.

We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on devices such as smart speakers and wearables. Our focus is on NN execution within devices with limited resources; thus, we suggest a Compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) architecture. This CNN features (i) reduced computation requirements via limited multiplications. (ii) an economical use of model parameters to minimize memory usage.

The partition function for the two-dimensional Dirac equation with a gauge field can be represented by an integral of a partition function of chiral matrix values, which is similar to the structure seen in the partition function for chiral conformal field theories. Isomorphisms with other mathematical structures, such as those involving the special unitary group and the projective special linear group, have also been established. We explore the properties of the Dirac partition function by examining its relation to these isomorphisms, demonstrating that it serves as a functional integral of a general observables partition function. Additionally, we derive explicit formulas for general observables in theories with Wilson lines and loop operators based on this isomorphic representation.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency in handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity and high dimensionality issues. To overcome these challenges, a new method called the Multi-Group Lasso has been developed for handling multi-response regression problems. By introducing a new algorithm for solving the ML-Group Lasso problem, the method's theoretical convergence is proven, and its performance is demonstrated through numerical examples and real-world applications.

In recent years, the need for embedded real-time systems to integrate general-purpose and embedded-specific workloads has driven the adoption of hypervisors for embedded devices. Despite this, the existing hypervisors have not fully lived up to the performance requirements of embedded real-time systems. Our research presents T-Visor, a lightweight and efficient hypervisor designed specifically for mixed criticality embedded real-time systems. By utilizing a multi-stage approach to schedule visisted tasks and implementing mode-based interrupt handling, T-Visor achieves superior real-time performance and energy efficiency compared to existing hypervisors. Additionally, T-Visor's architecture does not rely on a concept of domains which enables the direct integration with the embedded kernel. Our evaluation demonstrates that T-Visor's performance and energy consumption are comparable to that of native execution, while its scheduling capabilities meet the stringent requirements of hard real-time systems.

When capturing panoramic scenes, cameras are typically aligned either vertically or alternately rotated, leading to unique challenges in image stitching. Current methods often assume uniform camera alignment or employ costly 3D reconstruction to compensate for positioning errors. However, the association between camera configuration and stitching quality in panoramic images has yet to be systematically investigated. In this paper, we introduce novel datasets consisting of images captured with the primary axis horizontal (H-Dataset) and alternative (A-Dataset), totaling over 500 subjects. Our research reveals that camera orientation affects stitching quality, with vertical alignment resulting in reduced accuracy. Leveraging this insight, a new framework is proposed, comprising an alignment-aware feature extractor and a panoramic stitching algorithm, referred to as Panfoce. Panfoce employs an alignment-aware feature extractor to adapt current panoramic stitching techniques, enabling them to handle images captured with alternative configurations while achieving improved performance with both horizontal and alternative alignment images. Notably, Panfoce outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both H-Dataset and A-Dataset without utilizing 3D reconstruction information. Our source code will be made publicly available.

When two coupled populations of oscillators have synchronized and asynchronous elements respectively, a chimeric state can arise in such networks. We've analyzed chimeras in systems where one parameter influences an oscillator's behavior, drawn randomly from a uniform distribution, for oscillators in two-dimensional spaces. Our research builds on previous studies, such as Laing's 2019 findings on identical oscillators, to investigate the emergence and stability of these chimeras in diverse oscillator networks with a large number of elements. Interestingly, as heterogeneity in the oscillator network increases, it leads to the disappearance of stable chimeras through a saddle-node bifurcation. These outcomes shed new light on how robust chimeras are to varying levels of heterogeneity in diverse oscillator systems.

We examine if controllers obtained using model-based Reinforcement Learning, which employs an environment model to find the optimal policy, remain robust and adaptable when dealing with slight environmental variations. Typically, model-based methods offer better performance than model-free ones, but they assume environmental variations are limited. In real-world applications, environments often have inherent uncertainties and constraints. New methods aim to minimize the impact of inaccuracies in the environment model on policy decisions. We propose two approaches to tackle this challenge: using multiple models to track environmental changes and an uncertainty quantification framework. These strategies are evaluated in simulated scenarios and a robotic experiment, demonstrating their success. Interestingly, combining these methods surpasses previous techniques that targeted a similar problem.

We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, using which we can build a higher dimension (n+1) algebras of infinite complexity from a given n-dimensional algebra. This process enables the creation of such algebras in the form of matrix and tensor products of lower-dimensional algebras. Consequently, it results in equivalence of module categories for certain types of quivers and n-dimensional algebras.

Research in holographic theories reveals a duality between quantum information theories and gravity through specific constructions.  Reflection entropy in these theories displays singular behavior denoted by the entropy boom, specifically occurring during the page phase transition.  A random tensor network model, constructed using families of high dimensional tensors, has been developed and studied across different page phase transitions.  This model features a boom in reflection entropy along with a duality symmetry anomaly and an entropy condensation anomaly, both occurring at the tensor network level, independent of specific implementations.  A general framework has been established for general high dimensional tensor networks, extending beyond the specific "in-out" reflection and implementing various page phases.  This study supports the notion that holographic theories and their reflection encode fundamental principles of quantum information theories, while also exploring the underlying physics behind tensor network models.

We examine the relationship between a statistical system's properties and the durability of its long-lasting patterns, referred to as quasi-stationary states (QSS). By assuming the system undergoes a series of small changes, we develop two general methods for estimating the rate at which entropy is generated and the constraints preventing equilibrium in nonequilibrium systems. These methods are applied to two different types of systems: those influenced by kinetics and those impacted by dynamics. We find that the patterns which emerge in these systems are linked to periods of relatively slow entropy generation and that their longevity is determined by the strength of this constraint. Specifically, we demonstrate that the rate of entropy generation within a system is inversely related to the lifetime of its patterns when the system is in a QSS and that the patterns which emerge in these systems are linked to rates of entropy generation which occur via various routes to equilibrium. These routes, which include phase transitions and regular scenarios, are characterized by the divergence of the system from local equilibrium, and the rate of entropy generation within these routes can be estimated using a theoretical approach based on the perturbation of the linearized dynamics. This approach is applied to a number of different systems, including the Brusselator model, a model describing the early stages of the oscillating chemical reaction, the linearized dynamics of which diverges from local equilibrium, and a model explaining the pattern formation in the one-dimensional modulated oscillations of the extended system, which is found to follow a different route to equilibrium

We investigate the dynamics of a basic 3D version of the H\'{e}non map, specifically focusing on its dissipative and orientation-preserving variants. A thorough analysis of bifurcations in this system reveals that the emergence of periodic orbits, especially at specific resonant points, leads to distinct orbit patterns. The system's dynamic behavior can be visualized through 2D cross-sections, illustrating the appearance of periodic, quasiperiodic, and chaotic orbits. The occurrence of chaotic patterns is closely linked to the orientation-preserving variant and can be identified by specific ratio ranges between the parameter values. Ultimately, this study confirms that the system exhibits a rich set of patterns, including chaotic and quasiperiodic motions, arising from the intersection of stable and unstable linear trajectories.

The gravitational-gauge theory relationship known as the double copy is a well established concept that connects both three and four dimensional theories of gravity to electric and magnetic gauge theories. This relationship, which was first discovered in 1988, can be represented by the equation: 
GC = CA * BA. 
Where GC represents a gravitational field, and are the electric and magnetic fields derived from a common electromagnetic field, and A represents a gauge field. 
Research conducted recently in 2020 suggested that the equation GC = CA * BA holds true at a higher mathematical level than previously thought. 
In this study, both CA and BA are defined as matrix types known as the spin connection and flat connection respectively. 
These matrices can then be combined with a third matrix, referred to as the gauge field A, which is applied in the equation GC = CA * BA, 
resulting in the matrix representing the gravitational field GC. 
This study expands the existing knowledge of the double copy relationship by applying it to: 
Motion within a curved three dimensional space, 
The collision of particles with a cross section, 
The scattering of 2 and d dimensional particles, 
The rotation of black holes, 
The decay of gravitons, 
The bending and gravitational field formation observed in the context of photon motion in a gauge field environment.

We analyze the statistical behavior for specific $t = 2$ or $3$, examining how
the number of hook lengths divisible by $t$ in the partitions of $n$ varies.
The support of the resulting distribution, $Y_t(n)$, diminishes significantly
as $n$ approaches infinity for $t = 2$ or $3$. Specifically, we find that
$Y_2(n)$ is concentrated around its mean, $\mu_2(n)$, while $Y_3(n)$
is concentrated around its mean, $\mu_3(n)$. Furthermore, the ratio of the
standard deviation of $Y_2(n)$ to its mean, $\mu_2(n)$, approaches $\sqrt{
\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{6}{n-1}}$, and similarly, the ratio of the standard
deviation of $Y_3(n)$ to its mean, $\mu_3(n)$, approaches $\sqrt{\frac{24}
{(n-1)}}$. The research also demonstrates that $Y_2(n)$ and $Y_3(n)$ are
symmetric around their means and that their probability mass functions are
negative on certain intervals. The findings for $Y_2(n)$ extend earlier work
by G. K. Savchev and X. Zhang.

Quantum particles experiencing tunneling can be studied by analyzing the Larmor clock in a weak magnetic field. The clock registers two tunneling times, one associated with the wave function's peak and the other with its tail. Previous experiments failed to distinguish between these times due to the interferometric nature of the setup, which made it difficult to accurately measure the tunneling time. On the other hand, the present experimental method yields a clear value for the tunneling time without the ambiguity, which is found to be in line with existing theories. The new approach involves measuring the quantum action using a cycle-average technique, which provides a direct mean to verify existing theories and understand quantum phenomena. The results of the experiment can be used to test quantum theories such as the one posited by Birkhoff and Evans for the specific tunneling scenario of quantum particles passing through a barrier.

This research investigates the leading twist distribution amplitudes of P-wave non-relativistic mesons. Utilizing QCD light-cone sum rules, we place bounds on the universal function $\phi_P^{(J)}(u)$ for $0\leq|u|\leq 1$, where $J=0,1$ and the mesons are $s\bar{q}$ or $c\bar{q}$-flavored. We also derive sum rules for the P-wave meson distribution amplitudes from their soft limits and provide numerical range estimates based on current sum rules results. Our findings have implications for testing non-relativistic quantum field theory and constraining the P-wave meson light-cone sum rules.

Researchers have long assumed that the principles of quantum mechanics are universal and consistent across space and time.  However, recent breakthroughs in nonlinear quantum mechanics have the potential to revolutionize quantum information technologies and fundamental physics experiments. Our study delves into the nonlinear characteristics of Bose-Einstein condensates, finding that their nonlinear dynamics gives rise to a probability of measuring zero, susceptible to annihilation by quantum fluctuations. Additionally, we discover that nonlinear interferometry using orthogonal states yields a non-trivial phase, while our analysis of nonlinear mass terms in quantum field theories reveals the possibility of a massive Dirac fermion acquiring oscillatory'mass'. Our findings demonstrate the significant impact of nonlinear quantum mechanics on quantum physics, quantum information science, and interferometry, potentially enabling new technologies based on nonlinear quantum states.

The extended BMS algebra generated by supertranslation and superrotation vector fields at null infinity is known to be the asymptotic symmetry algebra of quantum gravity S-matrix. Researchers initially considered it to be a well-defined algebraic structure but, upon reevaluation, it's clear that this is not the case. Specifically, the extended BMS algebra is not a well-defined algebraic structure because its deformation map is not smooth in the deformation parameters. Consequently, it cannot be embedded in a Lie algebra as a deformations parameter-dependent structure. Despite this technicality, the extended BMS algebra is still a valuable tool for understanding asymptotic symmetries and its related charges are crucial components of the quantum gravity S-matrix. To make further progress, a deformation-dependent version of the symmetry algebra is necessary, and an investigation into the quantum gravity S-matrix is warranted using the charges associated with this algebraic structure.

The new paradigm of one-shot learning, specifically "from one example," has become prominent in the field of few-shot learning and has also been explored in the context of continual learning. However, the standard approach to combining one-shot and continual learning yields an unsatisfactory outcome, primarily due to the issue of class imbalance that results from the exponential growth of the set of learned classes in comparison to the base set of categories. To address this problem, researchers have developed a new training objective for the classifier component of the model, one that aims to ensure the classifier makes comparable predictions for all classes, including newly acquired ones, while also maintaining accuracy for the base set of categories. The proposed objective can be easily implemented by incorporating the cross-entropy loss for the new categories and applying a data augmentation technique to simulate the presence of multiple examples. The experiments conducted demonstrate that the proposed objective, specifically the comparative loss, leads to a significant improvement over existing methods in the one-shot and continual learning scenario, specifically "from one example." The results of the experiments show that the proposed objective enables the successful learning and representation of new categories in this challenging scenario, specifically "from one example."

In metric geometry and general relativity, specifically Einstein's vacuum equations, generalized differential forms play a significant role. They involve applying de Rham cohomology and generalized cohomology theories on various generalized manifolds. This discussion encompasses generalized differential forms of rank 0 and higher, as well as generalized vector fields, specifically generalized Killing vectors and fields. A focus lies on applying generalized differential forms to solve Einstein's vacuum equations by constraining general solutions of de Rham cohomology groups and generalized cohomology groups of generalized manifolds. This approach can be seen as a type of generalized Penrose transform. It hinges on developing generalized vector fields from given hypersurfaces, generalizing well-known techniques in 2 and 3-dimensional metric geometries and general relativity.

In the context of finite fields like F_9[x], we investigate new classes of permutation polynomials over finite fields with square-free underlying fields. Utilizing a multivariate method developed by Zhenchaol Fang et al., we establish novel categories of permutation polynomials with specific coefficients, while setting a universal maximum of 3 degrees of freedom in the coefficients for fields like F_9. This work also enables explicit construction examples that match certain constant fields, providing additional instances of permutation polynomials with fields like F_25. Notably, we establish one-degree permutation polynomials for fields like F_25, a previously unattained standard.

Approximately $4$ billion individuals worldwide are affected by intestinal
parasites. The health risks associated with these infections cause a multitude
of issues, including physical and mental disorders, often resulting in the
individuals being confined to bed. Research has identified $1,378$ species of
intestinal parasites, with $134$ species impacting humans. In this research
paper, we propose a machine learning model for automatically identifying
intestinal parasites in India based on host species, using digital images. A
study was conducted in three major cities in India: Mumbai, New Delhi, and
Kolkata, gathering images of the parasites from a diverse range of hosts. A
total of $2,548$ images were collected and processed, with the obtained data
being in the form of images and labels. We utilized the ResNet50 model to
accomplish the classification task, achieving a high $91\%$ accuracy rate for
the Mumbai dataset and $93\%$ for the combined Mumbai and New Delhi datasets.
When testing the model with the New Delhi dataset alone, we achieved a high
$87\%$ accuracy rate. Furthermore, we tested and evaluated our model using
different architectures, including VGG-16, Inception-V3, and ResNet-34, with
the results confirming the model's adaptability across various host species and
parasite types. A comparative analysis revealed that our model performed better
than the state-of-the-art

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, a Markov chain approximation approach and a dynamical programming technique are used to solve nonlinear integro-differential Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations. In addition, the research demonstrates the convergence of the approximating sequences to the accurate solution of the value functions and the Nash equilibrium. Ultimately, numerical examples confirming the obtained convergence are presented.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Accelerated (PIDA) control strategy, integrating a derivative filter, to enhance quadcopter stability in turbulent conditions. The theoretical foundation of this approach is presented through mathematical modeling followed by simulation validation using MATLAB/Simulink. Subsequently, the proposed PIDA control strategy was successfully implemented and tested on physical quadcopters using an Arduino Mega 644P microcontroller. The results demonstrate that this control method can effectively maintain the quadcopter's altitude and track target trajectories with high precision, while also ensuring the motor rotation speed does not exceed its maximum allowable value (10V).

A comprehensive investigation into one-pion exchange and nonrelativistic interactions between pions and nucleons at low energies can be found within the framework of chiral effective field theory, specifically in the $1/N_c$ expansion. The underlying principles of this theoretical model are discussed, including the derivation of the pion-nucleon $\Delta$-interaction from the $\beta$-function of the two-flavor baryon Chiral Lagrangian in the $1/N_c$ expansion. The findings reveal that the one-pion exchange and non-relativistic pion-nucleon interaction Lagrangians are intertwined in this effective field theory. The discussion also includes a derivation of the long-range part of the phase shift for one-pion exchange in the $1/N_c$ expansion to first order. The calculation of the $\pi$-$N$ scattering phase shift shows that the effect of wave function modification on one-pion exchange is negligible. The investigation further demonstrates that the Pauli term in the effective nucleon propagator does not impact the phase shift at this order. The phase shift is then compared with the one-loop $\Delta$-interaction calculation in the $1/N_c$ expansion, revealing a significant discrepancy. The analysis suggests that to resolve this discrepancy, it is necessary to incorporate a contact term into the effective field theory, and this contact term is then calculated within the $1/N_c$ expansion.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded version in 2017. During a period of prolonged disruption the International System of Units was modified, where the definition of the mole, ampere, Kelvin and others were revised. In this study, inaccuracy in the old measurement system was addressed where the values of physical quantities were expressed in terms of base units, by implementing appropriate conversion factors to the new system.

We have developed a machine learning-based system to accurately identify the types of Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) host galaxies within the existing knowledge framework. Utilizing a large dataset from the Palomar AGN spectroscopic survey, our research involved training algorithms on spectroscopic and morphological data, with a focus on correcting common classification errors. With the integration of established galaxy morphological classifications and spectroscopic data linked to the Palomar AGN survey, our system achieved high accuracy rates in categorizing early-type and late-type galaxies based on their characteristics. Late-type galaxies received a 100% accuracy rate in classification, with early-type galaxies demonstrating a 90% accuracy rate. Furthermore, our research demonstrated that incorporating spectroscopic data enhanced the performance of late-type galaxy classification and elevated late-type classification confidence while decreasing early-type classification uncertainty. This comprehensive system serves as a valuable tool for researchers to accurately identify AGN host galaxies within existing astronomical surveys, with notable improvements in the reliability of the classifications obtained.
