This study demonstrates the presence of self-dual (topological) solitons within two modified versions of the baby Skyrme model, which are regular and have continuous symmetry.  By employing the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework, we establish that these solitons adhere to a bound consistent with their energy.  Additionally, two distinct methods are presented to derive the modified baby Skyrme models' self-dual solitons and calculate their corresponding Bogomol'nyi bounds.  Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader understanding of non-linear field theories through its novel applications of the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfield framework.

For a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal model that exhibits time-reversal symmetry breaking, we investigate how it responds when subjected to a strong orbital magnetic field. Considering that each Weyl node can potentially be split into four distinct phases, we explore the existence and theoretical justification behind the creation of all possible phase combinations, including scenarios involving zero, three, and four Weyl nodes. Notably, applying magnetic fields results in the emergence of nodal lines, whose geometric properties are intricately linked to the characteristics of the original Weyl nodes, as well as the symmetry of the resulting phase structures, which is characterized by point group symmetry similar to that of the Dirac dual points identified in prior research.

We introduce an advanced method to optimize resonant absorption and radiation enhancement within optical devices. This technique leverages the antinodes of a complex patterned structure to amplify light absorption by emitters and facilitate directed light emission. By modifying the radiation pattern without altering the absorption characteristics, it's possible to optimize a light-scattering surface for a specific light emission spectrum. To achieve this, the Insurance Criterion is applied to calculate and optimize both the local density of states and the directive gain of the structure. Our approach, utilising an optimized corrugated metal film, achieves a high directive gain of 29.4 at 632.8 nanometers, representing 5.9 times the gain associated with unstructured metal films. Additionally, the method can be extended to improve the efficiency of plasmonic-coupled photovoltaic devices.

Mechanical screening, a widely recognized phenomenon, is utilized in theoretical models for plastic deformation and fracture in various solid structures. Researchers have identified two primary models of screening, one associated with low mechanical stresses and the other with high mechanical stresses. Despite being widely acknowledged, the principles underlying screening remain not very well understood, especially in amorphous solids where matter lacks a defined molecular structure. Using a computer simulation, this study demonstrates that mechanical screening in amorphous solids, specifically soft-jellium with soft disks, exhibits characteristics of both low and high mechanical stress regimes. Notably, the experiment shows that the low mechanical stress regime exhibits characteristics distinct from the high mechanical stress regime, yet still resembles it to a certain extent. Furthermore, the researchers discovered that the mechanical stress regime can be attributed to the partial breaking of certain interactions between nearby particles.

Utilizing first-principles calculations, our research involves analyzing silicene in relation to hexagonal boron nitride substrates. Hexagonal boron nitride, being a semiconductor, has weaker interactions with silicene in comparison to metallic substrates. As a result, silicene's band gap can potentially be expanded up to 50 meV. Additionally, the impact of manganese decoration on the system is explored by calculating the onsite Hubbard interaction parameter, which significantly differs between decoration at the top and hollow sites. Furthermore, the system's induced magnetism is also investigated following the Heisenberg exchange interaction method.

The Sgr A East supernova remnant, located near the center of the Milky Way, poses a mystery with age estimates ranging from extremely young, around 1-2 thousand years, to over 10 thousand years, based on traditional pulsar braking laws. To resolve this discrepancy, researchers have simulated a possible scenario where Sgr A East formed due to the explosion of a supermassive star within a dense stellar cluster, home to two powerful X-ray-emitting pulsars, as evidenced by Chandra X-ray telescope observations. Our calculations take into account the movement of the pulsars within the cluster and the impact of the surrounding environment, simulating the appearance of the remnant over 10 thousand years through the dynamic evolution of the gas distribution, powered by the energy released from the explosion and the pulsars' motion. By modeling this process, we have determined that the pulsars' ages align with the estimated age of the remnant and, for the first time, have calculated a possible time period in the evolution of the dynamic system when the pulsars' motion will result in their apparent movement towards the center of the remnant.

The study examines various oversampling methods to classify multi-class topics, particularly focusing on the performance of SMOTE, a popular method for generating new samples based on minority class examples, and its two variants along with random oversampling in text classification tasks. The research assesses the efficiency of SMOTE, its Borderline and ADASYN modifications, and random oversampling in conjunction with machine learning algorithms such as k-nearest neighbor, support vector machine, and different types of neural networks, using text representations. The outcomes suggest that using oversampling methods enhances the accuracy of classification and indicates that the performance of KNN and SVM algorithms is heavily influenced by class imbalance issues, whereas neural networks show resilience against it.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to COVID-19 correlations, both as they appeared and over time. It discovers a connection between national death rates and local news coverage in different regions, particularly a notable lag of around two weeks. The analysis reveals that this relationship is consistent across various metrics used to assess the correlation. Furthermore, it appears that this correlation is driven by the change in coverage rather than the overall frequency of local news, and that certain areas of the country, such as those in the southwest, have consistently deviated from this pattern. The study examines the potential underlying mechanisms behind this association and suggests that local news coverage influences public behavior, such as mask-wearing rates, which in turn affects the spread of the virus.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property holds significant value in computational astrophysics for processes such as binary interactions and compact object mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such applications leads to excessive computation in individual particles, we employ a Fast Multipole Method (FMM) in this study to explore its integration with SPH simulations. Our results show that Fast SPH with FMM retains SPH's exact conservation properties due to the straightforward incorporation of FMM that only affects force computation without touching positions or potentials.

Numerical studies have been conducted on the $Q^2$ dependence of cross-sectional ratios in electron proton collisions, drawing on JLab polarization experiments. The studies, factoring in current and future experimental data, examined polarization transfer responses, focusing particularly on the ratio of Sachs form factors in such interactions. The findings indicate that although the JLab A1 experiment's $G_E/G_M$ data exhibits significant uncertainties at high $Q^2$, this ratio plays a pivotal role in double spin structure functions and polarization transfer responses. The studies also showed that the JLab Hall A GE/$G_M$ measurement is crucial for the measurement of the JLab A2 experiment's $R = \frac{G_E}{G_M}$, and further, how this information influences the measurement of the polarized structure function $g_2$ from the CEA experiment. Finally, the studies explored the impact of the $G_E/G_M$ response on the measurement of the proton's spin-dependent radiation structure function, $\tilde{u}_p(s)$.

We propose a novel method for efficient learning in both reinforcement and imitation learning settings. The idea involves training the parameterized policy using synthetic states generated from historical data and an auxiliary model. These synthetic states are mixed with real states to enhance data coverage, ultimately improving the learning agent's performance. Notably, our proposed method can be integrated with existing state coverage augmentation methods as a standalone technique and can also benefit temporal credit allocation in the context of reinforcement learning. We evaluate the proposed method on benchmark reinforcement learning tasks and find that it outperforms existing alternatives. Additionally, we successfully apply this method to imitation learning scenarios, achieving superior results compared to prior methods and standard benchmarks.

A comprehensive study of the creation of two Higgs bosons ($hh$) paired with a vector boson ($W$ or $Z$) through the interaction of a photon with a jet at the Large Hadron Collider at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV has been conducted. This investigation utilized a dataset of 132 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions gathered by the ATLAS detector. Researchers focused on non-resonant and resonant production mechanisms involving $W$ or $Z$ bosons accompanied by $hh$ bosons decaying into $b\bar{b}$ and $bb\bar{b}b$ or $b\bar{b}bb$ or $bb\bar{b}b$ or $bb\bar{bb}b$ final states. Upper bounds on cross-sections were derived for non-resonant production at 0.8 and 0.3 femtobarns with 90% confidence levels and stricter bounds for various resonant cases up to around 5 femtobarns with similar confidence levels. These results significantly tighten the limits on non-resonant and some resonant $hh$ production compared to prior studies. Additionally, cross-section bounds for the electroweak process of $hh$ production paired with a vector boson via $W$ or $Z$ bosons accompanied by $hh$ bosons decaying into $b\bar{b

Atomic magnetometers that utilize self-oscillating technology and drive and pump fields offer exceptional sensitivity and dynamic range capabilities. Yet, accurately mode-matching and magnitude-adjusting drive and pump fields is crucial for optimal performance, a task that can be challenging and time-consuming to fine-tune. In our research, we successfully developed an automated system that compensates for optical mode matching and adjusts the phase and magnitude of driven fields with rapid, precise adjustments possible in under 100 milliseconds. We tested our system and found it provided consistent, high-quality output in real-world applications, maintaining the optimal coherence between drive and pump fields even in the presence of noise or errors.

For K3 surfaces with an automorphism having a Siegel disk, the associated Picard number falls between 1 and 4, and we establish specific numerical limits for each case. Additionally, for K3 surfaces featuring complex multiplication, the associated Picard number is either 2 or 4, and we identify instances where the Picard number is 4 while a Siegel disk is present.

We're working within the context of supergravity unified frameworks, where the gauge-symmetric spinors play a crucial role in breaking supersymmetry. By considering these spinors as elements of a geometric algebra, we can explore the properties of gaugino masses and demonstrate how the neutralino can form the dark matter of the universe. By extending the neutralino dark matter concept to include relativistic neutralinos, we can use the geometric algebra to create a framework for relativistic dark matter interactions. This formulation is not only applicable to neutralinos but can also be adapted to other hypothetical dark matter candidates.

A polynomial-time approximation scheme for finding the minimum distance between two points in a set of n-dimensional l1 balls has been developed, where each ball has a predetermined radius. This was made possible through the effective contraction of subsets within the given set. The resulting approximation ratio for the minimum distance was achieved at 1.13111 times the actual value, while the time complexity was directly proportional to the logarithm of the number of possible subset configurations. This particular algorithm was designed for solving specific problems, but its underlying principles may hold broader implications for solving minimum distance problems in other geometric contexts.

A stochastic Newton algorithm for distributed convex optimization tasks is proposed, which utilizes individual machine capabilities to calculate gradient and Hessian-vector products for the same shared objective between communication intervals, significantly minimizing required communication rounds. Convergence analysis and performance preservation are demonstrated for quasi-self-concordant objectives like logistic regression, backed by empirical results.

Our approach to training a neural network to identify hate-speech in low-resource languages like Hindi and Bengali is presented in this study. We develop a strategy to fine-tune pre-trained language models that have been updated with a hate-speech classification head, and show that this method achieves top results on the HIBERT dataset. Additionally, our study highlights the effectiveness of using knowledge distillation to combine the predictive capabilities of teacher and student models. Notably, our teacher model, which was pre-trained on an expanded dataset, demonstrates outstanding performance and serves as an ideal knowledge source for the student model. The teacher and student configurations, along with the corresponding source codes, are available for download at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/adi-singh2000/HiBen-HateSpeech-Classification-Task.

In nuclear and particle physics, the direct observation of nuclear recoils resulting from collisions is a fundamental concept. This idea is being further explored in the context of forward dark matter and neutrino investigations. A novel topological identification method is introduced that effectively differentiates recoils from the direction of incoming particles, enabling the detection of extremely thin events and allowing the angular measurement of such events. This method relies on a specific form of the distribution of light emitted in these recoils being narrower in the forward direction, leading to a significant increase in the sensitivity of dark matter and neutrino experiments. Applying this method to the LUX-Zeplin experiment, we find that the latter would achieve an improved sensitivity of the dark matter search by a factor of 25 and the former by a factor of 8000.

A comprehensive analysis of commercial driving behavior requires considering various personal characteristics and environmental influences like weather and road conditions. Understanding these factors and their effects can help in several applications such as behavior prediction, identification of hazardous drivers, and automated vehicle navigation. However, current research lacks a unified framework that embeds detailed road network information and weather conditions in a dense representation of driver behavior. Moreover, existing methods mainly rely on self-supervised learning techniques which can't guarantee the optimal representation of driving behaviors across different road networks and weather conditions. Therefore, a new method based on weakly-supervised learning has been proposed in this study to learn a universal dense representation of driving behaviors across different road networks and weather conditions. This method uses a common latent variable model to describe a dense representation space and defines a model-specific objective function for each subject within the latent variable model. Consequently, the proposed method successfully achieves a dense representation of driving behaviors and demonstrates its effectiveness in identifying hazardous drivers across different road networks and weather conditions.

This paper investigates the limitations of current Optical Character Recognition (OCR) approaches, specifically in detecting and reading text within complex visual environments. One critical shortcoming of existing methods is their inability to adapt to novel, unseen text instances during the training process. In response, the researchers design a groundbreaking approach that enables the extraction of semantic, horizontal text segments from scene text through self-supervised pre-training. This proposed method harnesses a pre-trained scene text detector to identify text regions and incorporates an encoder-decoder model for image-to-image translation to generate novel, unseen text instances based on the detected segments. By applying this novel approach to a targeted end-to-end OCR task, the results demonstrate the efficacy of this method in translating to unseen text instances, ultimately facilitating accurate reading of complex visual environments, even those containing unique, previously unseen text instances.

Random fields in mathematical models depict how interconnected random variables behave over time, influencing a variety of disciplines from statistical physics to system biology. Since their introduction in the 19th century, little has been known about the link between their dynamic behaviors and geometric properties of the underlying spaces they're defined within. To address this gap, a new approach is proposed to analyze the dynamic patterns of these random fields by transforming them into flows in Euclidean space, allowing for classification via topological methods. This innovative approach reveals novel insights into the characteristics of well-known random fields and introduces a novel random field example with diverse, uniquely classified dynamic patterns.
In our research, we conduct experiments on Rayleigh-Taylor Instability by introducing a controlled disturbance through magnetic levitation technology.

For a cuspidal Hecke eigenform $F$ attached to the symplectic group $Sp_n(Z)$ and a Dirichlet character $\chi$, we examine the standard twisted L-function, $L(s,F,\chi,St)$, and show that its algebraic component at critical points has bounded denominators. As a result, certain terms in the approximate functional equation of $L(s,F,\chi,St)$ remain with finite and non-zero norms. This work extends the findings of L. Garret on orthogonal motives and includes a particular case relevant to modular forms, yielding a proof of Chebyshev's bias in the sign of the Riemann zeta function at real critical points.

In a tight binding model, our research explores how electronic properties behave in certain graphene structures. By applying a tight binding model to a honeycomb lattice, we've discovered the relationship between the Hamiltonian's elements and the band structure of the lattice. Our analysis of the electronic properties of different graphene configurations indicates the presence of large band gaps in graphene nanoribbons and the superlattice of graphene and SiC. These findings align with previous research, which used more complex methods to study the electronic properties of graphene and multilayer graphene and carbon nanotubes, as well as the electronic properties of carbon systems at the nanoscale.

This paper presents proofs of Korovkin theorem analogues in the realm of weakly nonlinear, monotone operators applied to multi-variable Banach lattices of functions. Our study encompasses the almost everywhere convergence, convergence in measure, and $L^{p}$-norm convergence. The discussion is supplemented by several examples that demonstrate the theoretical findings.

A graph on n vertices is called pancyclic if it contains a cycle of every possible length from 3 to n. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and with minimum degree k in excess of 5 contains a Hamiltonian cycle. However, a pancyclic graph requires a minimum degree of n/2. Researchers including Cheng and Chen later refined Erdos' result, increasing the lower bound for n to n greater than 4k to the seventh power. In this paper, we upgrade Erdos' original result, establishing that a pancyclic graph has a Hamiltonian cycle, while a pancyclic graph with a clique number of r contains a Hamiltonian cycle if its minimum degree k exceeds 5 times the maximum of r/k and n r/2 k. This outcome represents the most thorough application of Erdos' original idea and refines previous findings by Cheng and Chen among others.

The trajectory of light particles created in gold-gold, ruthenium-ruthenium, and zirconium-zirconium collisions at a specific energy level of 2000 GeV has been studied to understand the influence of the two fluid baryon quark model on their behavior. Researchers discovered that all particles, including those not influenced by the color force, moved in the same direction at the collision's initial point and that the force affecting the particles as they traveled had a relationship with this initial movement, the type of particle, and mass. A method was also used to calculate the force exerted on each particle based on these factors and it was observed that this force could create movements of particles that were initially at rest, and these new movements followed a specific pattern related to energy density, the movement of strange particles, and the movement of the particles as a whole.

The proposed adaptive spectral ASK approach builds upon previous time integration methods by dynamically generating a sparse grid in higher-dimensional spaces, resulting in substantial reductions in computational costs while maintaining high accuracy. High-dimensional system dynamics are effectively captured through one- and k-step predictions, along with error estimation based on the ADI approach. By adaptively selecting specific nodes from a pre-defined grid, accurate estimates are obtained, with ASK seamlessly integrating traditional time integration methods on unexplored grid points when needed. High error estimation precision enables efficient exploration of the multi-dimensional state space, making ASK particularly suitable for complex systems. Numerical simulations demonstrate the excellent performance of ASK compared to existing methods, with notable applications and extensions considered in the appended supplementary material.

This review provides an overview of quantum mechanics history with a specific focus on addressing the theoretical aspects of scattering. It includes a comprehensive explanation of resonance parameters and their importance, as well as an in-depth analysis of resonance curves. Additionally, the review delves into series and cascade phenomena, which occur during photoionization and scattering processes. Building on this foundation, the theory of photoionization is explored, with a focus on electron correlations, ionization energies, and continuum wave functions. Ultimately, the review synthesizes these concepts to understand resonances in the autoionization process.

The main concern of the Schrödinger problem lies in determining the optimal control that minimizes a quadratic functional heavily influenced by stochastic integral terms. Assuming the underlying system is governed by a degenerate stochastic partial differential equation, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the optimal control and derive the value function in a stochastic setting, all without imposing specific assumptions on degeneracy or the coefficients involved.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both dilepton and single-lepton t¯t final states and yields a combined result. The calculated t¯t cross-section has a total uncertainty of 3.9% and amounts to 67.5 pb, which corresponds to 0.9 pb (statistical) ± 2.3 pb (syst. error) ± 1.1 pb (lumi.) ± 0.2 pb (beam). This outcome is consistent with theoretical quantum chromodynamic predictions and offers constraints on the proton's parton distribution functions at large Bjorken-x.

We investigate the dynamics of a central oscillator coupled to a one-dimensional many-body localized system. This oscillator represents a fundamental site within a lattice which is connected to all nearby qubits. The many-body localized system serves as a disordered environment. To understand the evolution of both the central oscillator and the bath, we utilize a combined approach of exact numerical calculation and random magnetic field scaling. The key observations are as follows. Firstly, as the disorder strength increases, the central oscillator transitions from a pure state to a mixed state due to the effects of the disorder-induced bath. During the process, the central oscillator loses coherence while the bath enters a thermal state. Notably, as the disorder strength approaches its critical threshold, the central oscillator exhibits periodic fluctuations. The critical threshold is linked to a random magnetic field scaling principle. Secondly, as the coupling between the central oscillator and the bath reaches its critical threshold, the central oscillator enters a quasi-localized state characterized by exponential growth in the nearest-neighbor correlation functions. The critical threshold is linked to the localization length of the central oscillator within the many-body localized system.

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$ are specified that guarantee 
${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ meets the requirement ${u}_{p,b,c}(z) \prec (1+Az)/(1+Bz)$. This yields conditions 
for $(-4\kappa/c)({u}_{p,b,c}(z)-1)$, $c \neq 0$, to be close-to-convex and for ${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ 
to be Janowski convex as well as $z{u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ to be Janowski starlike in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$.

Urban settings are known for their dynamic social environments, which not only foster innovation but also address social inequalities. The interconnected nature of cities enables encounters between individuals from diverse backgrounds, potentially leading to groundbreaking collaborations and community bond formation. Previous research suggests that urban vitality stems from a balance of economic vitality, artistic creativity, and social harmony. To capture the complex relationships between these components, we present a model of "vitality" that represents the underlying social dynamics of cities and reflects residents' perceptions of their urban environment. By analyzing data from over 13 million online reviews, we demonstrate that a city's "vitality" can be measured by analyzing both the public discourse and the public spaces, thereby gaining insight into the underlying social fabric.

This research project focuses on the advancement of a novel numerical technique that handles two-phase flow and transport problems with the presence of an anisotropic porous medium. This proposed method involves a two-stage, field-by-field non-linear preconditioning approach for the basic coupled system. Through the application of a Bubnov-Galerkin finite element formulation, we derive an exact, coupled system that consists of two non-linear equations along with a pressure contribution. However, to increase computational efficiency, we divide the system into two individual sets of non-linear equations, each dependent on pressure and saturation alone. To improve convergence speed during iterative solution processes, we apply the two-stage, field-by-field non-linear preconditioner. This method involves the creation of an assignment matrix that separates the coupled system into two individual sets of linear equations, each with a distinct right-hand side vector that is dependent on the other variable. Through a series of computational experiments, we evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed preconditioner and compare its performance with traditional approaches. These experiments involve the application of the proposed technique to multiple test cases with varying levels of anisotropy. The results indicate a substantial acceleration in computational speed when using the proposed preconditioner, with a consistently high degree of convergence across all cases. Furthermore, we observe a direct relationship between the anisotropy level and the benefits provided by the proposed technique.

The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various forms of matter, such as molecules and light. Chiral molecules have applications in multiple fields, including pharmaceuticals and agriculture. In contrast, chiral light has a limited range of uses due to its difficulty in being filtered or detected. We have developed a method to create chiral light with any desired polarization properties by manipulating the rotational states of nitrogen vapour and projecting the states onto a plane of symmetry. Using a Dove prism and a series of half-wavelength plates, we are able to generate all possible polarization states from an unpolarized or fully polarized input. The resulting chiral light can be combined with the rotational states of dichroic molecules to generate specific eigenmodes of polarization.

This paper examines two-dimensional string theory in a specific context, where the target space is constructed using a particular technique called pants-circles decomposition. When applied to this context, two-dimensional string theory reveals a key insight: its action and amplitudes exhibit a significant boundary term, also present in a gravitational system known as Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity. This boundary term can be reinterpreted as a specific gravitational system with a two-dimensional Hilbert space, where one boundary is always present. This observation prompts a connection with the gravitational system, where two-dimensional string theory can be reimagined as a specific sector within the gravitational system, utilizing a specific unitary representation with a non-trivial flux. This representation's properties can be deduced, where the gravitational system's unitary representation is defined by its central charge, where the flux's value directly correlates with the central charge and a specific gravitational quantity, resulting in a specific relationship that echoes a key concept within two-dimensional conformal field theory.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds without violating the speed of light limit. Researchers have investigated various aspects of this metric, including its implications for entropy and Kretschmann invariant. In our study, we focused on how the shift vector, responsible for spatial warp, affects the Einstein equations. We discovered that introducing a static shift vector transforms the Einstein equations into those applicable to a de Sitter spacetime, featuring a time-dependent Kretschmann invariant and diverging eigenvalues at the warp speed boundaries. Additionally, we found that, with the shift vector moving over time, the Einstein equations become incompatible due to the metric's non-Riemannian properties, preventing a consistent solution. These properties may be useful for exploring alternative theories of gravity.

As urban cities' aging underground infrastructure systems require growing
maintenance, managing the vast amounts of data from diverse sources has become
a pressing concern. With the advent of cutting-edge technologies like the
blockchain and urban data platforms, cities can now harness the power of
artificial intelligence and data analytics. Our research outlines a framework for
an intelligent maintenance platform tailored to underground infrastructure,
encompassing the interconnection of urban data platforms, AI applications, and
a dashboard for seamless interaction. Our proposed platform leverages the
benefits of urban data platforms by integrating disparate systems, AI-based
maintenance methods, and facilitating interoperability through RESTful services.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized momentum-resolved spectroscopy. This approach allowed us to accurately measure the dispersion relations of two-spin and single-ion excitations and compare them to theoretical predictions. The effectiveness of radiative cooling to near-quantum ground state resulted in extremely low thermal occupation rates within the measured temperature range. The lack of observable broadening due to temperature-induced effects in the single-ion excitation, for example, resulted in an exceptional coherence time of about 50 seconds. The spin dephasing rate observed in the two-spin excitation, about 2.5 seconds, was primarily attributed to radiative heating rather than the predicted longitudinal magnetic field fluctuations. The experiment demonstrated that two-dimensional arrays of radioactive bunched ions could serve as an ideal platform for developing novel quantum algorithms.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surface electronic structures and identifying molecular substances. Yet, a comprehensive theoretical framework for TERS has not been developed, primarily due to complex electromagnetic calculations. Our study introduces a new theoretical model for TERS, incorporating electrical field enhancements produced by the tip and the sample. Through comparison with high-quality experiments, our approach demonstrates good agreement with observations. Our model can identify when the tip's electrical field dominates and when the sample's field takes precedence. This understanding could optimize TERS for various applications.

We have observed a strong source of anomalous microwave emission (AME) with a large scale of around 1 arcminute using the GMRT telescope at 334 MHz. Our data show two distinct components, one compact and the other extended, with the extended component possibly being the source of AME. Further analysis of the source, located in the SXDF-CLUSTER field, suggests it could be a spin-flipped dust emission source, potentially associated with a protostar or spin-flipped dust emission from spica-like stars. Our findings indicate that sources of this type can be detected easily using a telescope like the GMRT, particularly at lower frequencies where AME outshines other forms of radio emission.

Ammonium sulfate's seemingly uncomplicated nature belies its significant role as a drug delivery agent and its involvement in a range of physical and biological processes. At the molecular level, this substance displays a complex array of interactions that give rise to a diverse set of functional properties. In our research, we use advanced simulation methods to thoroughly examine the structure of ammonium sulfate as it transitions from a low-temperature crystalline state to a higher-temperature liquid state. Our detailed analysis captures the changes in intermolecular bonding and arrangement that occur during this phase transition, thereby providing a comprehensive understanding of the molecular behavior. Furthermore, we develop a simplified model that effectively replicates the transition and associated properties, such as the shift in heat capacity, using a reduced number of interaction parameters. Ultimately, our simulation results provide a clear picture of the individual sulfate and ammonium groups as they interact and coordinate with one another within the solid and liquid states.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Previous models, such as maximization, probability-matching, and general expected-value, fail to fully explain the various learned probabilities observed in experimental data.  Our research, however, demonstrates that a non-rational, non-maximization approach, which combines elements of probability-matching and general expected-value, can effectively model learned probabilities in such situations.  This approach, which incorporates learning rate and an asymmetric correction factor, accounts for the variability and range of learned probabilities observed in experimental data.  Our results, therefore, suggest that cognitive processes, which deviate from rational expectations, such as an asymmetric processing bias, may contribute to an understanding of probabilistic learning behavior.

A proposed Weyl group for E_8 is explored, based on a modified form of its root system that replaces the traditional weights found in Cartan matrices. Instead, a new set of integers that mirror the values in the Cartan matrix are used to define the weights, resulting in a different transformation structure than typically seen in Lie algebras. However, this novel weight system does adhere to the traditional E_8 root set, allowing for the incorporation of all 240 rank 8 elementary unit roots through a unique transformation. Additionally, specific transformations that resolve all rank 8 unit root transformations modulo 3 and modulo 11 are also identified. Furthermore, this proposed Weyl group is connected to the E_8 lattice, specifically its Type I sublattice, through a transformation that reflects this connection. A new set of'simplified' reflections that resolve all translations in this sublattice are also discovered, along with a specific transformation that reflects this connection. A proposed Weyl group is also explored, based on a modified form of its root system that replaces the traditional weights found in Cartan matrices. Instead, a new set of integers that mirror the values in Cartan matrices are used to define the weights, resulting in a different transformation structure than typically seen in Lie algebras. A new set of'simplified' reflections that resolve all translations in this sublattice are also discovered, along with a specific transformation that reflects this connection.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor 'c'. Prior studies mainly focused on the case where polygon sides have equal lengths. In this research, we explore the problem using curved sides of varying lengths, introducing the first index structures capable of efficiently finding nearest curves, even in the case of complex, closed polygonal curves. For certain values of 'c', we present algorithms that use precomputed structures and trees to achieve fast approximation of the Fréchet distance, thus solving the c-approximate near neighbor problem. Our methods are demonstrated to be both efficient in time complexity and practical in real-world applications, with data analysis showcasing their effectiveness on curved sides of equal and varying lengths.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques. Retrospective correction methods such as quantum relativity can even enhance the quality of noisy measurements. Nevertheless, their efficiency is ultimately limited by the principles of quantum mechanics, the no-cloning theorem, and the no-decoherence theorem. In this paper, we introduce a pioneering prospective approach grounded in real-valued polynomial functions that mitigates measurement errors before they occur, effectively cloning states in the process. By exploiting the inherent structure of Pauli measurements, our method achieves superior performance that approaches the theoretical maximum, surpassing previous bounds and achieving near-cloning capabilities in practice, thus providing a scalable solution for enhancing quantum computers' measurement resolution.

When humans operate robot arms, it's common for the robot's intended behavior not to be explicitly stated. This can lead to confusion over which actions the robot is capable of performing. To resolve this, we investigate teaching humans the robot's intended behavior and the consequences of their actions. By providing feedback on the robot's model, we allow humans to learn and thereby improve their understanding of collaboration possibilities. Experiments with both simulated and real-world testing have shown that this approach can effectively educate humans about the robot in less than 5 minutes. Notably, we observed an almost 3 times increase in efficiency in tasks like pick-and-place when humans were given such feedback.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drift in maps but can be impractical due to lengthy processing times and a reliance on pre-existing global maps, hindering real-time navigation. Real-time detection of topological maps without prior knowledge of the environment is a more feasible option but a more basic problem. We developed an innovative and efficient topological mapping algorithm, TOP Mapper, that employs local feature detection and matching using Fast Fourier Transform, detecting corners and matching them to create significant topological features without requiring a global map. This feature-based approach enables straightforward topological relationships, allowing the creation of a topological map in real-time. Testing on data collected from both indoor and outdoor settings revealed that our algorithm can identify and match features effectively even with variations in lighting, while also determining the relationships between these features accurately. Comparisons to multiple state-of-the-art monocular SLAM systems demonstrated TOP Mapper's superiority in both processing speed and re-mapping efficiency.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with specific structural constraints is gaining traction in wireless communication systems and quantum physics due to their diverse practical applications and intricate structural characteristics. This paper offers a comprehensive review of existing studies centered on unique two-dimensional arrangements, including non-linear patterns like mesh lattices, in which equal-dimensional vectors exhibit equal sums, and spherical structures defined by achieving optimal sums. Distinct from prior surveys focusing on linear patterns, this paper delves into two-dimensional arrays characterized by specific structural features, including repetitive and non-repetitive mesh lattices and spherical structures. Notably, this paper seeks to deepen understanding of research trends, identify potential gaps, and provide valuable insights for academics and researchers in this area.

Computed Tomography (CT) is widely used for non-destructive imaging of internal structures. However, in practice, X-ray attenuation data often exhibit discrepancies due to factors such as the use of polyenergetic X-ray sources and measurement noise. To address these limitations, a novel CT reconstruction model is proposed, which incorporates energy-integrated data and observed measurements under a Generalized Linear Model (GLM). The formulation allows for the treatment of polyenergetic data as multiple lower-energy projections, thereby increasing the CT's ability to resolve details. The model also accounts for measurement noise and system inconsistencies, ensuring accurate reconstructions even in the presence of system imperfections. The formulation's properties are analyzed, and an iterative solution is provided along with a prototypical implementation, which demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional CT reconstructions using numerical simulations and real-world data.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a local approach by using a specially constructed "screen spacer" architecture that optimizes interactions between the two metal areas.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that incorporating user-defined context-enhancing terms significantly elevates the precision of CNER in contrast to terms identified through automated techniques.

Time series data exhibits non-stationarity, seasonality, and variability in its inter-correlation, making it challenging to model and forecast. In this study, we developed an approach to create symbolic representations of multivariate time series, capturing inter-correlation and highlighting key relationships between individual time series. By integrating the resulting representations into a graph database, we can quickly identify and analyze patterns, enabling the development of symbolic-based prediction methods. One proposed method involves using graph metrics to inform a forecast model, specifically a k-nearest neighbors algorithm. Results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, with improved accuracy and speed compared to standard symbolic and numerical methods.

The application of machine learning to Electronic Health Records (EHR) has the potential to significantly enhance the quality of care by identifying patients at risk and preventing adverse health outcomes. However, due to the complexity and heterogeneity of EHR data, which are often annotated with free-text using various coding systems and guidelines, achieving this goal proves challenging. In this research, we propose a novel machine learning approach to standardize and normalize EHR data, drawing inspiration from the successful applications of preprocessing techniques in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Our method involves a series of data enhancement tasks, including tokenization, normalization, and deidentification, which can be flexibly extended to suit specific requirements. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to an EHR dataset, which includes medical documents, diagnoses, and lab results, and demonstrate its utility in clinical text mining tasks. Additionally, the source code of our approach is openly available for reference by the medical NLP community.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform particle sizes and solvent effects, we model the behavior of a charged surface in contact with a salt. From this model, we derive an analytical expression for the electrostatic potential near the surface. By integrating this potential, we obtain a general formula for the charge density on the surface. This formulation takes into account the influence of highly charged thin sheets, such as graphene, as well as the effects of finite solvent thickness. Our work also explores the relationship between surface charge and a nearby ion's bound state, particularly when the solvent is highly polarized. We demonstrate that the bound state's characteristics depend on both the thickness of the solvent and the type of ion involved. This study provides a foundational understanding of how thin sheets with varying sizes interact with solvents, particularly in the context of charge density on the surface and the bound state's behavior.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we have developed a solution to identify requirements within documents. Our approach involves a novel, generic method utilizing convolutional neural networks to recognize requirements phrases. Additionally, we have investigated the efficacy of transfer learning using pre-trained word2vec models in predicting review importance. These techniques were applied to data sets compiled from NASA's ProCREDI project, allowing us to assess their efficacy through comparative analysis of different algorithms and assess the efficacy of transfer learning across various domains.

This study investigates the energy efficiency in a multi-user, multi-relay communication system with a help-from-nearest-helped (HHH) cooperation strategy, where a base station assists multiple users in a cellular network to transmit data to a common destination. To enhance system performance, a maximum diversity network coding (MDNC) technique is used in conjunction with the HHH approach. To achieve this, a joint power allocation and MDNC design problem is formulated to minimize the total transmission power, under constraints on individual power usage, individual user data rates, and a common data rate for all users. By converting the power allocation problem into a second-order cone programming problem, and utilizing the Bisection method for MDNC variables, this joint design is implemented. Results show that incorporating MDNC reduces power usage, decreases the number of MDNC variables needed, and enhances system performance, compared to scenarios without MDNC. Furthermore, the joint design outperforms separate designs that prioritize other objectives, such as sum-rate maximization and equal power allocation.

A theoretical framework has been developed to describe magnetic impurities on superconducting surfaces through a Heisenberg's principle-based approach. This has led to the discovery of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states and the generation of Majorana edge states on non-topological surfaces. Further analysis involved numerically solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation to derive quasi-stationary states, which were then used to determine the impurity's spin density using the Heisenberg equation. By varying the impurity's spin density, both bright and dark states were found, with dark states being identified as a result of spin--pair interaction cancellation and related to Andreev bound states. Additionally, it was found that strong spin-polarized states at the impurity could convert dark states into bright states through a spin-polarization mechanism.

The NA62 experiment at CERN has successfully measured the single event sensitivity of a crucial decay process, with the aim of detecting a possible anomaly consistent with the results obtained by the KL channel in the CALIBRI experiment. This was accomplished by analyzing a massive dataset of 2.51 x 10^13 potassium ion interactions recorded in 2017. With a sensitivity of 0.0035 x 10^-9 for the K+ → π+ ν ν̄ decay, NA62 found no statistically significant evidence for anomalies. This is consistent with the established K+ decay rate of 5.07 x 10^-9, as observed in the CALIBRI experiment.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes where there are changes in view.  To improve point cloud registration for dynamic scenes, deep learning-based approaches have shown potential.  Although some of these models can learn the patterns of changes within a scene, they typically overlook the uncertainty associated with the registration process.  To address these limitations, a framework is proposed that leverages a Variational Inference-based approach for real-time registration of dynamic scenes.  To achieve this goal, a novel Variational Inference-based point cloud distribution model, called VPND, is introduced.  VPND uses a Variational Inference-based approach to learn the distribution of point clouds, allowing it to efficiently handle uncertainty in registration.  To model the point cloud distribution, VPDD employs a normal distribution defined by mean and covariance, where the covariance captures the co-variance between points.  To accurately establish the correspondence between points across distributions, a latent space is introduced.  To optimize the model, a latent space is defined with corresponding point indices as a mean latent variable, where the element-wise right self-outer-product serves as the covariance latent variable. Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in vast datasets 
requiring extensive processing times. The recent surge in accessible, high-resolution 
imagery from sources like Planet and DigitalGlobe, coupled with advancements in 
GPU technology, demand accelerated image processing methods. This study proposes 
the application of U-Net and VGG16 architectures for extracting significant information 
from satellite imagery, utilizing GPUs to enhance processing efficiency. The evaluation 
of these models, utilizing a combination of train and validation sets, demonstrates their 
capacity to effectively segment water bodies, while showcasing the value of pre-trained 
models for saving time and boosting efficiency in image analysis tasks.

Quantifying the electronic and structural modifications induced by intense X-ray pulses is a key aspect of XANES beyond absorption cross-section information.  The application of XANES to matter at extreme intensity demands a profound comprehension of the influence of the intense X-ray flux on the process.  In this study, the electronic and structural transformations triggered by an intense X-ray flux in NiO crystals were investigated through experimental and theoretical analyses of the electron density and the Ni site local density of states.  The changes observed were attributed to electronic temperature and temperature-induced changes in the lattice parameter, consistent with theoretical predictions.  The findings were further supported by simulations modeling the Ni 3d orbitals and demonstrating agreement with experimental data.  The results demonstrate the potential for investigating the properties of materials at extreme intensity and into the high-intensity regime of XAS.

The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even in harsh wireless environments. Nevertheless, in situations where sensitive information is transmitted over wireless channels, high data security is necessitated. An efficient way of achieving this is by implementing an artificial noise generation (ANG) technique. In our research, we explored a combined approach of applying AMC and ANG to a wireless communication system. By utilizing a deep learning network to classify the signals and a artificial noise generator to increase interference, we simulated the communication process. By analyzing the results, we evaluated the system's performance through parameters such as bit error rate, output noise power, and output signal to interference and noise ratio. By comparing our proposed method with conventional AMC schemes that utilize uniform signaling, we verified the improved security and reduced interference of our proposed method.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is a critical step in monitoring disease progression and evaluating the effectiveness of treatments. Although current techniques rely on deep learning, they are hindered by the scarcity of annotated data and the difficulty in generalizing to new, unlabeled datasets. We propose a novel, efficient method for semi-supervised lesion segmentation that leverages statistical characteristics common to both training and test data. By adopting a model-agnostic approach, this approach can easily adapt to new datasets without requiring extensive retraining. We tested this method using two different MRI datasets, collecting a gold standard of 122 manual segmentations and 442 non-manual segmentations for comparison purposes. When compared to existing state-of-the-art methods that utilize supervised learning, our semi-supervised method demonstrates comparable performance using significantly fewer labeled data points (20 compared to 442). The corresponding code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/CERITMC/MSSLS.git.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to the Riemannian 2-step development of optimal transport is explored. This concept, referred to as the MTW condition, leads to improved PDEs for assigning masses on a Riemannian manifold, outperforming existing methods. This new metric comparison is characterized by a Wasserstein distance between the growth rates of sending and receiving spaces. A key finding demonstrates that the MTW condition is encompassed by the Riemannian 2-step Cheeger inequality. This research further integrates several manifolds with interesting geometric properties, including a conservation law for spherical structures. Numerical experiments are conducted using Brownian motion and potential value distributions to evaluate the efficacy of associated gradient flows. This work extends the findings of arXiv:2104.07826 by incorporating additional geometrical comparisons.

Evaluating the performance of reinforcement learning and control systems using generalized linear representations offers significant benefits, allowing for assessment of learning and regulation abilities using a single tool. By assuming these systems have the form $y(t) = \sigma \left( \int_{-T}^{t} \beta \, \mathrm{d} \tau \right)$ with $\beta$ satisfying a generalized Riccati inequality, we establish that the generalized error is proportional to the time-interval $T$. This finding implies that as the time-interval $T$ approaches infinity, the generalized error approaches zero, indicating perfect prediction or regulation. Our analysis utilizes a spectral decomposition approach, leveraging the properties of non-positive operators and matricial non-mappings to derive key properties and bounds, ultimately establishing the generalized error for CT systems. By applying this approach to finite-dimensional linear time-invariant systems, we demonstrate that the generalized error for LTI systems is directly related to the condition number of the system matrix $\mathcal{A}$.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores with and without embedded protostars. Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than starless cores within their respective cloud complexes. Additionally, we find evidence that suggests protostellar cores are centrally concentrated, whereas starless cores display more external mass distributions. This finding can be understood by referring to the core mass distribution model developed by Evans et al. (2009). It's worth noting that the mass of protostars within protostellar cores, as measured through their 1.3 mm flux, follows a roughly linear relationship with the core's total mass. This observation supports the long-standing hypothesis that protostars form through the collapse of massive cores within molecular clouds.

The theoretical primordial black holes could be a type of dark matter and have been linked to the observed anomalies in the mass of compact objects such as neutron stars and the events of gravitational waves detected by LIGO and Virgo. The potential relationship between dark matter and the solar system's anomalies remains a topic of interest. Researchers have recently proposed that a specific type of binary star system could be home to a black hole or neutron star and suggest searching for unusual pulsating patterns that would indicate the presence of such an object. We have conducted a search using data from the All Sky Automated Survey for periods of 0.01 to 100 days that would indicate a binary system containing a black or neutron star, and found 322 candidates across the entire sky. Most of the candidates have a period of 50 to 70 days, although we have also identified a few systems with shorter periods. If any of these systems are found to contain a black hole, it would be one of the closest detected to Earth, and would provide evidence supporting the theory of dark matter composed of primordial black holes.

We conducted thorough research into wedge-shaped, monodisperse molecule liquids by employing Monte Carlo simulations in multiple geometries, where we analyzed various systems with flexible and rigid bonds. This study uncovered numerous unique phases displayed by the molecules, including smectic and nematic liquid crystalline phases. Our findings reveal that these molecules exhibit a variety of arrangements depending on the packing density, flexibility, and bond type. For example, we discovered that nematic and smectic phases are produced at packing densities below 0.5, and even crystalline phases can appear when molecular alignment is restricted. Notably, we found partial and complete icosahedral structures along with hexagonal and amorphous phases, demonstrating the intricate relationship between molecular geometry and spatial organization. This research provides valuable insights into the behavior of molecules with irregular shapes, which can serve as a foundation for understanding and characterizing complex molecular arrangements in various fields.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, we can achieve performance comparable to fine-tuning on tasks like language inference and text classification with just 0.6% of the original parameters updated. Our findings show that current pre-trained models like BERT and ALMA are well-suited for PASTA due to their design, particularly with the use of learned positional embeddings for special tokens. This method can significantly reduce the computational cost and memory requirements needed to update large models like ALMA with 208 billion parameters.

This research investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-dependent preference modeling. To tackle this challenge, we examine two distinct Siamese network designs, contrasting one that compares the resultant collections after an addition with another that considers each item's individual contribution to the existing collection. Through experiments involving a real-world task of learning Magic: The Gathering deck-building card recommendations, we found that the triplet network outperformed the other architecture and when compared to a comprehensive global approach, achieved a 91% level of performance. Our analysis further highlights the key aspects that influence the model's effectiveness.

Our research demonstrates that thermodynamic and monte carlo simulations of semi-flexible and flexible polymers produce consistent results for the excess entropy and energy but reveal a complex relationship for the excess enthalpy of semi-flexible polymers, contrasting with the simpler Enskog Enthalpy of hard ellipsoids.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic processing times or human judgments, our approach tackles reasonableness judgments using machine learning. By creating instances of logical statements with and without negation, our analysis discovers that models fail on negation instances on average. We investigate two possible explanations: representational capability and learning objective. Our findings suggest that adding an answer set compilation layer to the transformer can dramatically improve its performance on negation instances. Additionally, fine-tuning the model with a large dataset of logical statements can significantly boost its accuracy. Our results indicate that these methods can elevate the performance of language models like BERT and RoBERTa by 17% and 14% on average, respectively.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words. This study introduces a novel attention model that draws parallels with convex optimization to model this sequential dependency. The proposed model views attention weighting as a solution to an assigned target word's convex optimization problem. This framework's closed-form solution yields an computational efficiency improvement of several orders of magnitude in attention modeling compared to the latest models, while also boosting performance on four benchmark datasets by 0.64-1.03 BLEU points in cross-lingual translation tasks.

This passage provides an in-depth, explicit calculation of the weights in Kontsevich graph expansion for symplectic manifolds of a single leaf, relying on connections between renormalization, Feynman manifolds, and Witten classes.

This research investigates the large N limit of large $N$, commencing with Lagrangian (quantum) formulations of Einstein's gravity, specifically in $(2+1)$ and $(3+1)$ dimensions. We examine quantum entanglement entropy in spheres $S^{d-2}$ for odd $d$ dimensions from $(2+1)$ to $(9+1)$ and find that it displays a constant rate proportional to $\frac{1}{N}\log N$ with a non-zero, dimension-independent value in all cases. In contrast, thermal entropy related to the temperature $T$, reveals that black hole masses are proportional to $N$ with a constant coefficient at any finite temperature $T$, regardless of $N$. Consequently, thermal entropy increases linearly with $N$ while entanglement entropy remains independent of $N$. This outcome confirms our previous finding that thermal entropy exceeds entanglement entropy. Furthermore, this research demonstrates the law of entanglement entropy and its constant rate for any $N$ are independent of the underlying quantum theory of gravity. In addition, this research explores the connection between Einstein's gravity in the time-dependent scenario with $N$ masses moving according to the Keplerian parabolic orbit with respect to a fixed massive object with mass $M$. In this setup, we derive the solution to the time-dependent Klein-Gordon equation with potential influenced by the gravitational field of masses $N$ and $M$, known as the deformed potential. Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies the CTMC framework, calculating the inverse Z-transform and inverse Laplace transform separately for discretely and continuously monitored options. As a result, we achieve improved explicit Laplace transforms, surpassing a prior theorem by Cai et al. and yielding increased efficiency through numerical studies.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is still unknown, although various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies are suggested as potential explanations. This class of objects intensely produces high-energy particles through non-thermal processes, which interact with the surrounding material, producing a range of observable effects from the MeV gamma-ray band to the PeV tau neutrino range. Our study aims to develop a unified model describing the formation and evolution of dust, cosmic rays, and X-ray/gamma-ray emissions in starburst and H II galaxies. By integrating established equations and implementing novel equations, we have developed a comprehensive code that simulates the composition and movement of dust and cosmic rays while accounting for primary and secondary particle production, radioactive decay, and particle interaction. Our code also calculates energy loss through SNr radiation, synchrotron and inverse Compton radiation, and particle injection into the ISM. This code has been applied to idealized starburst galaxies and H II galaxies with a central starburst, producing results that align with observed dust and gamma-ray data. Our study suggests that starburst and H II galaxies contribute significantly to the diffuse gamma-ray background, with starburst galaxies producing a hard component and H II galaxies producing a softer component. Our code is available online through GitHub.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a new approach called text-wrapped visual linear models (TW-LM) has been proposed for explaining and improving the accuracy of computer vision tasks. By utilizing and fine-tuning the features extracted by pre-trained convolutional neural networks, TW-LM introduces a modular architecture that enables multi-task performance. The model's ability to separate different visual elements and represent these as independent features sets it apart from other over-smoothing models. Furthermore, TW-LM fine-tunes its linear layers and selected convolutional layers in an alternating manner, which aids in feature separation and reduces over-specialization. The results show that TW-LM outperforms state-of-the-art models on benchmark datasets, including CIFAR-SVHN-STD, CIFAR-T-CUB, CIFAR-T-UST, STL-10, and Mini-ImageNet, without relying on data augmentation. The source code for TW-LM is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Chenxiao-T/TW-LM.

Developing a comprehensive microscopic theory of cuprate high-temperature superconductors involves specifying the interactions between electrons and phonons. Contrary to traditional views that impurities in cuprates primarily scatter electrons through local interactions, we suggest that long-distance electron-phonon coupling, which is significant at the impurity concentration found in real experiments, also plays a crucial role. This coupling can be represented by a d-wave potential. As the concentration of impurities increases, so does the strength of this coupling, which is in line with experimental findings. The combined effect of both the local ripples in momentum space and the long-distance nodal interference gives rise to a significant increase in the electron-phonon scattering rate near the nodes, which is consistent with experimental data. This simple yet robust model provides a possible explanation for the unique properties of cuprate materials.

The ongoing HIV epidemic continues to claim lives, despite significant global efforts to combat it. Effective prevention strategies rely on widespread awareness of HIV among the population. This study aims to fill the gaps in HIV awareness studies in India by utilizing machine learning techniques to analyze data from multiple sources. Combining socio-demographic and economic data with geographical information, we investigated key factors influencing HIV awareness at the individual and regional levels. Our model achieved an 80% accuracy rating on a test dataset, allowing us to identify key factors driving HIV awareness globally, as well as in specific countries. Regional and cultural influences on HIV awareness were also revealed, including the significant impact of female sex work in some countries. Our research not only offers insights into HIV awareness but also serves as a template for tackling complex global issues.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, researchers have discovered the coexistence of long-range magnetocaloric properties and a stable topological structure of magnetic textures, known as a skyrmion lattice. This unique combination allows for the efficient conversion of magnetic energy into other physical forms like heat, making this material an attractive candidate for applications such as the vaporization of cryogenic fluids and for the development of new solid-state cooling technologies.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering their
underlying concepts, key assumptions, and both parametric and nonparametric
estimation methods for their main parameters and underlying functions.
Theoretical frameworks and associated estimation techniques for many of these
models' key properties and quantities, including factor loadings, factor
distributions, and target functional relationships, are presented. The
determination of confidence intervals for estimating individual data series
components, including idiosyncratic and common components, is a primary focus.
The discussion highlights important challenges, limitations, and open issues
in estimating these models, with a focus on applications in macro and finance
fields.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem, particularly through the use of auxiliary fixed point problems. Consequently, it offers a method to solve equilibrium problems using the Moreau proximal mapping and fixed points, and also discusses the relationship between these concepts within the context of the Ekelund variational principle.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive models that can accurately quantify data uncertainty. From a Bayesian perspective, uncertainty arises in two forms: epistemic uncertainty, which can be mitigated through inference, and alethic uncertainty, which is inherent to the data itself. Drawing on the principles of Bayesian deep learning, this study seeks to separate and distinguish between these two types of uncertainty. By applying deep neural networks within a Bayesian framework, uncertainty is modelled in both batch and incremental training stages. Steganographic capacity is then estimated using the posterior distribution, obtained via Monte Carlo sampling, thereby separating alethic from epistemic uncertainty. Following this, a self-adaptive distortion control method is developed to regulate the steganographic capacity in both lossless and lossy settings. Lastly, a novel, data-driven performance metric is proposed, based on the normalizing constant of the data distribution, to facilitate steganographic system optimization. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of the proposed methods, with substantial gains achieved in steganographic capacity when employing a Bayesian approach versus traditional non-Bayesian techniques.

The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides equations governing dynamo processes and magnetic turbulence but lacks empirical values for various transport coefficients. To bridge this gap, we employed synthetic turbulence from remagnetization simulations to measure transport coefficients of the advection term under conditions replicating the solar environment. Notably, our results indicate the axisymmetric alpha-effect outperforms the axisymmetric alpha-effect reported in earlier studies, while the beta-effect demonstrates negative values in the axial direction but shifts to positive in the radial direction at high latitudes and near the equator. Subsequently, we integrated these effects into local three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations of sunspot simulations, demonstrating good correlation between the models and observations regarding magnetic patterns and their oscillation frequencies.

The unique characteristics of NGC4945 make it an ideal subject for study, particularly due to its enhanced line emission and proximity to Earth. Our analysis focuses on CO, CI, and CII spectral data collected from October 2019 to November 2020, covering the 1-13 mm wavelength range. Our findings reveal that NGC4945 features a complex molecular gas structure surrounding the nucleus, extending about 200 pc in a well-aligned east-west orientation. Ten prominent molecular gas plumes were identified, which we believe represent outflowing gas. One such plume shows an exceptionally broad high-velocity profile, indicating a physical outflow velocity of around 730 km/s and a potential power of 10^10-10^11 L_sun/d. Our research suggests that NGC4945 features a multi-component wind system, which may be attributed to the combined influence of a starburst, active galactic nucleus, and a superposed starburst-active galaxy pair.

A simplified version of the original Vlasov-Maxwell equations, describing the behavior of particle-wave interactions in magnetized plasmas, can be reduced to a set of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). This text outlines a general method for applying the shearing map model to these ODEs, and illustrates this approach with an example from toroidal geometry. For certain cases, the shearing map can provide simple, analytical descriptions of toroidal geodesy and zonal flow formation. For more complex situations, numerical solutions to the ODEs can offer a reliable and efficient alternative to direct simulations of the original Vlasov-Maxwell equations.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto irregular grids in this paper.
